description: An early self-released Spencer Radcliffe LP of sparse, home-recorded songs. Its hushed vocals and simple guitar sketches anticipate the twangier, more rock-oriented turn of his later solo work.
lineage: An early entry in Radcliffe's long solo catalogue that eventually feeds into the twangier Ohio Vision.

description: Ratboys' debut LP: unhurried, twang-flecked indie rock built around Julia Steiner's plainspoken voice and long, patient song structures. A quieter, more folk-adjacent record than the band's later output, closer to their alt-country roots.
lineage: Grew out of Steiner and Sagan's college-band beginnings at Notre Dame; set the twangy-indie template the band expanded on GN and Printer's Devil.

description: Radcliffe's first Run For Cover full-length: patchwork indie pop and lo-fi textures held together by his flat, equivocal voice. It is homemade and a little strange, for listeners who like bedroom pop with rough edges.
lineage: Sounds part of the same Run for Cover/Topshelf-adjacent 2010s indie underground as Ratboys.

description: Second Ratboys LP: warm, unhurried indie rock with country phrasing and Steiner's conversational storytelling. Quieter and more spacious than the band's later, harder-rocking records.
lineage: Bridges the band's early alt-country leanings with the bigger, distorted guitar sound they'd bring on Printer's Devil.

description: A small bedroom EP, quieter and rougher than anything he would release later. It already carries his plainspoken, half-joking phrasing over hissy home-recorded guitar.
lineage: Sounds like an early sketch of the bedroom-recorded songwriting Lenderman developed on his Dear Life releases.

description: Lenderman's home-recorded debut: hissy four-track guitar songs, half-mumbled vocals and jokes buried in genuine heartbreak. It is rougher and slower than his later work but already has the deadpan, small-town eye for detail that defines his writing.
lineage: Grew out of Asheville's DIY bedroom-recording scene before Lenderman joined Wednesday full-time; a direct line to the funnier, sadder songwriting of Boat Songs and Manning Fireworks.

description: Ratboys' loudest, most confident record to that point: bigger choruses and full-band muscle layered over the same plainspoken, twang-inflected songwriting. It suits listeners who like their indie rock warm, hooky and a little country.
lineage: Marks the move from their earlier folk-adjacent sound toward the anthemic guitar rock of The Window and Singin' to an Empty Chair.

description: Florry's turn toward Gram Parsons-style Cosmic American Music: pedal steel, honky-tonk piano and Neil Young-indebted guitar wrapped around Francie Medosch's songwriting. It is warm, loose and hopeful, made for fans of ragged '70s country-rock.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Parsons' Cosmic American Music and Neil Young; precedes the caustic barroom twang of The Holey Bible.

description: A scrappy, tossed-off-sounding set of slacker-rock songs that bridges his earliest bedroom tapes and the more assured Boat Songs. It is full of one-liners about basketball, bad decisions and long-gone relationships, delivered in his flat, dry voice over loose, fuzzy guitars.
lineage: A Dear Life Records release recorded as Lenderman's own songwriting was starting to draw notice alongside his role in Wednesday.

description: A short stopgap EP released ahead of Boat Songs, loose and quick in feel. It carries the same wry, downbeat humor as his full-lengths in miniature, with fuzzy guitars and his dry, understated voice.
lineage: Fits between Ghost of Your Guitar Solo and Boat Songs as Lenderman's songwriting sharpened toward the deadpan style that broke through in 2022.

description: A tenth-anniversary record revisiting older songs with the full band, playing them at their most direct and hooky. It sits between the loose twang of GN and the polish of The Window.
lineage: A victory-lap record marking Ratboys' first decade before their Chris Walla-produced pivot.

description: Dave Benton's Trace Mountains project leans further into warmly recorded, country-tinged indie pop on this record, mixing jangling guitars with synths and unhurried melodies. Benton's soft, conversational voice keeps things intimate even when the arrangements fill out. It suits listeners who like gentle, twang-flecked indie rock.
lineage: A former LVL UP member's move toward twangier songwriting, released on Philadelphia's Lame-O Records alongside Slaughter Beach, Dog; its country tint sounds akin to the wider indie-twang turn.

description: Austin quartet's debut: blue-collar, plainspoken indie rock with Replacements swagger and War on Drugs-style desert-rock riffs from guitarist Jake Ames, writing about home and growing up around conservatives.
lineage: Bandleader Tyler Jordan met Jake Ames at Kerrville Folk Festival song swaps (where they also crossed paths with Buck Meek and Adrianne Lenker); Keeled Scales labelmates of Katy Kirby.

description: Freeman's quietly released debut: thunderous overdriven guitars and plaintive pedal steel under vivid, semi-biblical images of shipwrecks and doomed drifters. Word of mouth turned it into a cult favorite well after its original release.
lineage: Part of the Burlington, Vermont scene around Freeman and Lily Seabird; it set up his later label releases.

description: The album that put Lenderman on the map: loping, overdriven guitar rock with a country tilt, sung in a bone-dry deadpan about Dan Marino, Michael Jordan's baseball career and other small American humiliations. Funny and sneakily devastating within the same verse.
lineage: Builds directly on Neil Young & Crazy Horse's guitar tone and the deadpan-funny-sad lineage of Drag City songwriters; opened the door to Manning Fireworks and his growing profile in Wednesday.

description: Thomas Dollbaum's debut LP: dark rural storytelling sung in a rangy baritone, with Southern gothic detail and spare, dusty arrangements. It is for listeners who like their country songs literary, slow and haunted.
lineage: Sounds rooted in the alt-country storytelling lineage of Townes Van Zandt and Jason Molina.

description: Zachary James's efficient, hooky home-recording project: '90s alt-rock and Pavement/Big Star-style jangle folded into twangy, deceptively simple songs. It is short, bright and replayable, for fans of warm, lo-fi guitar pop.
lineage: Part of the same Burlington scene as Greg Freeman; its songwriting sounds indebted to Judee Sill, Alex Chilton and Elliott Smith.

description: A short, ramshackle punk-country EP that sounds built for beers in a small, sticky room. It works as a loose bridge between Big Fall and the fuller-band Holey Bible, with rough guitars and Medosch's warbling voice up front.
lineage: Part of the same Dear Life Records-era run of scrappy, caustic Philly country as The Holey Bible.

description: Florry's Dear Life Records debut proper: raucous, barroom-ready country-rock with a half-broken pedal steel, fiddle and a full band behind Francie Medosch's caustic, warble-voiced songwriting. It sits somewhere between the Replacements and Drive-By Truckers, built for loud rooms and cold beer.
lineage: A Dear Life Records release that sounds of a piece with the indie-twang of Greg Freeman and Lily Seabird.

description: A loose, rowdy live document of the Boat Songs-era band, billed as MJ Lenderman & the Wind. The studio songs stretch out with extra guitar interplay and the crowd noise left intact, making it a good fit for fans who want the band's ragged, Crazy Horse-style side.
lineage: Captures the touring band that would carry over into the Manning Fireworks era, showing how the songs mutate on stage.

description: Chris Walla-produced fifth LP blending alt-rock, country twang and a little emo, the fullest version of Ratboys' patient songwriting. Highlights include the elegiac 'Black Earth, WI' and the wired 'Morning Zoo'.
lineage: Sounds of a piece with Wednesday and MJ Lenderman in the current wave of twangy Midwest/Southern indie rock.

description: Ella Williams's fourth Squirrel Flower album is dense, expansive guitar rock about work, anxiety and climate dread, cut with Alex Farrar (MJ Lenderman, Wednesday) and players from Wednesday, Bon Iver and the War on Drugs.
lineage: Farrar's production ties Squirrel Flower directly into the Asheville Drop of Sun network that also produced Wednesday and MJ Lenderman.

description: Debut LP from Norwich's Brown Horse: stark, road-worn alt-country with twangy guitars and weary, shared vocals. It establishes the band's slow-burning songwriting before the fuller sound of All the Right Weaknesses.
lineage: A UK band that sounds steeped in the American alt-country/Crazy Horse tradition, close in spirit to Wednesday and Greg Freeman.

description: The Clearwater Swimmers' self-titled debut flips between hushed intimacy and full electric-guitar surges, recalling Neil Young's Harvest Moon and Jason Molina's Magnolia Electric Co. It suits listeners who like quiet folk that can suddenly turn loud.
lineage: Sounds indebted to the Neil Young/Crazy Horse and Molina/Magnolia Electric Co. lineage that defines indie twang.

description: Nance's record with his full band Mowed Sound: interlocking, jammed-out guitar rock that sounds deeply indebted to Crazy Horse. Long, ragged solos and a heavy, loose rhythm section push the songs well past the three-minute mark.
lineage: Sounds like a Midwest continuation of the Crazy Horse guitar-jam trunk line that also runs through Wednesday and MJ Lenderman.

description: A Nashville band's ramshackle, woozy-twang record with fiddle and Built to Spill/Elephant 6-style energy. The songs are loose and wordy, with homemade production and big, sloppy singalong moments.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Neil Young and Silver Jews, sitting within the same trunk lines as the rest of the Core.

description: Good Looks' second LP: conversational, big-hearted indie rock with big riffs and a steady, resilient mood. Its plainspoken storytelling about working people sits over warm, twangy guitars.
lineage: Continues the band's blue-collar Austin storytelling from Bummer Year into a bigger, more electric sound.

description: The Pittsburgh songwriter's breakout LP: warbling steel and outlaw-tinged guitars swelling into feedback-heavy catharsis. Her songs of loss, land and family community are sung in a clear, plain voice that the band slowly overwhelms.
lineage: Sounds close to the Asheville indie-twang of Florry and Wednesday.

description: Lenderman's breakthrough on a bigger indie label: warmer production, pedal steel and long, unhurried guitar solos wrapped around some of his sharpest, saddest jokes yet. The songs circle men who can't quite say what they mean, sung in his dry drawl over a loose, Crazy Horse-style band.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Neil Young's guitar sound and the funny-sad Drag City songwriting tradition; released the same year he played a key role on Waxahatchee's Tigers Blood.

description: Songs about aging, addiction and small-town North Carolina life, told in long, wry, half-spoken verses that turn dark memories into deadpan jokes. Unhurried heartland-rock backing with warm, fuzzy guitars keeps it plainspoken and barroom-adjacent, for fans of conversational, funny-sad songwriting.
lineage: Sounds close to the Asheville guitar tone of MJ Lenderman's circle, applied to Prine-style conversational storytelling.

description: Blair Howerton's second Why Bonnie LP: twangy, expansive rock that widens the country-coded debut 90 in November into more cinematic, ambitious soundscapes. Fiddle and harmonies still anchor the quieter moments, while the louder songs swell into big, glossy guitar rock.
lineage: Follows 90 in November, whose country sound sits near Waxahatchee and Wednesday, before opening out toward Broken Social Scene/HAIM-style pop-rock.

description: Columbus songwriter Abel's self-lacerating, ramshackle country-jangle LP. It is loud guitar music for quiet people, with jangly guitars, clattering drums and bruised, self-deprecating lyrics.
lineage: Sounds part of the small-label DIY twang network alongside Ohio- and Midwest-based indie-country peers like Spencer Radcliffe.

description: Brown Horse's second LP: soaring guitars, blissful pedal steel and earnest vocals melding slacker rock, folk and alt-country. It sits near Greg Freeman, Wednesday and Neil Young in feel, loud but tender.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Lucinda Williams, Jason Molina and Silver Jews; part of the UK's small but active indie-twang scene.

description: Joseph Barresi's Chico States LP: dusky, encyclopedic Americana with pedal steel and scrappy harmonies. It mixes personal minutiae with train-line and travel history, like a homemade folk archive.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Lomax-style folk documentation and cosmic Americana, close to the Northeast's alt-country underground.

description: Florry's second full-band album: rambunctious barroom twang with Rolling Thunder-style energy alongside quieter, more understated songs. Fiddle, pedal steel and loose group vocals keep it feeling like a party that occasionally sobers up.
lineage: Continues the Dear Life Records run of The Holey Bible; sounds close to the Asheville indie-twang of MJ Lenderman and Wednesday.

description: Freeman's proper label follow-up melds energetic indie rock with an ambling twang and Americana touches. It is explosive and purposeful, with wordy, hooky songwriting that sometimes recalls Elvis Costello.
lineage: Builds on the cult success of I Looked Out and Freeman's place in the Burlington scene alongside Lily Seabird.

description: Oldstar's studio debut: raucous, meaty overdriven country rock with fiddle and outlaw phrasing, recalling Lenderman, Steve Earle, Drive-By Truckers and Being There-era Wilco. A concept record about highway wandering, bar to bar.
lineage: Sounds indebted to outlaw country and Wilco's Being There; close in spirit to young Southern indie-twang songwriters like Thomas Dollbaum and i26connector.

description: A surprise-released full-band project pairing Katie and Allison Crutchfield (Waxahatchee, P.S. Eliot) with MJ Lenderman and Brad Cook. It is warm, harmony-driven indie rock with country edges rather than a solo Lenderman vehicle, built around the sisters' blended voices.
lineage: Connects Lenderman's Asheville circle directly to Waxahatchee's through shared members.

description: Radcliffe's twangy return: fuzzy, hypnotic rock and rambling jams chronicling a return home to Ohio. It is propulsive and relaxed by turns, Midwest indie rock with a country lean.
lineage: Sounds of a piece with the current wave of Midwest indie-twang alongside Ratboys and i26connector.

description: A short EP of hushed, tragic story-songs set on Florida backroads. It works as a brief bridge between Wellswood and Birds of Paradise, with Dollbaum's baritone close to the mic over quiet guitar.
lineage: Brings Dollbaum's alt-country storytelling into the Dear Life Records fold alongside Florry.

description: Brown Horse's third LP: brooding, twangy guitar rock with fuzzy riffs, pedal steel and country-rock arrangements. It keeps the band's weary vocals and slow-building dynamics but leans heavier than before.
lineage: Continues the band's alt-country arc from Reservoir and All the Right Weaknesses.

description: A.S. Wilson's second Convinced Friend LP: compact, forceful tracks fusing serene twang with apocalyptic indie rock. The songs reflect on home, loss and a changing coastline, moving from calm to loud without warning.
lineage: Sounds close to the Northeast slowcore/twang orbit of Horse Jumper of Love and Friendship.

description: Freeman's third full-length pushes his indie-twang songwriting toward heavier, more fractured arrangements. Pedal steel still runs through it, but the guitars are knottier and louder.
lineage: A more ambitious, geographically displaced follow-up to Burnover, reflecting Freeman's move from Vermont odd jobs to full-time touring musician.

description: An Asheville project's debut, self-tagged 'Emo Southern Rock': wailing pedal steel and booming riffs under conversational lyrics. The songs swing from barroom talk to apocalyptic brooding.
lineage: Sounds close to the Asheville scene around MJ Lenderman and Wednesday, blending twangy Southern rock with an emo-adjacent intensity.

description: Kevin Copeland's solo debut: punchy, twangy pop-rock and winsome folk. 'That's All Over Now' is an outright country barnstormer, while 'MONEY' leans into a bluesy stomp.
lineage: Sounds part of the Vermont/Northeast indie-folk-to-twang orbit of Greg Freeman and Lily Seabird.

description: Owen Burton's debut as Ovven: a fuzz-guitar alt-country record with loud, driving arrangements and a drawled, plainspoken voice. It suits listeners who like Crazy Horse-style guitar under country song shapes.
lineage: Sounds close to the Asheville-adjacent indie-twang of Wednesday and MJ Lenderman.

description: Ratboys' latest LP: massive-sounding, anthemic indie rock with lilting twang and frantic shredding. Julia Steiner's plainspoken voice holds the center while the guitars push the songs toward big, cathartic endings.
lineage: Continues the arc from AOID's quiet twang through The Window's alt-rock/country/emo blend.

description: Dollbaum's second LP: roaring Americana shading into tender folk, sung in a rangy, raspy baritone with strong harmonies. It plays like a goodbye letter to lost loved ones, set among Florida's pine flatwoods.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Townes Van Zandt and Jason Molina while stepping out of their shadow.

description: New Orleans band's 13-song LP steeped in Gulf Coast heat and road-worn twang; loose, rowdy cowpunk energy carried across tracks like the title cut and 'Swamp'.
lineage: Part of the current New Orleans indie-twang scene alongside Thomas Dollbaum, touring with Kurt Vile.

description: Wild Pink's most twang-coded record: driving, intense indie rock with pedal steel threading through the arrangements. Its lyrics about contemporary malaise are searing, funny and wrenching by turns.
lineage: Sounds like Wild Pink's turn toward the Core indie-twang sound; ruled into C1 as a specific stylistic pivot rather than the band's whole catalogue.

description: Owen Ashworth's post-Casiotone project sets deadpan, plainly sung short stories about Michigan, Christmas and lost people over minimal drum machine and synth. The songs are small and exact, with the quiet electronics leaving the narratives in front.
lineage: Carries the deadpan storytelling of the Drag City school (Silver Jews) into Ashworth's own Orindal Records orbit, following directly from his Casiotone for the Painfully Alone records.

description: The former Pearls and Brass drummer's third album drapes his cavernous, deadpan baritone over sampled loops and drum machines rather than a bar band. Its storytelling core of plainspoken, dark, small-town character studies fits the same funny-sad lineage as his songwriting peers.
lineage: Follows All Hell (2012) and Me Moan (2013), both pre-2014 and outside this lane's window; Carnation extends his baritone-narrator style into a more electronic production.

description: A punked-up country record steeped in Louisville's weird, unassuming rock scene, with fiddle and banjo scrapping against fuzzy guitars behind Ryan Davis's character sketches of postmasters, coroners and drinkers. It sounds close to Souled American and Palace Brothers, rough and funny.
lineage: Early-period State Champion, before Davis's Roadhouse Band turn; sounds indebted to the Drag City/Palace lineage that runs to Silver Jews and Purple Mountains.

description: Fritz folds synths and drum samples into his unconventional, wisecracking country songwriting, moving past the straighter honky-tonk of Dad Country toward a more hopeful, idiosyncratic sound. Titles like 'Chihuahua Rescue' signal the deadpan comic streak underneath.
lineage: Follows Dad Country (2013); as Jonny Corndawg-turned-Fritz's later work, it sits at the more experimental, funny-sad end of the outlaw-adjacent Nashville scene.

description: Poole's self-released debut, a bedroom-recorded set built from drum machines and synthesizers under twangy vocal melodies, already showing the wry, deadpan lyric style he'd sharpen on later records. Rougher and more lo-fi than what followed, it is a deep cut for fans who want the beginning of the story.
lineage: The starting point for Poole's country-by-way-of-DIY-indie sound that would develop through The Freelancer's Blues and The Rainbow Wheel of Death.

description: Ryan Davis's main band before his Roadhouse records: loose, twangy full-band arrangements built to carry his dense, surrealist wordplay. Send Flowers is their most fully realized record, with fiddle and ragged guitars under long, funny-sad verses. It sounds like a missing link between Silver Jews and the current Louisville deadpan-songwriter scene.
lineage: Direct predecessor to Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band through Davis himself; sounds rooted in the Drag City deadpan lineage.

description: A scrappy pop-punk and emo-pop record with late-'90s-indebted alt-rock energy. It is much more hook-driven and busy than the noise-country of the atlas core, with fast tempos and crowded arrangements.
lineage: Sounds rooted in scrappier punk and emo rather than the storytelling style of the countrygaze bands.

description: Poole's second LP graduates from bedroom drum-machine country to a full honky-tonk band with wailing pedal steel. It updates classic countrypolitan storytelling for a young, broke, romantically alienated urban narrator, sung in his dry baritone.
lineage: Follows his debut Wideass Highway; sounds like Haggard/Nelson/Kristofferson-style storytelling country moved into an ironic, digital-age idiom.

description: David Berman's only album after retiring Silver Jews a decade earlier, made with members of Woods as his backing band, is his most bluntly autobiographical record, its jokes about divorce, depression and aging landing harder for being sung in the same flat, wry voice as ever. Berman died less than a month after its release, days before a scheduled tour, which makes songs like 'All My Happiness Is Gone' retroactively devastating. It stands as the culmination of his songwriting and a touchstone for the deadpan storytellers of this lane.
lineage: David Berman's return after Silver Jews, rooted entirely in the Drag City deadpan lineage that runs from Starlite Walker through this final album.

description: Halper's debut mixes wry self-reflection with intricate fingerpicked instrumentals. Its title, Yiddish slang for a crass nouveau-riche success story, sets up the self-deprecating tone he'd carry into Schlemiel.
lineage: Debut predecessor to Schlemiel; sounds indebted to Elliott Smith and fingerstyle players like Leo Kottke and William Tyler.

description: Tre Burt's debut sets talky, literary verses over lo-fi fingerpicked guitar and rootsy production, favoring character sketches and slow-building narrative over hooks. It was independently released in 2019 before John Prine himself signed Burt to Oh Boy Records for its wider 2020 release. It plays like a front-porch reading more than a rock show, aimed at listeners who want the Prine lineage of plainspoken, half-sung storytelling.
lineage: Directly anointed by John Prine, who signed Burt to his own Oh Boy Records, tying Burt's storytelling explicitly to the Prine/Tom T. Hall deadpan tradition that feeds the modern barroom-storyteller scene.

description: Friendship frontman Dan Wriggins' solo debut strips his prose-poem lyrics down to quiet drums, classical guitar, and a big melodic organ, letting a wounded, deadpan voice turn diary-plain lines into gutting little jokes. Produced by bandmate Michael Cormier, it is five songs of fragmentary memory and small-town Maine imagery delivered with total seriousness despite the title. It works as a quieter, more confessional companion to Friendship's barroom rock.
lineage: Extends the Philadelphia Friendship/Orindal circle's plainspoken, half-spoken songwriting, itself indebted to the Drag City deadpan school of Silver Jews and Smog that runs through the whole 2020s barroom-storyteller scene.

description: Burt's second album narrates a cast of invented heroes and villains with a poet's eye for detail, closer to short fiction than confession. Fuller band arrangements surround his plainspoken, slightly raspy delivery without softening it, for listeners who want storytelling folk with some groove.
lineage: Released on John Prine's Oh Boy Records, keeping Burt's storytelling tied to his mentor Prine and the plainspoken folk tradition he represents.

description: A live set cut at Levon Helm Studios, revisiting Made In America highlights in a stripped, in-the-room performance. Goodall's rolling piano and wry vocals come across warm and direct, with the room sound left in.
lineage: Live companion to Made In America, recorded shortly after that LP's release.

description: The ex-Ona keyboardist's debut swaps that band's rock for piano-man virtuosity and Zevon-ish snark. It is funny without playing as a comedy record, closer to plainspoken confession set to rolling piano.
lineage: Follows Goodall's time in Ona; sounds indebted to the Randy Newman/Warren Zevon line of wry piano storytelling.

description: A piano-led, songs-first country record from the Fust bassist and Dear Life Records co-owner, mixing Neil Young-style keyboard balladry with Lambchop-esque narrative turns and field-recording interludes.
lineage: Meadows co-runs Dear Life Records and plays in Fust, linking this solo record directly to that North Carolina/Brooklyn alt-country network.

description: Smart, unfussy, mildly twangy folk built around dry, plainspoken wit about small-town Montana life. It sounds as gentle as Bahamas or Andy Shauf, but the lyrics carry the same funny-sad economy as his barroom-storyteller peers.
lineage: Missoula, Montana songwriter whose work sits at the folk/country-adjacent end of the deadpan-storyteller lineage.

description: Miller's debut full-length: hushed, homespun songwriting set against tape-hiss production and found-sound experiments. Pump organ, dulcimer-like textures and quiet guitar give it a front-porch, family-archive feel.
lineage: Predates Losin'; sounds close to the Asheville scene around MJ Lenderman and Wednesday.

description: Poole's third solo LP pairs his golden, deadpan baritone with a live band plus old-school synthesizers, widening his millennial-malaise persona into songs about mortality and time rather than just dead-end jobs. The title track, named for the Mac beachball icon, is eerie and gently funny.
lineage: Poole's country songwriting sounds descended from Haggard/Nelson/Kristofferson filtered through Brooklyn's DIY scene; the drum-machine-plus-pedal-steel sound recalls Silver Jews.

description: Bradshaw's character-driven songwriting captures life split between the north Georgia mountains and the touring road, recorded in five live days at Fellowship Hall Sound. Reviewers place him alongside Jason Isbell for narrative-driven, plainspoken Southern songwriting shot through with dry humor.
lineage: Follows his 2021 LP Calico Jim, cut at the same Little Rock studio; part of a loose north-Georgia Appalachian storytelling trilogy completed by Thus Spoke the Fool.

description: Davis's first billed Roadhouse Band record: a double-LP set of long, expansive songs that mix folk-rooted wordplay with synth textures, organ swells and pedal steel. The mood is melancholic and gentle rather than rowdy. A good entry point for the barfly-poet strain of the scene before New Threats from the Soul refined it further.
lineage: Follows Davis's work fronting State Champion; sounds indebted to Souled American, David Berman and Neil Young.

description: A compilation of Aaron Dowdy's early home-recorded songs, released as a single sprawling document of the years before Fust became a full band. Rough, home-taped country songs with Dowdy's drawl up front show the roots of the band's later, fuller storytelling. It is for fans who want to hear the sketches behind the band records.
lineage: Predates and directly seeds the full-band Fust sound heard on Genevieve and Big Ugly; a look at the songwriter's home-recording origins before the Dear Life Records band era.

description: A sprawling album that gathers Jesse Welles' viral topical folk songs into a full deadpan-protest record, delivered in a flat, half-amused talk-sing that turns the grimmest subjects into wry asides. Built mostly on acoustic guitar and harmonica, it sounds like a modern update of Woody Guthrie topical folk filtered through Prine's dry humor. It suits listeners who want current-events songwriting that jokes its way toward grief rather than shouting.
lineage: Sounds like a revival of the Guthrie/Prine topical-folk lineage for the social-media era, reaching listeners through viral video rather than the club circuit.

description: Bradshaw's character-driven historical songwriting, humanizing north-Georgia history and working-class locals. His rough, drawled voice sits over sparse, Appalachian-rooted arrangements.
lineage: Follows Calico Jim and North Georgia Rounder in his run of north-Georgia story records.

description: Three Nashville songwriters trading instruments and lead vocals on an easygoing patio album with shaggy-dog charm. Feelies-ish jangle and Little Feat-style tempo shifts run through their group songwriting.
lineage: Sounds close to the Nashville dive-bar scene of Lambchop and Silver Jews, and to Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band.

description: A bittersweet, sharpened set of folk-rock songs full of shared-memory and loss storytelling drawn from his Asheville circle. Miller's plainspoken, half-sung delivery and homespun production put the focus on the writing over any studio polish.
lineage: Follows Miller's debut Haw Creek; sounds of a piece with the Asheville scene around MJ Lenderman and Wednesday.

description: A cellist-songwriter's wry, meticulously detailed record, pairing relaxed, lush chamber-pop arrangements (cello interludes throughout) with DIY-punk detours and dryly funny lyrics. Closer to bedroom chamber-folk than a bar band, but its joke-then-gut-punch songwriting places it near the deadpan storyteller lineage.
lineage: A borderline Core inclusion: less bar-band than her C2 peers, but shares the funny-sad lyrical mode with Prine/Berman-style songwriters.

description: Fritz's return after a long break turns blue-collar everyday life into wry, anthemic country songs. Honky-tonk band arrangements back his nasal, joke-laced delivery, with the humor always edging toward sadness.
lineage: Follows Sweet Creep (2016) after a near-decade recording gap; continues his idiosyncratic, joke-laced country songwriting.

description: A keys-heavy, conversational sophomore album about relationships, mixing fingerpicked folk, indie rock and pop confessionals. The Yiddish title signals the same rueful, self-deprecating humor that runs through his songwriting.
lineage: Follows Halper's 2020 debut Alrightnik; a Nashville songwriter working the same wry, wordy vein as his singer-songwriter peers.

description: Mess Esque is Helen Franzmann (McKisko) and Mick Turner (Dirty Three), and this is a twisted, handmade folk record that builds a warm, dreamlike world out of plainspoken vocals and loose, unhurried arrangements. Turner's shimmering guitar loops circle under Franzmann's voice. It sounds openhearted and slightly askew at once.
lineage: Released on Drag City alongside Bill Callahan and Bonnie 'Prince' Billy, placing Mess Esque within that label's wry, left-of-center songwriting world.

description: Mildred's debut EP introduces the four-singer, four-songwriter format they'd expand on Fenceline. It is homemade and intimate, with trading lead vocals over living-room-scale guitar arrangements.
lineage: Precedes Fenceline as the band's first release.

description: Janky, livewire guitars and winking humor meet surprisingly massive choruses, somewhere between Amen Dunes and a Lou Reed doing country. The title alone sets the funny-sad tone that carries through songs about content-creation anxiety and modern malaise.
lineage: Sounds close to the Northeast indie-twang of Greg Freeman and Lily Seabird; extends jokey, confessional indie-folk songwriting into anthemic rock territory.

description: A sprawling seven-song double LP of conversational barfly rock, Davis half-sings dense, punning verses over a loose Roadhouse Band arrangement that folds pedal steel and violin into synths and programmed beats. It is dark, funny and grand at once, with guest harmonies from Will Oldham, Catherine Irwin and Lou Turner deepening its Drag City-indebted, David Berman-adjacent lineage. For listeners who want the modern high-water mark of wordy, tragicomic songwriting.
lineage: Davis fronted the earlier Louisville band State Champion before going solo with the Roadhouse Band; the record extends the Silver Jews/David Berman line of deadpan storytelling into the 2020s.

description: Sam Sodomsky's songwriting project sounds akin to David Berman, John Darnielle and Dan Bejar: clever, plainspoken songs balancing folksy earnestness against wry self-awareness. Gentle guitar arrangements leave room for the lyrics to do the work. It suits listeners who come to songs for the words.
lineage: Sounds indebted to the deadpan-songwriter lineage of Berman and Darnielle, within the small Brooklyn Ruination Record Co. circle.

description: A piano-driven, introspective record about returning to his West Virginia hometown, with the sophisticated melodic sense of Made In America turned toward homesickness rather than jokes. It rounds out Goodall's small catalog of plainspoken, piano-led songwriting.
lineage: Follows Made In America and a Levon Helm Studios live set; continues his piano-based storytelling, which sounds indebted to Zevon and Newman.

description: Gibson's fourth full-length, a slow-building record of Florida noir vignettes that trades his earlier sample-collage approach for a more spacious, bar-at-closing-time mood. His deep, deadpan baritone carries Southern gothic storytelling over sparse arrangements.
lineage: Fourth Daughn Gibson LP, following Carnation (2015); continues his deadpan-narrator persona in a stripped-down mode.

description: The Oakland quartet's breezy, affecting debut LP, with four singers and songwriters trading lead vocals from laconic to full-throated. Conversational lyrics and a living-room-session intimacy carry its funny-sad, plainspoken storytelling.
lineage: Sounds of a piece with the funny-sad, plainspoken songwriting in the barroom-storyteller lane.

description: The trio's follow-up to Real Time leans further into playful genre-hopping, with lounge, B-52's pulse and Glen Campbell dust. It keeps the same trading-instruments, trading-verses songwriting method.
lineage: Sounds close to Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band and MJ Lenderman and the Wind.

description: London songwriter Michael Rea's charming, conversational folk-rock record moves at an ambling, unhurried pace, its plainspoken verses and breezy melodies squarely in the wordy funny-sad tradition despite its UK setting.
lineage: A non-US example of the Prine/Berman deadpan-storyteller mode, showing the style's reach beyond its American scenes.

description: Meek's solo debut, looser and more overtly country than Big Thief. It is built on plain, warm Telecaster twang and easygoing melodies, with his reedy voice sitting relaxed in front of the band.
lineage: Establishes Meek's separate honky-tonk-adjacent solo identity outside Big Thief, rooted in his Texas upbringing.

description: Ruston Kelly's debut is the sound he calls 'dirt emo': confessional, downcast lyrics about addiction and heartbreak set over pedal steel and plainspoken country-rock arrangements, closer in mood to emo than to Music Row polish. It moves between hushed acoustic laments and fuller, rootsy full-band tracks without losing its diary-like intimacy. It is a gateway record for listeners coming to alt-country from indie/emo rather than from classic country.
lineage: Draws on Nashville's neo-traditional and outlaw country vocabulary but bends it toward emo's confessional mode, a hybrid Kelly himself named 'dirt emo' and one that seems to echo across later indie-adjacent country songwriting.

description: A full-band collaboration with New Zealand's Marlon Williams, Plastic Bouquet brightens Kacy & Clayton's usual spare Canadian prairie folk into warmer, harmony-heavy country rock. Williams and Kacy Anderson's voices trade and blend across a set of plainspoken duets.
lineage: A one-off widening of Kacy & Clayton's traditional-leaning catalog through collaboration with Marlon Williams, closer to breezy country rock than their usual austere folk.

description: Kentucky songwriter S.G. Goodman's debut is a rocking, rootsy country-folk record steeped in her rural western-Kentucky upbringing, produced by My Morning Jacket's Jim James. Her keening voice and reverb-heavy guitars make it a stark, plainspoken start to her catalog.
lineage: Sounds close to Tyler Childers and Ian Noe in the Kentucky storyteller wing of the new country scene.

description: Katie Crutchfield's fifth Waxahatchee album traded her indie-rock guitars for a warmer, twangier palette of pedal steel and loping tempos, written in the wake of getting sober. The plainspoken lyrics about family, memory and the South made it one of the most acclaimed records of 2020. It is often cited as a turning point for indie musicians leaning into country.
lineage: Grows out of Crutchfield's earlier lo-fi indie-rock work into full country songwriting, leading directly to the Plains project with Jess Williamson and sitting at the front of a wider wave of indie musicians leaning into twang.

description: A warmer, more full-band record than his debut, with ramshackle, patient country-rock songs and groove-locked guitar interplay.
lineage: Deepens Meek's alt-country songwriting voice ahead of his move to 4AD for Haunted Mountain.

description: Aaron Dowdy's self-released full-length debut as Fust is a lo-fi, plainspoken alt-country record, its narrators drifting through small Southern towns and bad decisions. It set the template the band expanded on with a full lineup on Genevieve and Big Ugly. A quieter, more private-sounding entry point into the band's catalog.
lineage: Fust's founding document, before the fuller alt-country sound the band pursued once signed to Dear Life Records.

description: Chapel Hill songwriter and literature professor Florence Dore blends classic-rock hooks, Americana twang and 1980s college-radio jangle. Narrative-heavy lyrics and a lived-in, veteran band sound keep it far from Nashville polish. It is built for listeners who want literate, well-crafted country-rock steeped in the history of the genre's indie wing.
lineage: Sounds steeped in the 1980s-'90s college-rock and No Depression alt-country lineage that C3 grew from.

description: A duo album pairing Katie Crutchfield (Waxahatchee) with fellow songwriter Jess Williamson, built around plush '90s-country vocal harmonies and pedal steel over breakup-and-friendship songs. It plays like a loving homage to Lucinda Williams and Trisha Yearwood-style country radio filtered through two indie songwriters. A key document of the indie scene's 2020s country turn.
lineage: A direct collaborative offshoot of Waxahatchee's country pivot, pairing Crutchfield with Jess Williamson's own move from folk toward country songwriting.

description: Goodman's second album sharpens her rural-Kentucky storytelling into a bleaker, more electric record about depression and rural isolation. The arrangements lean harder into fuzzy guitar than her debut without losing its plainspoken drawl. A more confident, harder-hitting follow-up.
lineage: Extends Old Time Feeling's western-Kentucky storytelling into darker territory; sounds close to Ian Noe and the post-Childers Kentucky scene.

description: Calgary-born, bluegrass-trained singer Bella White's second album pairs striking opening lines about moving on with Appalachian-rooted picking. It widens her sound with country, indie and classic-rock textures without losing the traditional bluegrass core.
lineage: Sounds like the Appalachian bluegrass tradition seen through a young Canadian songwriter's lens.

description: Blue County Pistol's EP is a rollicking, banjo-heavy alt-country release, warm and instantly familiar in its melodies. It plays like a tight, focused introduction rather than a sprawling statement.
lineage: Part of the wider Bandcamp-driven alt-country underground, sharing the banjo-and-drawl approach of countless small self-released country EPs of the early 2020s.

description: Meek's 4AD debut, patient, ramshackle folk-rock songs built on groove-locked guitar work, sung in his easy, unhurried drawl.
lineage: Meek's first release for 4AD, the label Big Thief also records for, bringing his alt-country solo work to a wider audience.

description: Fust's Dear Life Records debut fills out Aaron Dowdy's plainspoken songwriting with a full band. The songs mix wry, character-driven storytelling with a loose, unhurried alt-country backing of pedal steel and piano.
lineage: Expands Evil Joy's lo-fi songwriting into a fuller band sound after signing to Dear Life Records, setting up Big Ugly.

description: Jobi Riccio's debut is coming-of-age country songwriting built on pedal steel, fiddle, and small full-band arrangements, moving from tender acoustic ballads to fuller alt-country arrangements without losing its intimate, diaristic voice. Songs about self-love, loneliness, and growing up in your twenties are sung plainly, without Nashville gloss. It suits listeners who want 2020s indie-scene country that still plays like a singer-songwriter record.
lineage: Sounds of a piece with 2020s indie-Americana peers who bring 2010s indie-folk intimacy into recognizably country arrangements.

description: The Chicago band's debut mixes cosmic country and psychedelic choogle with straight honky-tonk, split between co-lead singers Chris Coleslaw and Lexi Goddard. Pedal steel and reverb-soaked guitars sit under barroom, heartbreak-and-hangover songwriting. It is an unpolished debut that established the band's neon-lit, small-hours sound.
lineage: Draws on classic honky-tonk duet singing and cosmic country in the Gram Parsons/Emmylou Harris mold, feeding directly into the band's more widely reviewed follow-up Horses.

description: John Prine's son makes an unhurried, plainspoken singer-songwriter record about grief and inheritance, built on fingerpicked acoustic guitar and a warm, understated voice that avoids leaning on his father's shadow. Songs like the title track work through loss directly rather than cleverly, closer to quiet country-folk than to barroom wit. It gives the C3 scene a straight-line link back to the '70s country-folk storytellers by blood as well as sound.
lineage: The most literal lineage in the atlas: son of John Prine, carrying the plainspoken country-folk storytelling tradition (V25) directly into the 2020s indie-country scene.

description: Jesse Daniel plays it straight: shuffling honky-tonk rhythms, crying pedal steel and a plain, traditionalist voice on songs about recovery, the road and old-school country. Coming out of California punk rather than a Nashville pipeline, Daniel's traditionalism is a chosen, DIY revival rather than an inherited style. It is a straightforward entry point for listeners who want honky-tonk played by someone raised on punk rock.
lineage: A cowpunk-to-honky-tonk arc in miniature: Daniel's background in California punk bands leads into a self-consciously traditionalist sound that recalls Bakersfield, released through the independent, Nashville-based Lightning Rod Records.

description: Nashville honky-tonker JP Harris makes self-aware, satirical country songwriting here, gutting and funny often in the same verse. Fiddle, steel and a tight honky-tonk band back a pointed, personal voice.
lineage: Follows Harris's years fronting JP Harris and the Tough Choices, landing him on Bloodshot's insurgent-country roster.

description: Halfsies is Lizzie No's modern Americana record, carried by a genre-fluid songwriting voice and her harp alongside twangy band arrangements. It balances pedal-steel warmth with sharp, personal storytelling. It suits listeners who like country with a wry, independent streak.
lineage: Sounds akin to the wider Black country and cosmic-country revival within the neighboring C3 scene.

description: Waxahatchee's sixth album deepens the country turn of Saint Cloud with a full touring-band feel, guitar and harmonies from MJ Lenderman, and some of Crutchfield's most direct, hook-driven songwriting. It is a good entry point for the wider indie-to-country scene of the mid-2020s.
lineage: A continuation of the country-facing sound Crutchfield established on Saint Cloud, cementing the connection between the Waxahatchee/Plains circle and the Asheville MJ Lenderman scene.

description: Case Oats' debut album, led by singer Casey Gomez Walker, is an assured set of character studies backed by pedal steel and fiddle. It moves easily between confessional-poem weight and conversational ease. A confident debut from a young Chicago band.
lineage: Sounds of a piece with Chicago's indie-country circle and the wider Waxahatchee/MJ Lenderman scene.

description: Fust's third album is a detail-rich, character-driven record about visiting a grandmother's childhood Appalachian neighborhood, cut with help from Alex Farrar and members of Sluice. It is the band's fullest and most widely heard record to date.
lineage: Continues Fust's Dear Life Records run, cementing the North Carolina country-textured songwriting line that runs alongside Wednesday and MJ Lenderman's Asheville-adjacent scene.

description: Kentucky songwriter Grace Rogers' debut LP puts conversational, character-based storytelling over jangly electric guitar and a friendly, unpolished full-band sound. Her lyrics have a poet's eye for small-town and family detail. A warm, inviting entry point into the Louisville indie-country scene around Sophomore Lounge.
lineage: A Sophomore Lounge release from the same Louisville scene as Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band; sounds rooted in old-time and string-band music.

description: Hedley's third album keeps building on his throwback Nashville-Sound sound with New West, continuing the honky-tonk revivalism of Neon Blue. It is the most recent entry in a catalog built entirely around classic-country authenticity rather than novelty. A steady, dependable extension of his sound.
lineage: Extends Hedley's classic-country throwback catalog for a third record on New West Records.

description: Tulsa songwriter Ken Pomeroy's stripped-back, autobiographical collection of contemporary folk-country, drawing on her Cherokee heritage and coming-of-age stories. It is a brutally honest, unshowy record built around voice, guitar and close harmonies.
lineage: Sits alongside the Oklahoma/Texas red-dirt songwriter tradition, sharing an audience with the Sturgill Simpson/outlaw-adjacent wing of the new country scene.

description: Goodman's third album turns toward the folk-magic and planting traditions of rural Kentucky for its imagery. It keeps the plainspoken, rootsy sound of her earlier records while widening its spiritual and agricultural language. A settled, personal record from one of the scene's most distinctive Kentucky voices.
lineage: Continues Goodman's western-Kentucky storytelling; its imagery draws on the region's folk traditions.

description: Tobacco City's second album widens their neon-lit country sound with more players and fuller arrangements while keeping the boozy small-town nostalgia of their debut. It channels '70s country touchstones like Gram Parsons, with duet vocals and pedal steel. A confident, more fully arranged follow-up to Tobacco City, USA.
lineage: A direct sequel to Tobacco City, USA; sounds indebted to Gram Parsons-style cosmic country.

description: Nashville songwriter Brennan Wedl's self-titled debut full-length blends arena-scaled country-rock hooks with swaggering, confessional lyrics. It moves between honky-tonk pastiche ('Fake Cowboy') and glammy indie rock without losing its country backbone.
lineage: An Anti- release that sounds close to the Waxahatchee/Snocaps country-rock circle.

description: Meek's latest solo album, built around his wiry guitar lines and reedy, gentle voice as he digs into questions of love and self-reflection. It is for listeners who like their alt-country relaxed and a little off-center.
lineage: Continues Meek's alt-country solo catalog after his earlier records.

description: Nenni widens her honky-tonk base with soul horns and organ while keeping her focus on the dancefloor as a place of escape and self-acceptance. The songwriting turns more explicitly toward self-forgiveness and imperfection, sung in her bright, twangy voice.
lineage: Extends Nenni's honky-tonk catalog toward Southern soul, a crossover that sounds close to Margo Price's and Jaime Wyatt's later albums.

description: Kiely Connell's debut record is sparse, unburdened alt-country songwriting. The arrangements stay spare and intimate, built to foreground her plainspoken, unsettled lyrics. A quietly confident debut steeped in Midwestern small-town detail.
lineage: Sounds like a Midwestern-to-Nashville songwriter story typical of the current alt-country scene.

description: Chicago's National Photo Committee plays raucous, country-tinged bar rock, with spidery pedal steel lines cutting through gravelly, shouted vocals. Its songs favor an unresisting, rowdy energy over polish, closer to a loud honky-tonk stage than a studio. A record built to be heard live.
lineage: Part of the same Chicago DIY-country circle as Tobacco City and Red PK, connecting the city's cowpunk-adjacent bar-rock scene to the wider Bandcamp alt-country revival.

description: A Chicago songwriter's hushed, banjo-and-pedal-steel folk-country. The songs are intimate and unshowy, closer to a bedroom recording than a full-band statement.
lineage: Sounds close to the Chicago cosmic-country scene around Tobacco City.

description: Chicago-by-way-of-Minnesota songwriter Tommy Goodroad's debut studio album mixes Midwestern folksy roots music with rollicking classic honky-tonk, co-produced by Amos Pitsch (Tenement, Hotline TNT). Backed by his touring band the Highway Birds, it leans on fiddle and pedal steel over a rowdy country-rock backbone. A confident full-band debut after years of live shows.
lineage: Part of the same Chicago DIY-country network as Case Oats and Tobacco City, blending Midwestern roots music with classic honky-tonk and outlaw touches.

description: An early, quietly-released Wednesday EP from just after the band's formation, rawer and more hushed than anything on their later Dead Oceans records.
lineage: Part of the pre-Lenderman early catalog that shows the band's sound before its shoegaze/noise elements arrived.

description: Wednesday's self-released debut: hazy, unpolished indie rock recorded long before the band's louder albums. It already leans on Karly Hartzman's diaristic, Southern-gothic lyrics, sung plainly over rough, lo-fi guitars.
lineage: The starting point of Hartzman's project, years before the shoegaze/country fusion of Twin Plagues and Rat Saw God.

description: A self-titled EP from the band's early period, cheaply recorded and rough around the edges. It points toward the heavier guitar textures of the albums to come, with Hartzman's plainspoken vocals up front.
lineage: Bridges yep definitely and the fuller-band sound of I Was Trying to Describe You to Someone.

description: Wednesday's first proper album and first for Orindal: thick, shoegaze-leaning guitars wrapped around Hartzman's vivid, small-town storytelling. It is quieter than Rat Saw God but has the same eye for uncomfortable detail.
lineage: First album to show the full band's mix of noise rock and alt-country, setting up Twin Plagues.

description: Fuzzed-out, noisy indie rock that sits near countrygaze without being built around it. 'Kerrytown' is the clearest crossover point, its Americana tinge recalling Wilco and Silver Jews inside a record otherwise driven by distortion.
lineage: Sounds akin to Wednesday-adjacent noise/twang bands, though it arrived alongside rather than after them.

description: A debut of loose demos that set Dutch Interior's template: scuzzy tape hiss, wandering slide-ish guitar leads, and a slack, almost countrified drawl buried under distortion. Rougher and stranger than the records that followed, it plays like a sketchbook for the noisy-Americana sound they'd refine on Moneyball.
lineage: Grew out of the LA DIY scene alongside bands trading Crazy Horse fuzz for twang; feeds directly into Blinded by Fame and Moneyball.

description: Will Anderson's debut full-length as Hotline TNT buries plainspoken pop melodies under thick sheets of guitar fuzz and noise, setting up the countrygaze-adjacent wall-of-sound style he'd refine on Cartwheel. It's rawer and murkier than the later records but already has the hooks. It's for fans who want the noisiest end of the jangle/shoegaze crossover.
lineage: Kicks off Hotline TNT's run from DIY noise-pop toward the more country-tinged, festival-ready sound of Cartwheel and Raspberry Moon.

description: A short, sparsely produced EP from the band's early period. It is rough and home-recorded, with Hartzman's plainspoken voice over loose guitars.
lineage: Sounds like a transitional sketch between the band's first two albums.

description: The album where Wednesday's mix of shoegaze fuzz and country twang really locked in. Loud, blown-out guitars and pedal steel sit under Hartzman's plainspoken lyrics about small-town Southern life, with songs like 'Cliff' swinging between hush and roar.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Velvet Underground-descended noise textures grafted onto Southern storytelling in the Skynyrd-to-Drive-By-Truckers line.

description: A radio-session live album cut around the Twin Plagues era, rougher and noisier in the room than the studio versions, capturing the band's live intensity before they broke through more widely.
lineage: A snapshot of the band mid-transition from lo-fi project to full-throated noise-country outfit.

description: A road-trip-ready tour tape from an Inland Empire band splitting the difference between fuzz-caked shoegaze riffs and a plainspoken country vocal delivery. It is short, hazy and rough, a sketch of the sound they would build on.
lineage: Sounds close to the countrygaze Bandcamp scene around Wednesday; precedes There You Ain't.

description: A full-band covers record pulling from country, indie and classic-rock sources, filtered through Wednesday's blown-out, pedal-steel-laced sound. It's a covers set rather than original songs, released just before the band left Orindal for Dead Oceans.
lineage: Shows the covers/tribute strand of the countrygaze scene and the band's own influences in plain sight.

description: Thicker and more purposeful than the debut, this set pairs a ratty, bubblegum drum feel with whiny, screaming lead guitar and a cathartic, a-rhythmic sense of collapse. It blends country, folk and grunge, which is the whole Dutch Interior pitch in a sentence.
lineage: Bridges Dutch Interior's tape-hiss beginnings and their Fat Possum signing; sounds like the Wednesday-style countrygaze template with a heavier '90s alt-rock skew.

description: A short follow-up EP built around small, specific images (a fruit arrangement, a golf dream about Willie Nelson) delivered through thick, honeyed distortion. Its sound splits the difference between Dinosaur Jr.-scale guitars and an unmistakably country vocal cadence.
lineage: Extends the sound introduced on 2022 Tour Tape; sounds close to Wednesday's countrygaze.

description: This home-recorded set mixes shoegaze walls of guitar with Primal Scream-style melodic touches and loose, woozy energy. It sits at the loud, twangy edge of countrygaze rather than its center, for listeners who like their noise-pop hazy and homespun.
lineage: An off-kilter entry in the countrygaze lineage, closer to noise-pop than to Wednesday's overt country phrasing, but sharing its shoegaze-scale guitar walls.

description: Shallowater's debut earns the 'dirtgaze' tag: dusty, string-bent guitar figures get swallowed by walls of overdriven noise, with a drawled, half-buried vocal riding on top. It is rougher and more shoegaze-indebted than the band's later work, closer to noise rock with a country skeleton than to polished Americana.
lineage: Debut full-length that establishes the dirtgaze sound Shallowater expand on with God's Gonna Give You A Million Dollars; part of the small post-Wednesday wave of Texas and Southern bands mixing noise-rock scale with country phrasing.

description: Wednesday's breakthrough: a widescreen mix of Dinosaur Jr.-style guitar theatrics and vivid, novelistic Southern storytelling, from car crashes to church parking lots. 'Bull Believer' is the album's noisiest, most cathartic centerpiece.
lineage: Sounds like the Skynyrd-to-Drive-By-Truckers storytelling line fused with Sonic Youth/Dinosaur Jr.-style guitar noise; a defining Core record for this atlas.

description: Dutch Interior's Fat Possum debut pushes the noisy-twang formula into a more cohesive, full-band record without losing the ragged edges. Its golden-hour twang swings between sunny and haunting, the clearest statement yet of the band's noise-wall-over-country-changes sound.
lineage: Third album for a band who came up recording to tape; sounds of a piece with Wednesday and Shallowater in the 2020s countrygaze scene.

description: Long songs, several stretching well past the usual length, swing between ear-splitting guitar walls and glacial, delicate melodies. It is the fullest realization yet of the band's dirtgaze idea: country-song bones dressed in noise-rock scale.
lineage: Second Shallowater LP, expanding the noise/twang balance of There Is A Well into longer, more patient song structures; sounds of a piece with Dutch Interior and Wednesday.

description: Wednesday's latest album pushes further into explosive shoegaze and grunge territory while keeping classic country song structures underneath. Songs like 'Elderberry Wine' show the quieter, twangier side, while the loud tracks bury Hartzman's storytelling under huge guitars.
lineage: Continues the countrygaze sound of the band's own Twin Plagues and Rat Saw God, now bigger and more anthemic.

description: Ella Williams' enveloping voice sits against crunchy, wall-of-guitar production on this Squirrel Flower record. Big, distorted guitars swell under slow, open melodies, giving the songs a live, room-filling weight. It suits listeners who like loud guitars wrapped around intimate songwriting.
lineage: Continues Squirrel Flower's move toward the countrygaze-adjacent, guitar-wall sound of Wednesday's circle.

description: A teenage solo record made years before Big Thief formed, simple acoustic songs that already show Lenker's fingerpicking and plainspoken emotional directness in embryonic form.
lineage: An early, little-heard document of Lenker's development as a songwriter well before Hours Were the Birds or Big Thief.

description: An early Lenker solo album, recorded around the time Big Thief was forming. It is spare and intimate, mostly voice and acoustic guitar, in the same vein as her band's early records.
lineage: A parallel solo thread running alongside early Big Thief.

description: A short duo release of stripped-back, harmony-driven folk songs recorded before Big Thief formed. It shows the songwriting chemistry between Lenker and Meek that carried into the band, with two acoustic guitars and close harmonies.
lineage: An early document of the Lenker-Meek creative partnership that predates Big Thief and continues through Meek's own solo work.

description: The companion release to a-sides, with more spare, harmony-focused acoustic duets from Lenker and Meek. Recorded just before Big Thief's formation, it is quiet, loose and intimate.
lineage: Completes the a-sides/b-sides pair documenting Lenker and Meek's pre-Big Thief songwriting collaboration.

description: Native State is Jess Williamson's early, spare full-length, plainspoken folk songs recorded with minimal backing that let her voice and guitar carry the weight. Her high, quavering voice and slow tempos give it a haunted, desert-folk stillness.
lineage: Predates the cosmic-country turn of Cosmic Wink and Sorceress, an early document of Williamson's move from Austin's DIY folk scene toward the wider Mexican Summer roster.

description: Shelley's No Quarter debut is patient and unadorned folk songwriting sung in a clear, plain alto over sparse fingerpicked guitar. Light touches of accompaniment never crowd the voice.
lineage: Her first record for No Quarter, the label she'd stay with through Real Warmth, part of the Louisville folk scene alongside Nathan Salsburg.

description: Recorded with Mike Mogis in Omaha after signing to ANTI-, Dark Arc pairs dulcimer-and-mandolin folk instrumentation with denser production. The electric edge gives the stomping group vocals more push.
lineage: Zac Little's Columbus, OH string-band project, drawing on Appalachian instrumentation (balalaika, dulcimer, mandolin) filtered through indie folk-rock.

description: Released as Erin Rae and the Meanwhiles, this is a self-released early record of warm, plainspoken country-folk. It predates her solo billing.
lineage: An early document of Rae's Nashville scene before Putting On Airs brought her wider attention.

description: Pratt's second album is warbling, hazy fingerstyle folk sung in her distinctive high, cracked vibrato. It is associated with the freak-folk revival but closer in spirit to Vashti Bunyan than to any twang scene.
lineage: Her only album for Drag City, between her 2012 debut and Mexican Summer's Quiet Signs.

description: A quietly assured second No Quarter record, continuing Shelley's plainspoken, guitar-and-voice folk songwriting. It has a warmer, more settled tone than the debut and subtle full-band shading.
lineage: Bridges Electric Ursa and her self-titled 2017 breakthrough.

description: A pop-structured folk-rock record built on the band's trademark mix of banjo, dulcimer and balalaika. Synths and electric guitars push the songs outward.
lineage: Zac Little's Columbus, OH string-band project, drawing on Appalachian instrumentation (balalaika, dulcimer, mandolin) filtered through indie folk-rock.

description: Recorded at La Frette studios near Paris, Loyalty is warm, unhurried indie folk with Tamara Lindeman's plainspoken alto out front and light Americana touches (pedal steel, brushed drums).
lineage: Tamara Lindeman's long-running Toronto folk project, moving from 2000s singer-songwriter records toward the more expansive, band-driven indie folk of its 2020s run.

description: Big Thief's debut: raw, guitar-driven indie folk built around Adrianne Lenker's cracked, intimate voice. Her vivid, sometimes violent storytelling about family and coming of age sits over a band that can swing from whisper to loud electric surge.
lineage: Sounds indebted to the folk-songwriting line running from Gillian Welch and Elliott Smith, and starts the 2020s Big Thief/Lenker axis.

description: Marten's teenage debut is hushed and delicately fingerpicked. It is a precociously assured folk record built around her breathy, unadorned voice.
lineage: Marten came up through YouTube covers and the UK singer-songwriter circuit before signing to RCA; this debut set the hushed template she has expanded over five albums.

description: Cornfield's early full-band folk-rock record. It carries plainspoken road-life songwriting delivered in her low, conversational alto.
lineage: An early entry in Cornfield's Canadian folk-rock catalog, well before the more widely noticed Could Have Done Anything.

description: Jacklin's debut pairs a plainspoken alto with spare, twang-tinged arrangements. Its coming-of-age songs sit closer to country-folk than to polished pop.
lineage: Grew from Australia's singer-songwriter scene; its countryish edges look ahead to the twang overlap of later records like Pre Pleasure.

description: A quieter, more interior record than Masterpiece, digging into childhood trauma and family history. The close-miked intimacy that became the band's signature is everywhere, with Lenker's voice nearly whispering over spare guitar on songs like 'Mythological Beauty'.
lineage: Deepens the confessional folk songwriting that would open out into the more exploratory U.F.O.F. and Two Hands.

description: Shelley's self-titled record, made with Jeff Tweedy producing, widened her audience. It keeps the same plain, guitar-and-voice core in her clear alto.
lineage: Her most widely reviewed record before Like the River Loves the Sea, connecting her to the Wilco/Chicago folk-adjacent circle.

description: Hushed, minor-key indie folk built from finger-picked guitar and Lucille's airy, wavering voice, with lyrics circling grief, darkness and the underworld. The arrangements stay sparse and patient, leaving plenty of silence around the voice. It is for listeners who want folk that feels like a quiet room at dusk.
lineage: Sounds akin to the 2010s Bandcamp-era hushed indie folk around Keeled Scales, closer to private chamber folk than to country.

description: Shame is iconoclastic bluegrass-rooted folk with pointed, feminist political songwriting. Baiman's fiddle playing anchors the lean arrangements.
lineage: Oak Park, Illinois-raised fiddler turned Nashville songwriter; sounds rooted in the politically engaged old-time and bluegrass-folk tradition.

description: Living Water is a spare folk record built on close-mic'd guitar and Lay's airy voice. It sounds indebted to Nick Drake and Vashti Bunyan.
lineage: Lay's second solo album, made while she played in the LA punk band Feels; sounds akin to the LA cosmic-folk revival around Ty Segall's circle.

description: The self-titled fourth album is Lindeman's most purely indie-folk record, wistful full-band songs about love and self-doubt. Jangling guitars sit under close, conversational vocals.
lineage: Tamara Lindeman's long-running Toronto folk project, moving from 2000s singer-songwriter records toward the more expansive, band-driven indie folk of its 2020s run.

description: Stratton's sixth album is a hushed, meticulously fingerpicked set that pairs Nick Drake-indebted guitar work with chamber-folk strings. It's patient, literate songwriting built for close listening rather than singalongs.
lineage: Grew from Stratton's decade-plus run as a solo-guitar folk songwriter; sounds indebted to Nick Drake and John Fahey.

description: A hushed, largely solo-acoustic record, sparer than any Big Thief album. Lenker's voice and fingerpicked guitar get room to breathe on songs about grief, healing and impermanence, including 'symbol' and 'cradle'.
lineage: Establishes Lenker's solo catalog as a genuinely separate, quieter project from Big Thief rather than a side effort.

description: Rae's breakthrough solo debut is warm and searching country-folk. It examines faith, sexuality and family with unusual gentleness and directness.
lineage: Signed her to Single Lock Records and set the plainspoken, gospel-tinged style she carried into Lighten Up.

description: Heynderickx's debut is conversational, fingerpicked folk that finds grace in the mundane, from housework to horticulture. Her voice can turn from a murmur to a full-throated cry within a verse.
lineage: Emerged from Portland, Oregon's folk circuit; later plainspoken songwriters such as Lily Seabird sound indebted to its patient observation.

description: I See You Among the Stars is Chicago songwriter Jessica Risker's delicate, minimal psych-folk record, brief vignettes built on bouncing acoustic guitar and quiet, wood-grained atmosphere. It recalls Nick Drake and Sibylle Baier in its unhurried, slightly askew calm.
lineage: Predates Risker's more ornate, psychedelic later work (Calendar Year) and sounds of a piece with Chicago's hushed folk scene.

description: A low-key set released between her main label albums. It stays in the same patient, plainspoken guitar-and-voice vein as her No Quarter records.
lineage: A stopgap independent release showing Shelley's steady, unhurried songwriting pace.

description: An unexpected folk-rock record mixing Appalachian string-band instrumentation with contemporary electronic touches. Zac Little's high, urgent voice leads the layered arrangements.
lineage: Zac Little's Columbus, OH string-band project, drawing on Appalachian instrumentation (balalaika, dulcimer, mandolin) filtered through indie folk-rock.

description: Recorded in Texas as U.F.O.F.'s rawer twin, largely captured live by the full band. It trades that album's haze for folk-rock urgency and blunt, plainspoken lyrics about love and the state of the world, with 'Not' as its jagged, guitar-heavy centerpiece.
lineage: The heavier, more grounded counterpart to U.F.O.F., closer to the band's live sound.

description: The dreamier, more abstract half of Big Thief's 2019 double-album year. Its hushed, almost whispered songs drift rather than build, closer to folk-inflected ambient music than rock, with 'Cattails' as one of its gentlest moments.
lineage: Shows the band pulling folk songwriting toward atmosphere and space, a contrast to the rockier Two Hands released the same year.

description: A slightly fuller-band second album than the debut, still built around Marten's hushed, breathy delivery and fingerstyle guitar. The production is subtly more textured, with a touch more low-end warmth in the arrangements.
lineage: Continues the debut's hushed folk approach before Marten's move to Fiction Records for Flora Fauna.

description: A drummer-turned-singer-songwriter's plainspoken record of quiet, groove-aware folk-rock, continuing her steady, road-worn songwriting.
lineage: Bridges Cornfield's earlier folk-rock records and the sharper, Tom Petty-esque songwriting of Could Have Done Anything.

description: Jazzy, warm-toned folk mixing loose acoustic guitar and piano with unhurried melodic turns that owe as much to Randy Newman as to any folk revivalist. Durant's relaxed, conversational singing keeps the songs intimate. It suits listeners who like their singer-songwriter records warm and a little old-fashioned.
lineage: Sounds indebted to '70s piano-and-guitar singer-songwriter craft more than to the folk revival, sitting at the jazzier edge of 2010s indie folk.

description: A more finely produced, flute- and piano-inflected record, still built on Pratt's warbling voice and fingerstyle guitar. The pace is warmer and more meditative than before.
lineage: Her Mexican Summer debut, expanding her sound just ahead of Here in the Pitch.

description: Recorded in Iceland, this is a warm and unhurried record. It continues Shelley's plain, guitar-centered songwriting with subtly expanded arrangements.
lineage: Follows her self-titled record on No Quarter, keeping the same patient, guitar-centered approach.

description: A breakup record about bodily autonomy and the end of a long relationship, delivered in Jacklin's plain, unadorned voice. The spare full-band arrangements lean acoustic more than electric.
lineage: Sits alongside Australian songwriters such as Stella Donnelly and, later, Maple Glider in plainspoken, folk-rooted heartbreak writing.

description: Sam Swinson's band makes its debut with dark, twangy country-Americana about addiction and recovery. Sauntering guitars and a weary, close-up vocal give it a lived-in storytelling core.
lineage: Its dark, lived-in country-folk storytelling sounds akin to rural-leaning indie bands like Wednesday.

description: Lay's first album for Sub Pop, co-produced with Ty Segall. It dresses her fingerpicked folk with a wider array of instrumentation than her earlier records.
lineage: Marks Lay's move from Feels' punk records into a dedicated solo folk career.

description: Donnelly's debut pairs plainspoken, funny-sad lyrics, many of them pointed portraits of bad men, with light, jangly indie-folk arrangements. The songs are sharp and conversational, and the quiet backing leaves the wit and anger right at the front.
lineage: Grew out of Donnelly's 2017 Thrush Metal EP and the Perth DIY scene; part of the same wry Australian singer-songwriter lineage as Julia Jacklin.

description: Hollie Fullbrook's Tiny Ruins widens its hushed, literate folk with warmer full-band arrangements. Her soft, precise voice stays at the center, for fans of patient, wordy indie folk.
lineage: Grew from Fullbrook's solo Tiny Ruins recordings into a full band; sounds akin to Southern Hemisphere songwriters like Julia Jacklin.

description: A companion set of wordless guitar pieces recorded during the same cabin sessions as songs. It is ambient and meditative rather than song-based, with long acoustic passages and room sound left in.
lineage: A rare instrumental branch of the folk-songwriting lineage, released as a direct pair with songs.

description: Recorded alone in a cabin during a breakup and the start of the pandemic, an extremely intimate set of largely unadorned acoustic songs, among her most stripped-down work.
lineage: Deepens the solo-cabin-recording strand of folk songwriting, released alongside its instrumental companion piece the same day.

description: Krieger's early Northern Spy record: undulating, plainspoken diaristic songwriting over spare acoustic arrangements, quieter and rawer than her later, more piercing work.
lineage: The start of Krieger's run of prolific, mortality-fixated songwriting that continues through I Keep My Feet on the Fragile Plane and Art of the Unseen Infinity Machine.

description: Anaïs Mitchell, Eric D. Johnson, and Josh Kaufman's debut as a trio reworks traditional British and American folk ballads into warm, harmony-driven arrangements. Fingerpicked guitar and close three-way singing give old songs like 'Deep in Love' and 'The Roving' a hushed, lived-in glow.
lineage: A modern-folk supergroup drawing directly on the Child ballad and Appalachian folk-revival tradition, feeding into the wider Big Thief-adjacent folk circle via shared label 37d03d.

description: A stark breakup record built from voice, piano and sparse accompaniment, Old Flowers is Courtney Marie Andrews at her most unadorned, with a big, Ronstadt-like voice carrying every ounce of the heartbreak. It is the quietest, most direct record in her catalog, for listeners who want grief sung plainly.
lineage: Sounds indebted to 1970s Laurel Canyon songwriting (Ronstadt, Mitchell), carried into the modern indie-folk scene; her later records lean further into full-band cosmic country.

description: Hill's debut sets intricate fingerpicking under a plainspoken, nature-fixated songwriting voice. It sounds indebted to Michael Hurley and Karen Dalton, for listeners who like patient solo-guitar folk.
lineage: Sounds rooted in the American Primitive fingerstyle tradition, opening onto her fuller-band later records.

description: A lo-fi indie-folk EP of intimate, close-mic'd acoustic songs, with soft vocals sitting right up against fingerpicked guitar. It is bedroom-scale and diaristic, for listeners who like quiet, unvarnished songwriting.
lineage: Sounds akin to the hushed, Bandcamp-era indie folk of artists like Julia Lucille.

description: Dan Knishkowy's Adeline Hotel project offers gentle, fingerpicked indie folk with plainspoken, slightly wry lyrics about memory and routine. Soft vocals and small arrangements keep it homey and understated. It suits listeners who like quiet, detail-focused songwriting.
lineage: Sounds akin to a small Brooklyn songwriter circle around Ruination Record Co.; fingerpicked folk with a deadpan streak.

description: A newly confident, full-band-driven record made after a period of writer's block. It is warmer and more rhythmically alive than her first two RCA albums.
lineage: Marks Marten's move from RCA to Fiction and a fuller, more grounded folk-pop sound.

description: A patient, plainspoken folk-rock record with a drummer's ear for groove. It continues Cornfield's steady run of low-key songwriting in her warm, conversational voice.
lineage: Sits between The Shape of Your Name and the more widely reviewed Could Have Done Anything.

description: Meg Duffy's most ambitious Hand Habits record to date, produced by Sasami Ashworth; folk-rooted songwriting opened up into lusher, more adventurous arrangements after a pandemic-forced pause, with Perfume Genius guesting on one track.
lineage: Duffy came up as an in-demand guitarist for Kevin Morby and War on Drugs before Hand Habits' own records; Fun House marks the point where the project moved from insular bedroom folk toward fuller studio arrangements.

description: A Tucson artist's record blending Americana-tinged songwriting with ambient sound design: synthesizer, tape loops, field recordings and desert-referencing lyrics. Songs dissolve into long drones and hiss before re-forming around her voice and guitar. It is for listeners who like folk that shades into ambient music.
lineage: A joint release between Keeled Scales and Orindal Records, connecting Tucson's desert-folk scene to both labels' networks.

description: Kirby's Keeled Scales debut is sparkling, precisely arranged indie folk-pop with an unusually sharp ear for melody. Singles like 'Cubic Zirconia' pair bright, layered arrangements with careful, searching lyrics.
lineage: Established Kirby as a defining voice of the 2020s indie-folk wave that runs from Nashville through Big Thief's circle.

description: Lauren Spear's debut as Le Ren is ten hushed, plainspoken folk songs, with a guest turn from Tenci. The arrangements stay spare and the delivery direct, letting the songs sit close to the listener.
lineage: Montreal songwriter whose spare, direct folk songwriting fits the same lineage as Gillian Welch by way of Joni Mitchell.

description: The Ohmme co-founder's solo debut: spare piano- and violin-inflected songs moving between chamber-folk intimacy and quiet dissonance. Her clear voice sits close to the listener while strings scrape and hover at the edges. It suits listeners who like experimental folk that stays tender.
lineage: Grows out of Chicago's overlapping indie-folk/experimental scene, tied to Orindal labelmates Gia Margaret and Macie Stewart's other Chicago projects.

description: Tori Zietsch's debut as Maple Glider, produced by Tom Iansek, draws on vignettes of her life and travel. The spare, intimate folk songs center her clear, hushed voice.
lineage: Launched Zietsch's solo folk career on Pieater/Partisan.

description: Erin Birgy's surrealist song-world turns painterly and desert-lit on this record, co-produced with Big Thief's James Krivchenia. Avant-pop arrangements of horns, synths and loose guitar wrap around plainspoken, image-dense lyrics. It suits listeners who like their indie folk strange and colorful.
lineage: Connected to the Big Thief/indie-folk network via Krivchenia's production; sits at the arty edge of the twangy indie-folk lane.

description: A transitional second record that opens Hill's solo fingerstyle sound to a small circle of collaborators. The warm, unhurried arrangements stay close to her voice and guitar.
lineage: Follows Azalea, expanding her palette ahead of the full-band Hopeful Woman.
