description: Burton's debut LP pairs a high, Roy Orbison-like wail with moody, echo-laden country-rock production. Fingerpicked guitar and a hushed drawl give it an old, lonesome feel that plays as timeless rather than retro. It suits listeners who like crooned, reverb-soaked heartbreak songs.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Roy Orbison's balladry and 1970s cosmic country, akin to the Woodsist circle's hazy country rock.

description: Nashville pedal-steel sideman Spencer Cullum's debut as a bandleader is a sunny homage to '60s-'70s British and American folk-rock, cut with a cast of Music City players. It's less about his usual session role and more about letting his own songwriting lead, suited to fans of gentle, steel-soaked folk-rock.
lineage: Grows out of Cullum's work as a Nashville session pedal-steel player, channeling his English folk-rock upbringing through the city's cosmic-country underground.

description: A career-spanning live document assembled from years of shows, capturing how the band stretches its Dylan/Springsteen-via-Neil Young songs into extended, synth-lit jams on stage. It works as both a best-of and proof of the band's live reputation.
lineage: Distills a decade of The War on Drugs' guitar rock, which sounds like Crazy Horse meeting motorik drive, into its most expansive, jam-lengthened form.

description: Woods work in synths and drum machines alongside their usual guitar interplay here, giving the record a hazier, more nocturnal feel than their jam-band-leaning mid-2010s albums. It's still built on Earl's falsetto and the band's loping, Dead-adjacent chord changes.
lineage: Shows the Woodsist scene absorbing softer, synth-touched textures while keeping a backbone that sounds indebted to Crazy Horse and the Dead.

description: A fuller-band, more overtly country-rock record than Hanson's debut, with pedal steel and long, winding guitar solos running through desert-toned songs. It leans into the sound of vintage Neil Young and Gene Clark records without straight pastiche. It suits listeners who want wide-open, sunburnt guitar music.
lineage: Pulls Hanson's solo work closer to what sounds like classic Cosmic American Music in the Neil Young and Gene Clark mold.

description: A quieter, more reflective Hiss Golden Messenger record that folds subtle home-studio textures into the band's usual country-soul without losing the pedal steel and warm harmonies. The songs reckon with stillness, isolation, and small-town North Carolina life. It suits listeners who want gentle, unhurried roots music for late evenings.
lineage: Shows Taylor bending his sound, which sounds rooted in the Grateful Dead and the Band, toward home-studio textures while keeping the same cosmic-country core.

description: Andrews leads this loose, sunny record of ramshackle country-folk. Ringing guitars and easygoing tempos carry conversational, unfussy songwriting throughout. It sits comfortably in the Woodsist label's twangy, DIY take on Laurel Canyon songwriting, for listeners who like their folk hazy and homespun.
lineage: Sounds akin to the hazy, harmony-driven country-folk of Woodsist labelmates Woods.

description: Kazar's debut solo album is joyful, unhurried rock built on winding jams, pedal steel, and close harmonies. It mixes Band-style looseness with a glammy, playful pop streak. It suits listeners who want warm 1970s-leaning rock with a grin.
lineage: Released on Kevin Morby's Mare Records imprint; its loose, harmony-rich rock sounds indebted to the Band and 1970s pop-rock.

description: The duo keeps refining their guitar-and-harmony formula, with intertwined acoustic guitars and close, easy vocals. It is short, warm and unpretentious, songs built for a porch or a campfire rather than a festival stage.
lineage: A continuation of Mapache's California country-duo sound, which sounds indebted to the Everly Brothers and the Flying Burrito Brothers.

description: Rosali's first collaboration with David Nance's Mowed Sound band opens up her songs into looser, more guitar-forward arrangements, closer to Neil Young or Yo La Tengo than singer-songwriter folk. Her plainspoken drawl rides warm Telecaster lines and harmonized guitars at easy tempos.
lineage: Marks the start of her ongoing partnership with the Mowed Sound band, a key thread connecting Philadelphia and Omaha DIY scenes.

description: A patient, groove-heavy record that leans further into the band's live-jam side, with extended guitar and pedal-steel interplay over motorik rhythms. It is psychedelic country rock for a long, stoned drive, trading drone-rock heaviness for open-prairie ease.
lineage: Continues Johnson's arc from Wooden Shjips' drone-rock toward fully-formed cosmic country.

description: A trip into '70s classic-rock territory, all chiming guitars, T-Rex stomp and Lou Reed-style breeziness. The band favors warmth and laid-back groove over polish, evoking the late-'60s and early-'70s golden era rather than throwback pastiche.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Britfolk- and glam-inflected early-'70s classic rock, with a garage-rock looseness.

description: Other You folds subtle synth textures into Gunn's guitar-first sound without losing its unhurried, sun-bleached feel. Soft drums, layered guitars and his relaxed voice give it a hazy, meditative calm. It plays like a gentler sibling to Way Out Weather.
lineage: A late-period Matador record that keeps Gunn's cosmic-country songwriting intact while widening its palette with electronics.

description: Ben Schwab's Sylvie project trades the psych-pop of his Golden Daze work for spare, warm country-folk arrangements. It's a slight but gorgeous record of soft vocals, brushed drums and gentle guitar, for listeners who like their '70s revival hushed.
lineage: A side project of Golden Daze's Ben Schwab, carrying that LA psych-pop scene toward softer '70s-style country-folk.

description: A slightly brighter, more direct record than its predecessors, with tighter songwriting and guest vocals from Lucius. Still built on the band's signature long crescendos and Telecaster shimmer, it is a comfortable, confident continuation rather than a reinvention.
lineage: Continues the band's cosmic-Americana lineage into the 2020s, an established touchstone for younger heartland-adjacent songwriters.

description: Wild Pink's breakout record layers pedal steel and strings under John Ross's introspective, plainspoken lyrics, arriving at a lush, heartland-scaled sound. Mid-tempo songs build slowly to widescreen peaks, for listeners who want indie rock with a country sheen.
lineage: Wild Pink's fullest realization of pedal-steel-dressed indie rock, sounding like a crossover point between heartland rock and the C1 twang scene.

description: This album keeps McCombs' warm, unhurried guitar-rock sound while turning toward more openly emotional lyrics about grief and love. The tempos stay breezy and the arrangements uncluttered, closer to Mangy Love than to Tip of the Sphere's jams. It is for listeners who want his songwriting at its gentlest.
lineage: Continues McCombs' ANTI- era guitar rock; its softer edges sound indebted to classic Laurel Canyon songwriting.

description: Loose Future opens Courtney Marie Andrews back up into full-band, '70s-flavored arrangements after the bare-bones Old Flowers, with buttery lead guitar and warm harmonies replacing the earlier record's silence. The mood is lighter and more hopeful, suited to listeners who like breezy, sunlit country rock.
lineage: Sounds indebted to the country-rock/Cosmic American Music lineage, following her own path from stripped-down folk into the cosmic country revival.

description: A more textured, golden-toned record than Putting On Airs, layering Rae's strong, unhurried voice over arrangements that borrow from 1970s AM radio without tipping into kitsch. Every arrangement stays tasteful and uncluttered, with pedal steel and close harmonies giving it a breezy, cosmic-country glow. It suits listeners who want warm, soft-focus country-folk.
lineage: Extends Rae's Nashville country-folk into a sound akin to 1970s AM-radio soft rock and Cosmic American Music.

description: New Jersey's Garcia Peoples keep working the dual-guitar-jam vein of their earlier records, all extended solos and interlocking leads in the spirit of the guitarist their name nods to. It's dense, riff-forward psych-jam rock built for headphones or a long drive.
lineage: Takes its name from Jerry Garcia and sounds directly indebted to his lead style and the Dead's long-form jamming.

description: Sparked by an old photograph of his father found after a family health scare, this album is a warm, mid-tempo meditation on mortality and memory, built on breezy country-rock arrangements with pedal steel and horns. Recorded partly in Memphis, it draws on that city's soul and gospel history as much as on Laurel Canyon songwriting. It suits listeners who want reflective songs with a big, generous band sound.
lineage: Continues Morby's move toward a fuller folk-rock and country sound that sounds indebted to Dylan, the Band, and Memphis soul; it was followed by the companion More Photographs (A Continuum).

description: Microcosmos is a spacious cycle of cosmic country songs from Lou Turner, her warm, conversational voice finding humor and grace in small domestic moments. Its deadpan warmth recalls Silver Jews and Lambchop, for listeners who like country songs slow and wry.
lineage: Sounds indebted to '70s singer-songwriters like Joni Mitchell, with touchstones in Bill Callahan and Silver Jews' wry, plainspoken style.

description: A long, generous set of earnest, classic songwriting built on intertwined acoustic guitars and close duo harmonies. It is an unpretentious road-trip record from a duo comfortable with letting songs breathe. It suits listeners who want easygoing California country-folk to play front to back.
lineage: The most expansive entry in Mapache's catalog, extending their duo-harmony format across a longer set.

description: Whitney's most ambitious record, grown from acoustic demos into full arrangements, folds synths and programmed textures into their usual horn-and-guitar warmth. It's a left-field stretch for the band without losing the easy melodicism and falsetto of the debut.
lineage: Whitney's furthest reach from their country-soul debut, though still built on the same warm, horn-inflected songwriting core.

description: Written and recorded after John Ross's cancer diagnosis, ILYSM is a more inward, cathartic record than its predecessor, its heartland-scale arrangements now carrying real emotional weight. Synths, guitars and pedal steel swell around Ross's soft, conversational voice.
lineage: A personal, health-crisis-driven turn within Wild Pink's pedal-steel-and-synth heartland sound.

description: Gabe Birnbaum's band shares out lead vocals over extended, guitar-forward jams and replayable choruses. It is a generous, collaborative record built for a full band stretching out live. It suits listeners who like storytelling songs with big, harmonized guitar breaks.
lineage: Sounds indebted to 1970s long-solo rock and New York indie songwriting.

description: St. Louis's second album opens up her stark debut into brighter, more orchestral arrangements of strings, piano and fingerpicked guitar. It trades the gritty apparitions of her first record for patient, present-tense contentment, sung in her low, unhurried voice.
lineage: Connects directly to the Woodsist label that released her debut, and sounds of a piece with the West Coast singer-songwriter circle of Jess Williamson and Kacey Johansing.

description: Yonder is Arbor Labor Union's most introspective, nocturnal record, cleaner and more inward than the kaleidoscopic New Petal Instants but no less indebted to the Allmans and Neil Young. Unhurried guitar lines wind around each other at walking tempos, suited to late-night listening.
lineage: A quieter turn within Arbor Labor Union's catalog that still sounds drawn from the same Dead/Allman Brothers well as their earlier fuzzed-out records.

description: A provocatively titled record built around long guitar-solo epics, closer to Hanson's Wand side than his quieter solo debut. Country-rock tempos and pedal steel still anchor the songs even as the guitar playing stretches out at length. It suits listeners who want shredding that still feels warm and melodic.
lineage: Reconnects Hanson's solo work to long-form guitar jamming that sounds indebted to the Dead and Crazy Horse.

description: The self-titled album pares Cut Worms' sound back to a leaner, more direct country-pop. Melodies stay bright and hooky, riding on the same twangy, harmony-laden guitar interplay as his earlier work. It reads as a mid-career consolidation rather than a reinvention, for fans of sweet, retro-minded songcraft.
lineage: Keeps Cut Worms in a country-pop vein that sounds indebted to the Everly Brothers and Gram Parsons, as across his whole catalog.

description: Warm harmony vocals sit against loose, breezy guitar arrangements on this full-length. The songs move at an easy tempo somewhere between cosmic country and dream-pop, with fingerpicked acoustic lines and a gentle drawl. It suits listeners who like soft, sunlit harmony songwriting.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Laurel Canyon-style harmony songwriting filtered through DIY self-release culture.

description: A relatively lean, upbeat record with brighter tempos and some of Taylor's most direct choruses. Pedal steel and harmony vocals sit up front, in keeping with the buttery, breezy sound that defines his Merge catalog. It suits fans who want Hiss Golden Messenger at its most sunny and hook-driven.
lineage: A late-period return to a communal, road-band version of Hiss Golden Messenger's cosmic country, sounding indebted to the Band and Grateful Dead country rock.

description: Silverstein alternates expansive pedal-steel-laced instrumentals with songs sung in a delivery pitched between Bill Callahan's deadpan and Kurt Vile's drift. It's cosmic country in the vein of Beachwood Sparks and Silver Jews, slow and sunlit.
lineage: Sounds of a piece with the Pacific Northwest cosmic-country instrumentalists around Rose City Band, sharing their pedal-steel drift.

description: Williamson's most fully country-identified record, with pedal steel, warm harmonies, and road-song imagery throughout. It works through the end of one relationship and the start of another with plainspoken directness, her voice sitting close and unhurried over two-step and ballad tempos. It suits listeners who want classic country feeling from an indie-bred songwriter.
lineage: Brings Williamson's cosmic-country sound closest to what sounds like Gram Parsons and outlaw-country roots; she also records with Katie Crutchfield as Plains.

description: A gentle, warmly produced set of songs about distance and homecoming, Year Away favors soft-focus folk-pop arrangements over the twangier end of the C6 sound. It's closer to a hushed Laurel Canyon lullaby than a jam band, for listeners who want close harmonies and patient tempos.
lineage: Sounds of a piece with the West Coast singer-songwriter circle around Anna St. Louis and Jess Williamson, sharing their soft-focus Laurel Canyon warmth.

description: A relaxed set that continues the duo's front-porch harmony sound with a slightly fuller band arrangement. Intertwined acoustic guitars and unhurried tempos keep the mood warm and easy. It suits listeners who like classic California country rock played with gentle sincerity.
lineage: Extends Mapache's ongoing homage to what sounds like Flying Burrito Brothers-style California country rock.

description: Davis's harp anchors a full-band record that weaves '60s pop melodies, psychedelia and driving folk rock. Steel guitar and close harmonies give it a country-rock backbone, and the band's interplay recalls Fleetwood Mac at their most collaborative. It suits listeners who want sunny, harmony-rich rock with a cosmic tilt.
lineage: Leans into a harmony-driven jam-pop sound that sounds akin to the Grateful Dead's gentler side and Fleetwood Mac.

description: A tighter, hookier set than its predecessors, with the band sounding fully locked in. Pedal steel and harmonized guitars balance sunlit pop songcraft with room to stretch out at breezy, anthemic tempos. It suits listeners who want cosmic country at its most concise and summery.
lineage: Part of Rose City Band's steady evolution of a cosmic-country template that sounds indebted to Gram Parsons and the Grateful Dead.

description: Mapache's Sam Blasucci steps out solo, trading intertwined acoustic guitars for piano and writing autobiographical songs about settling into adult life. Close harmonies and hushed, breezy arrangements keep it intimate. It suits listeners who like gentle, diaristic singer-songwriter records.
lineage: A solo detour from Blasucci's work in the California country duo Mapache.

description: Burton's second album trades some of I Can Go With You's stark folk for fuller, Laurel Canyon-style arrangements, with pedal steel and strings framing his warm, unhurried baritone. It's gentler and more polished than the debut without losing its plainspoken sadness.
lineage: Moves Burton from the Tompkins Square country-folk revival roster to Partisan, with a sound indebted to '70s LA soft country rock.

description: James Wallace's kaleidoscopic project mixes piano-led psychedelic rock with dense, spacey arrangements and strings. Opaque, mystic lyrics sit over swampy, soulful, gospel-tinged production. It suits listeners who want anthemic, cosmic songwriting with a spiritual bent.
lineage: Sounds indebted to 1970s gospel-tinged psychedelic rock and cosmic country.

description: Cullum's second Coin Collection album pulls further from his English folk-rock reference points toward stranger, more subconscious songwriting, with layered arrangements from Nashville players. It keeps the pedal-steel-led warmth while hiding its influences further from view.
lineage: A step deeper into Nashville's instrumentalist underground, still rooted in Cullum's pedal-steel session background.

description: Woods' 2023 album settles into a warm, unhurried guitar-band sound full of long fades, loops and gently interlocking leads. Two decades in, it plays like a settled, confident restatement of what the band and the Woodsist label have stood for. It suits listeners who like hazy, patient psych-folk.
lineage: A late-career synthesis of the Woods catalog, still released on Jeremy Earl's own Woodsist label, whose scene it sounds central to.

description: The 2000s cosmic-country revivalists' first album in over a decade, mixing pedal-steel-laced country rock with the band's longtime dreamy, harmony-driven sound. The songs drift at easy tempos with jangling guitars and soft group vocals. It is a warm late-career return for fans of their early records.
lineage: A late-career return from one of the foundational 2000s cosmic-country revival bands (C6); their sound is indebted to V21 country rock and the Paisley Underground's jangle.

description: Made with contributions from Jeff Parker and Josh Johnson, this record keeps Cohen's subdued psychedelia while adding jazzier color and understated hooks. It moves through hazy, mysterious moods without ever raising its volume. It marked Cohen's move from Captured Tracks to Hardly Art.
lineage: Extends Cohen's breezy, Laurel Canyon-adjacent pop songwriting into jazzier arrangements, deepening a catalog that has quietly run in parallel to the wider cosmic-country revival.

description: Color Green's second album is a meditation on grief and clarity delivered through loose, live-feeling jams, from the hush of '5:08' to the sprawling 'Kick the Bucket.' Guitars trade lines and voices stack into harmonies the way a band that treats every gig as improvisation would.
lineage: Sounds indebted to '60s SoCal folk-rock and the Dead/Allmans jam vocabulary, delivered with a live-band looseness.

description: Wilder Maker frontman Gabriel Birnbaum's solo album mines character studies of quiet desperation over lush, psychedelic-tinged folk-rock, closer to Paul Simon's narrative songcraft than his main band's more experimental side. It's a mature, unhurried record built on empathetic detail.
lineage: A solo outlet for the Wilder Maker frontman that leans further into plainspoken, character-driven folk-rock storytelling.

description: A debut LP from a loose LA collective, Aventurine spreads out into sprawling, heady grooves that recall electric-era Miles Davis and Can as much as the Dead. Its jam-length instrumental patience and synth textures put it at the far cosmic edge of this lane.
lineage: Sounds like the cosmic-jam end of the scene stretched into krautrock and fusion territory, indebted to Can and electric Miles as much as the Dead.

description: Kate Bollinger's kaleidoscopic full-length debut ranges from homespun folk songs to warmly psychedelic rock. Her airy soprano and jazzy, organic arrangements give it a Laurel Canyon-adjacent glow.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Françoise Hardy, the Velvet Underground and Teenage Fanclub as much as country, landing at the pop-facing edge of this lane's '70s revival strand.

description: Baggett makes crunchy, warm Crazy Horse-style rock here, all snaking guitar solos and B3 organ. It sits comfortably alongside the mellower, jam-friendly end of this lane, for listeners who like their fuzz relaxed.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Crazy Horse's loose guitar rock, filtered through the relaxed sensibility of West Coast lo-fi songwriters like Little Wings.

description: Sam Cantor's Chicago band mixes alt-country songwriting with adventurous, Dead-like guitar theatrics and pedal steel. Storytelling lyrics sit over harmonized guitars that stretch out without losing the songs. It suits listeners who want Midwestern alt-country with a cosmic streak.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Grateful Dead and Crazy Horse guitar playing filtered through Midwestern alt-country songwriting.

description: Rosali's Merge Records debut, again with Nance's Mowed Sound band, elaborates elliptical folk songs into full-bodied guitar rock reminiscent of Yo La Tengo or Neil Young. Her voice carries a mesmerizing pull in the vein of Sandy Denny or Will Oldham, over long solos and harmonized guitars.
lineage: The full flowering of her Mowed Sound collaboration, moving her from DIY folk circles onto a larger indie label.

description: Sam Owens's fourth album as Sam Evian chases a warm, early-1970s Laurel Canyon feel across loose, groove-driven songs. Soft vocals, relaxed tempos and a live-band warmth make it for listeners who like cosmic-country-tinged soft rock.
lineage: A Catskills singer-songwriter whose sound is indebted to the Laurel Canyon and Gram Parsons-adjacent cosmic-country lineage.

description: An Auckland quartet's sophomore LP mixes desert twang, brooding psych atmospherics and country phrasing into immersive, dynamically wide-ranging arrangements. It swings between rowdy and delicate, for listeners who like cosmic country with a darker, more atmospheric edge.
lineage: Part of a small but growing Antipodean cosmic-country scene taking the Dead/Beachwood Sparks lineage outside the US.

description: Down Home is a Dead-inspired set of psychedelic twang, warm, loose and collaborative in feel. Its front-porch take on cosmic country favors easy grooves, harmonies and winding guitar over polish.
lineage: Sounds of a piece with Nashville's Dead-indebted country-rock scene around acts like Coin Collection and Rich Ruth.

description: A follow-up live set drawn from the I Don't Live Here Anymore tour, again showing how songs built in the studio around layered synths and guitar loops unfurl even longer on stage. Adam Granduciel's guitar solos get plenty of room to stretch.
lineage: Second entry in the Live Drugs series, continuing the band's arena-scale guitar rock, which sounds indebted to Crazy Horse and Dylan, in concert form.

description: Dylan Young's Way Dynamic studies mellow '70s songwriting in the Carole King, Jackson Browne, Harry Nilsson and Todd Rundgren mode, dressed in baroque-pop string arrangements. It is playful and melodic rather than jam-heavy, closer to chamber-pop revivalism than Dead-style sprawl.
lineage: Young also leads the Melbourne band Cool Sounds; here he channels what sounds like '70s Laurel Canyon songcraft into a minimalist folk-pop frame.

description: Wild Pink's fifth album trades some of ILYSM's studio polish for a rougher, heavier rock palette. The title track is a fist-raising ode to moving on, with louder guitars and a more direct band sound than before.
lineage: Wild Pink's rawest, most rock-forward record to date, still carrying the heartland/pedal-steel DNA of their Royal Mountain years.

description: Ada Lea's third album is her most playful and breezy, trading the moodier indie rock of her earlier records for '70s Laurel Canyon folk warmth and slice-of-life humor under a Dylan-borrowed title. Alexandra Levy's plainspoken voice carries loose, sun-drenched arrangements built for driving.
lineage: Sounds like a late turn toward Cosmic American Music textures for a Montreal songwriter previously closer to art-rock; it sits alongside Kate Bollinger and Courtney Marie Andrews' own Laurel Canyon-leaning records in this lane.

description: A short follow-up EP to Yonder that keeps the same winding, left-field guitar grooves and Dead-indebted chord changes in a tighter package. The playing is crunchy and unpredictable, a quick fix for fans of the band's longer records.
lineage: A compact continuation of Arbor Labor Union's post-Yonder sound, still sounding indebted to the Dead/Allman Brothers vein.

description: Interior Live Oak returns to the more economical song structures of McCombs' earlier records while keeping his prime-era wit and melodic ease. Relaxed guitars and his low, conversational voice give it a warm, unhurried feel. It's a hopeful, clarifying record from an artist who's spent two decades circling extremes.
lineage: Marks McCombs' return to Domino after his ANTI- Records albums, circling back to his earlier songwriting style.

description: A full swerve from Hanson's scorching guitar-rock records into piano-led, orchestral balladry in the Nashville Sound mold, carrying sarcastic, well-built songs. It keeps the breezy tempos of his earlier work while trading long solos for lusher, more classic-country arrangement. It is his most stylistically surprising solo record, for fans of wry, lushly dressed songcraft.
lineage: Bends Hanson's solo catalog toward orchestration that sounds indebted to the classic Nashville Sound.

description: A self-released Los Angeles record built on warm, breezy guitar interplay and easygoing tempos in the Dead-revival mode. The songwriting stays understated rather than showy, favoring feel over flash.
lineage: Part of the same self-released, Dead-indebted West Coast guitar-band underground as Garcia Peoples and Cass McCombs' looser records.

description: This self-titled record blends Radiohead-style atmospherics with Nilsson-esque psychedelic pop and woozy, pub-rock-adjacent Americana. Synths and pedal steel drift together at breezy, hushed tempos. It suits listeners who like country textures pushed into dreamy, experimental pop.
lineage: Sounds akin to Nashville's instrumentalist-led cosmic country scene (Rich Ruth, Spencer Cullum), taken in a more song-based, psychedelic-pop direction.

description: Glyders' second full-length was flagged by Josh Terry as a forthcoming record to watch, continuing the duo's mix of breezy, harmony-driven guitar pop and cosmic-country tempos. It builds on Maria's Hunt with slightly fuller, more anthemic arrangements. The band remains a self-released Chicago project more than a decade after forming.
lineage: Continues Glyders' Laurel Canyon-indebted harmony songwriting within Chicago's independent DIY scene.

description: Cohen's fourth album, made with partner and producer Sam Evian at their Catskills studio Flying Cloud, is a hazy collage of memory built from years of home recording. Its soft-focus folk-pop favors atmosphere over hooks, with hushed vocals floating over gentle acoustic and keyboard textures.
lineage: Grows out of the Flying Cloud/Sam Evian Catskills recording circle, the upstate-New York studio and label run by her partner.

description: Kazar's second solo LP is cozy, conversational folk-rock in a New Morning and Wings register, with pedal steel and fiddle threading through warm, unhurried songs about everyday intimacy. It suits listeners who like homey, melodic 1970s-style songcraft.
lineage: Continues Kazar's post-Due North songwriting in a mode that sounds indebted to early-'70s Dylan and Paul McCartney.

description: Johnson's most emotionally shadowed Rose City Band record, letting a melancholy undertone sit alongside the band's usual sun-kissed grooves. Pedal steel remains the glinting through-line, with long, harmonized guitar solos stretching over relaxed tempos. It suits listeners who like their cosmic country with a dusk-colored edge.
lineage: The latest chapter in Johnson's long arc from Wooden Shjips/Moon Duo psych-drone to widescreen cosmic country.

description: An airy, piano-led set that trades some of Off My Stars' folk directness for a more sophisticated pop croon. Tasteful rather than showy, it continues Blasucci's move away from Mapache's guitar-forward sound.
lineage: Follows Off My Stars in the solo evolution of Mapache member Blasucci away from the duo format.

description: Thompson's debut full-band LP trades some of his earlier twang for exploratory, cosmic territory, with easygoing songs about country living and long drives. It is a step forward from the project's 2022 self-titled EP, built around his guitar playing and loose, jam-friendly arrangements.
lineage: Builds on Thompson's Nashville session career and his earlier Weird Ears EPs into a fuller cosmic-country-jam statement.

description: An instrumental trio's debut built from long-drive jamming with pedal steel, guitar, and synths. It luxuriates in kosmische, ambient and jazz-fusion textures rather than song structure, Dead-adjacent in spirit but closer to Alice Coltrane or Ashra in execution. It suits listeners who want slow, glowing instrumental music.
lineage: Sounds akin to Nashville's instrumentalist-led cosmic country, with debts to kosmische and spiritual jazz.

description: A playful cosmic-pop record that sits somewhere between New Riders of the Purple Sage and the Clientele, released on the Curation label. Pedal steel from Luke Schneider and flute from Rex Gregory widen the band's palette beyond their glammier debut.
lineage: Deepens Silver Synthetic's turn from garage punk toward cosmic country, aligning them with the Curation Records/Beachwood Sparks lineage.

description: A return to fuller, more assured songwriting after SPARK's detour into synths, Small Talk puts Whitney's warm country-soul back at the center. The horns and Julien Ehrlich's falsetto are still the core of the sound, delivered with more confidence and a gentle pedal-steel sheen.
lineage: A confident late-career synthesis of Whitney's country-soul debut and their more expansive mid-period records.

description: A brief, folk-based debut built on plucked strings and a mallet-driven pulse, with playful, transcendental lyrics floating over spare, exploratory arrangements. The mood is spectral and cosmic, a little spooky despite its lullaby-like gentleness. It suits listeners who want hushed, spiritual folk-pop to sink into.
lineage: A hushed, folk-song take on cosmic music that sounds closer to Vashti Bunyan than to full-band jam-rock.

description: Angela Autumn folds American folk and bluegrass roots into a hybridized, big-sounding record on Believer, blending indie, psychedelia and gothic country. Twangy picking sits under heavy, reverb-washed production. It suits listeners who like old-time roots pushed toward the psychedelic.
lineage: Sounds rooted in Appalachian old-time and bluegrass tradition, recast through the 2020s cosmic-country revival's bigger, more psychedelic production.

description: Valentine finds Courtney Marie Andrews leaning further into ornate, Laurel Canyon-styled folk, her Ronstadt-range voice wrapped in ethereal harmonies and a warm, '70s Nashville palette. Slow-rolling piano, pedal steel and brushed drums keep it intimate, for fans of classic country-folk heartbreak.
lineage: The latest chapter for a songwriter who stays close to the Cosmic American Music revival this lane tracks, sounding indebted to '70s Ronstadt and Emmylou Harris records.

description: Davis's debut draws on pristine Laurel Canyon songwriting from the '60s and '70s and dresses it in gentle country phrasing, all warm harmonies and unhurried tempos. It reads as a straight continuation of the soft-rock/country-rock lineage this lane traces back to.
lineage: A newer voice working directly in the Laurel Canyon/country-rock tradition that feeds this lane, closer to '70s soft rock than jam-band twang.

description: Samuels' songs sit somewhere between wry confessional folk and loose country rock, working through coming-of-age memory with a deadpan, conversational delivery. It's plainspoken songwriting in the Drag City tradition dressed in warmer, twangier arrangements.
lineage: Part of the LA singer-songwriter circle overlapping several C6/C5 field-guide artists, working the same funny-sad songwriting vein as the Drag City deadpan school.

description: Streetsweeper is a tranquil, piano-and-guitar record from Andrews' long-running Yawns project. It's quieter and more contemplative than his fuller band records, closer to Little Wings' loose, handmade songwriting, for listeners who like soft-spoken, homespun songs.
lineage: The latest entry in Andrews' long-running solo project, which sounds close to Little Wings' loose DIY songwriting.

description: Morby's latest album works in a bucolic folk-rock palette, continuing the warm, unhurried style of This Is a Photograph with an even more pastoral, near-spiritual tone. Pedal steel and acoustic textures dominate over the breezy tempos. It suits listeners who want gentle, open-hearted songwriting.
lineage: Extends Morby's Dead Oceans-era folk-rock songwriting, which sounds indebted to Dylan and cosmic country.

description: A 'canyon country' record that balances light and dark more explicitly than Davis's earlier work while keeping her harp and full-band folk-rock sound intact. Harmonized guitars and road-song imagery push it toward neo-western country rock. It suits listeners who like breezy, anthemic California-style songwriting.
lineage: Continues Davis's arc from harp-led pop toward songwriting that sounds indebted to Laurel Canyon and cosmic country.

description: Recorded at Chicago's Thawed Out festival, this live document catches Sam Cantor's band stretching their warm, Dead-adjacent country-rock songs out on stage. Guitars trade lines over an easy groove, for fans who want the band looser than on record.
lineage: A live snapshot of Chicago's small cosmic-country scene, sounding close to the city's guitar-forward underground around acts like Ryley Walker.

description: Cogan's Sacred Bones record mixes haunted folk, psych rock and a shadowy strain of country. Pedal steel and mandolin ground the record's smoky, '70s-inflected atmosphere, with her voice hushed and drawling. It suits listeners who like their country dark and dreamlike.
lineage: A shift for Cogan from her earlier dream-folk toward country and psych-rock textures that sound akin to the wider cosmic-country revival.

description: The third entry in pedal-steel player Spencer Cullum's Coin Collection series, built around English folklore. Pedal steel and fingerpicked acoustic guitar drift through a kaleidoscopic, hushed mix of folk, jazz and pop. It suits listeners who like pastoral, gently psychedelic folk.
lineage: An English-born Nashville pedal-steel player's solo series, sounding indebted to English folk-rock and pulled into a cosmic-country frame.

description: Ballgame's full-length debut sets warm, '70s-inflected songwriting inside commanding, theatrical vocal performances and tasteful, non-pastiche arrangements. It leans closer to Laurel Canyon soft-rock revivalism than jam-band twang, but fits the same '70s-revival umbrella.
lineage: A newer entry in the '70s soft-rock/country-rock revival that runs alongside this lane's jammier, Dead-descended wing.

description: Way Dynamic continues Dylan Young's painstaking attention to '70s-styled folk-rock harmonies and drum sounds, mixing sincere songwriting with oddball funk detours. Strings and close harmonies keep the mood hushed and breezy.
lineage: Continues Young's Melbourne chamber-pop lineage established on Duck and So Familiar.

description: Vile's debut is a hazy, homespun collection of fingerpicked drones and mumbled melodies recorded largely at home. It set the template for his sleepy-eyed guitar style before Matador came calling, for listeners who want the slacker-rock revival at its most unpolished origin point.
lineage: Grew out of the Philadelphia scene around the War on Drugs, which Vile co-founded; its haze sounds like a direct precursor to the countrygaze and slacker records of the 2010s.

description: Vile's Matador debut adds full-band muscle and squalling guitar solos to his stoned drawl, making it one of the most rock-and-roll records in his catalog. The driving opener 'Hunchback' shows him leaning into Crazy Horse-style fuzz. It's the record where the War on Drugs alum became a solo guitar hero in his own right.
lineage: Signing to Matador connected Vile's Philly lo-fi scene to the wider indie-rock world, and its sound looks ahead to the 2010s slacker and jangle revival.

description: A compilation of early home-recorded tracks that bridges Constant Hitmaker and his Matador debut, showing the same murmured vocals and unhurried acoustic-electric picking before a full band thickened his sound. It's a stopgap for completists tracing his rise from bedroom tapes to indie stardom.
lineage: Part of the same lo-fi Philadelphia tape underground that produced Constant Hitmaker; a bridge into the more full-band Matador era.

description: A hazy, reverb-soaked debut about suburban New Jersey boredom, built on interlocking clean-toned guitar lines and unhurried tempos. A foundational record for the 2010s jangle revival.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Flying Nun/Feelies-style jangle guitar pop; a key node connecting classic jangle to the 2010s slacker/jangle scene.

description: Another early self-recorded Bandcamp album from Alex G's prolific pre-label period, built from warbling home-studio pop songs and pitched vocal manipulation. The songwriting is skeletal and the fidelity is intentionally rough, but melodic hooks poke through the murk. It's for listeners tracing the earliest roots of his songwriting before Domino signed him.
lineage: Shares the same DIY home-recording aesthetic as Winner, part of the flood of Bandcamp full-lengths that built his cult following before DSU broke through.

description: One of Alex Giannascoli's earliest self-released Bandcamp full-lengths, built from home recordings with warped, pitch-shifted vocals and drum-machine loops. It's rougher and stranger than the records that made him famous but already shows his knack for a warped melodic hook, for deep-catalog listeners.
lineage: Part of the early-2010s Bandcamp lo-fi boom, the self-released run that fed directly into DSU and the rest of his catalog.

description: The Melbourne band's debut is loose, plainspoken jangle-pop full of local color and wry deadpan vocals. Drawled, small-town observations sit over relaxed, chiming guitars, a key early record of the 2010s Australian slacker-pop scene.
lineage: Sounds descended from Flying Nun jangle, by way of Melbourne's Chapter Music scene.

description: A quieter, more assured record than its predecessor, built on fingerpicked acoustic figures and Vile's half-asleep drawl, this is often cited as his creative breakthrough. It slows the tempos down and lets the songwriting carry the weight rather than the guitar pyrotechnics. It's the album that turned casual fans into believers ahead of his commercial peak.
lineage: Refines the Crazy Horse-and-folk hybrid of Childish Prodigy into the more meditative style that would define his Wakin on a Pretty Daze and B'lieve I'm Goin Down eras.

description: Parquet Courts' scrappy, self-released debut, full of talky, deadpan vocals and loose, Pavement-indebted guitar interplay recorded on the cheap.
lineage: A direct extension of Pavement's slacker guitar-pop songwriting into a Brooklyn DIY setting.

description: A cleaner, more melodic refinement of the band's suburban jangle-pop sound. Warm, mid-tempo guitar interplay sits under gentle, nostalgic lyrics, for listeners who like their indie rock hazy and summery.
lineage: Continues Real Estate's jangle catalog, which sounds indebted to Flying Nun and the Feelies.

description: A hazy, unhurried debut of ramshackle jangle-pop from Melbourne, indebted to the Flying Nun and Feelies sound. The vocals are offhand and half-mumbled, for listeners who like their guitar pop loose and sunlit.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Flying Nun jangle-pop and the Go-Betweens/Clean lineage; part of the same 2010s Australian guitar-pop wave as Rolling Blackouts Coastal Fever and The Goon Sax.

description: A collection of short, murky home recordings that lean further into the pitched-vocal manipulation and tape-hiss atmosphere that became his early trademark. Songs blur together into a woozy, half-remembered whole rather than standing as individual singles. It's a transitional record for fans tracking his path toward DSU's breakout.
lineage: Sits in the same self-released Bandcamp run as Winner and Race, the DIY foundation that eventually caught Orchid Tapes' and then Domino's attention.

description: The last of Alex G's run of purely self-released Bandcamp full-lengths before signing to Orchid Tapes, still built on lo-fi four-track pop songs with warped, childlike vocals. Melodically it's a bit more confident than Rules, hinting at the songwriting leap DSU would make. It's for listeners who want the full arc of his self-taught bedroom period.
lineage: Closes out the self-released Bandcamp era that set up his signing to Orchid Tapes for DSU and eventually Domino Recording Co.

description: DeMarco's Captured Tracks debut coined the woozy, chorus-pedal 'jizz jazz' sound that defined blog-era slacker rock: loose, warbly guitar lines, half-mumbled vocals and a stoned, unhurried tempo throughout. It set the template for a decade of goofball-slacker singer-songwriters.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Pavement's shambling guitar pop and Flying Nun-style DIY jangle; its own influence on the 2010s slacker-rock and bedroom-pop wave that followed is well established.

description: The breakout record: rambling, funny, deadpan talk-singing over tight guitar interplay that recalls Pavement and the Modern Lovers. It is half stream-of-consciousness and half punk energy, with songs like 'Stoned and Starving' stretching into wiry jams.
lineage: Sounds like the clearest 2010s inheritor of Pavement's slacker guitar-pop songwriting.

description: Allison Crutchfield and Kyle Gilbride's band debuts with scrappy, fuzzed-out guitar-pop that splits the difference between 90s indie rock and Philly basement-punk. Direct, unpolished and hook-driven.
lineage: Grows out of the same Philadelphia DIY scene as Waxahatchee and Radiator Hospital, with a guitar-pop sound that seems indebted to Pavement and GBV.

description: Katie Crutchfield's bedroom-recorded debut, written and tracked in a week at her family home, is just acoustic guitar and a cracked, plainspoken voice working through devastation and longing. It is the rawest end of the slacker/DIY spectrum this lane covers, closer to a diary than a studio record.
lineage: Grows out of the DIY punk and cassette/Bandcamp network Crutchfield came up in, and sounds indebted to the deadpan funny-sad songwriting line; it seeds her entire catalog, including her later, more country-leaning work covered elsewhere in this atlas.

description: A compilation pairing Barnett's first two self-released EPs, introducing her rambling, deadpan talk-singing and wry observational lyrics to an international audience for the first time. The guitar tone is loose and unpolished, closer to garage rock than the more produced records that followed. It's the release that put her on critics' radars before her proper debut LP.
lineage: Grows out of Melbourne's DIY scene and Barnett's own Milk! Records label, the base for the deadpan Australian songwriting wave around her.

description: This second Dick Diver LP is loose, warm and conversational, built on ringing guitars and half-sung, half-spoken vocals in the vein of the Go-Betweens and the Clean. It's a high point of the early-2010s Melbourne jangle-pop revival, for fans who want the sound that shaped a wave of Australian slacker-pop bands.
lineage: Grew out of Melbourne's Chapter Music scene alongside Boomgates and Twerps; its sound feels like a template for later Melbourne jangle bands such as Chook Race.

description: Vile's fifth album stretches sun-baked slacker rock into sprawling, double-LP length, blending gorgeous fingerpicking with heavy guitar drift. The mood is unhurried and half-stoned, closer to a daydream than a statement. It is the record where his Pavement/Crazy Horse-indebted sound became widescreen.
lineage: Vile was a founding member of The War on Drugs in Philadelphia; his sound here seems descended from Pavement's loose-limbed guitar rock and Neil Young's amp-drone side.

description: Sam Cook-Parrott's project delivers scrappy, hissy, hook-filled songs with a plainspoken, earnest voice at the center. It is unpretentious DIY power-pop-punk in the classic Philly basement mold.
lineage: Part of the same Philadelphia DIY network as Swearin' and Waxahatchee, with a lo-fi guitar-pop sound that recalls Guided by Voices.

description: Sadie Dupuis's knotty, GBV/Pavement-indebted guitar riffs collide with tossed-off, sardonic lyrics across a record that swings between melody and noise. A key 2010s document of the slacker-noise-rock crossover.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Guided by Voices/Pavement's loud-quiet guitar-pop songwriting.

description: A noisier, more layered second record, with dual songwriters Allison Crutchfield and Kyle Gilbride trading lead vocals. Dense, fuzzed guitar interplay drives short, urgent songs built for basement shows.
lineage: Continues Swearin's Philadelphia DIY guitar-pop songwriting, which sounds indebted to Pavement and GBV.

description: Twin Peaks' scrappy debut is all ragged garage-jangle riffs and teenage swagger. Short, shouted songs and loose, bashing drums capture a young Chicago band playing fast and not overthinking it.
lineage: Rooted in Chicago's teenage DIY scene, with a sound that recalls garage rock and Pavement-style slacker guitar-pop.

description: Recorded at home with Swearin's Kyle Gilbride, this is a fuller-sounding but still homemade record about family, addiction and young adulthood in Alabama. The song-to-song shift between fragile acoustic pieces and full-band fuzz set the template for a decade of Waxahatchee records.
lineage: Extends American Weekend's DIY lo-fi songwriting with Swearin'-band muscle; a key transitional record between bedroom-pop slacker rock and Crutchfield's later, more countryish songwriting.

description: Alex G's breakthrough, a warm and melodic leap from his earlier tapes released by Orchid Tapes, mixing pitch-shifted vocals with genuinely gorgeous pop songwriting. It's still lo-fi but far more melodically assured than his self-released run. It's the record most people point to as his arrival as a songwriter to watch.
lineage: The culmination of his self-released Bandcamp period, and the record that plugged him into the Orchid Tapes/bedroom-pop scene before Domino signed him.

description: DeMarco's best-known record is a warmer, more melodic take on his slacker sound, about the anxieties of encroaching adulthood delivered with a shrug. The title track and 'Passing Out Pieces' became blog-rock standards.
lineage: Refines the '2' blueprint into DeMarco's signature sound; a touchstone for the 2010s jangle/slacker revival.

description: Nigel Chapman's conversational, half-spoken vocals ride over loose, unhurried jangle-rock guitar, closer to Jonathan Richman or Silver Jews than most of their slacker-rock peers. Bookish, philosophical lyrics over simple, warm arrangements.
lineage: Sounds indebted to the deadpan funny-sad songwriting line (Silver Jews/Drag City) crossed with VU-style jangle guitar; the start of one of the decade's most consistent guitar-rock runs.

description: A kinetic Chicago DIY debut mixing jangly, interlocking guitar lines with garage-rock urgency. It is the first half of a strong two-album run, for listeners who like their jangle fast and loud.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Flying Nun/Feelies jangle crossed with garage-rock energy, rooted in Chicago's DIY venue scene.

description: A denser, more collaborative record built on Cook-Parrott's plainspoken, hook-first songwriting. Short, bright pop-punk songs about love and small humiliations fly by, for fans of basement-show intimacy.
lineage: Continues Radiator Hospital's lo-fi pop-punk songwriting within the Philadelphia DIY scene, with a sound that recalls Guided by Voices.

description: Released while the band was still called Sports, this self-released debut is scrappy, hooky basement pop-punk. Fast, fuzzy guitars and wry, confessional lyrics set up everything the band would polish later.
lineage: Sounds indebted to GBV/Pavement guitar-pop songwriting by way of the East Coast DIY scene.

description: A Busan band's debut full-length, applying warm, ringing jangle-pop guitar tones to plainspoken, sea-town songwriting. It is the start of a consistently pristine throwback indie-rock run, understated and melodic.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Flying Nun/Byrds-style jangle-pop, transplanted to the Korean indie scene.

description: A tighter, more craft-oriented second LP that mixes ragged jangle-pop with rowdy garage energy. Multiple singer-songwriters trade short, catchy songs, making it the band's most instantly fun record.
lineage: Continuation of Twin Peaks' garage-jangle songwriting, moving toward wider recognition.

description: Warehouse's self-released debut is a kinetic, interlocking-guitar record fronted by Elaine Edenfield's commanding, sing-shouted vocals. It sits closer to Sonic Youth's angularity than to straightforward jangle-pop, but is still built on tightly wound guitar jams, for fans of wiry post-punk.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Sonic Youth's interlocking-guitar vocabulary, part of the Atlanta post-punk/jangle underground.

description: Alex G's Domino debut pushes his warped pop songs into stranger, more processed territory, with pitch-bent vocals sitting alongside skeletal drum machines and unsettling interludes. It's a deliberately harder listen than DSU, trading immediacy for atmosphere. It's for fans who like the unease under his prettiest melodies.
lineage: First release for Domino after his Bandcamp/Orchid Tapes run, expanding his cult audience while keeping the same bedroom-pop DNA.

description: Will Toledo's Matador debut re-records and remasters highlights from his sprawling self-released Bandcamp catalog, bringing his hyper-verbal, deadpan songwriting to a wider audience for the first time. It's noisier and more chaotic than his later full-band records. It's for fans curious how his bedroom-era songs sounded once given an actual budget.
lineage: Bridges Toledo's run of self-released Bandcamp albums with the full-band Matador era that produced Teens of Denial and beyond.

description: A tightly recorded set of plainspoken, jangling Melbourne guitar pop, in the same scene as Dick Diver. Deadpan vocals and short songs keep it brisk and unfussy.
lineage: Sounds descended from Flying Nun jangle, within Melbourne's jangle-pop scene.

description: Barnett's debut is a wry, rambling slacker-rock landmark, its deadpan run-on lyrics detailing house-hunting anxiety ('Depreston') and open-mic dread ('Pedestrian at Best'). Loose, twangy guitars and a conversational drawl carry the songs.
lineage: Sounds heir to Pavement's talky slacker rock, alongside Australian jangle peers like Dick Diver.

description: A more introspective turn with banjo and piano alongside the guitars, led by the single 'Pretty Pimpin'. Vile's cracked, mumbling delivery and stream-of-consciousness lyrics stay pure slacker even as the arrangements soften toward folk.
lineage: Sounds akin to the Pavement-to-Silver Jews thread of deadpan funny-sad songwriting, in a more folk-inflected register.

description: Remember Sports' second album and first for Father/Daughter tightens the basement pop-punk of their Kenyon College beginnings into brisk, hook-first songs. Carmen Perry's elastic voice leads scrappy, fast guitar-pop that suits fans of loose, energetic DIY indie rock.
lineage: The scrappy basement pop-punk starting point of Remember Sports' own arc, which grows toward the more collaborative, fuller songwriting of Slow Buzz and Like a Stone.

description: A more confident, bigger-sounding follow-up, with Dupuis's guitar leads pushed further forward and her lyrics turning more pointed and political. Still rooted in the band's angular, GBV-descended riffing.
lineage: Continuation of Speedy Ortiz's Pavement/GBV-indebted noise-pop songwriting.

description: A more polished, dreamier follow-up, with brighter production but the same loose jangle songwriting at its core. Male and female vocals trade off over chiming guitars, keeping the debut's casual charm.
lineage: Continues Twerps' jangle-pop, which sounds indebted to Flying Nun and the Go-Betweens.

description: Waxahatchee's Merge debut loosens the structure further, mixing drum machines and organ drones into the guitar songs for a woozier, more experimental slacker record. It is the least polished-sounding of her Merge albums and the closest to classic 90s indie rock.
lineage: Bridges Cerulean Salt's basement sound with a more expansive, era-blurring indie rock palette; part of the same Merge-era run that established Crutchfield as an indie rock and later Americana songwriter.

description: Will Toledo's first full-band studio album turns Bandcamp-honed bedroom pop into classic-rock-scaled narrative rock, nodding to the Cars, Pavement and Jonathan Richman. It is a sprawling, self-lacerating song cycle of long, anthemic, funny-sad songs.
lineage: Toledo self-released many albums on Bandcamp before signing to Matador; the result sounds fused with Pavement's slacker irony.

description: Casper Skulls' debut EP introduces the Toronto band's dual-vocal, college-rock-indebted guitar pop, drawing on Pavement and R.E.M.-style jangle with conversational, story-driven lyrics. It's shorter and scrappier than their later full-lengths but sets the band's voice from the start. It's for fans who want the earliest version of their sound.
lineage: Part of Toronto's Buzz Records jangle-pop roster alongside acts like Weaves; a direct forerunner to Mercy Works and Knows No Kindness.

description: A shambling, K Records-worthy set of hooky, unhurried indie pop from this Melbourne trio, all ringing guitars and plainspoken vocals over loping tempos. It's cheap, cheerful, and unfussy in a way that recalls the DIY jangle-pop of decades past. It's for fans of Flying Nun-descended guitar pop with an Australian slacker drawl.
lineage: Part of the Melbourne DIY jangle-pop scene that also produced Dick Diver and Terry, distributed internationally by the American slacker-rock label Trouble in Mind.

description: Matt Scottoline's Hurry plays tight, hook-forward power pop with an easy, unfussy jangle and plainspoken lyrics about heartbreak and self-doubt. The songs are short, sunny-sounding and quietly anxious underneath. It is for listeners who like their guitar pop clean and catchy.
lineage: Part of Philadelphia's Lame-O Records power-pop circle; the sound is indebted to Big Star and Superchunk.

description: Mo Troper's scrappy, hook-crammed debut packs GBV-scaled power pop into a lo-fi, fast-moving set, full of pop-culture non-sequiturs delivered with a snotty, deadpan sneer. Songs rush by on buzzing guitars and sticky melodies, for fans of four-track power pop with attitude.
lineage: Sounds squarely indebted to the Guided by Voices four-track power-pop tradition, filtered through the 2010s Portland DIY scene.

description: A more assured, road-tested version of the band's talky jangle-rock, with Chapman's lyrics turning toward philosophy and self-doubt over bright, ringing guitar lines. Songs like 'Stargazer' stretch out patiently, for listeners who like their indie rock literate and unhurried.
lineage: Continues the band's jangle songwriting, which sounds indebted to Silver Jews and the Velvet Underground.

description: The Melbourne five-piece's debut EP sets out the template their albums would follow: three guitarists trading tightly interlocked jangling lines over driving, motorik rhythms. It's unpretentious, sun-bleached guitar pop that announced the band before Hope Downs.
lineage: Grows out of the Go-Betweens/Triffids strand of Australian jangle-pop filtered through a more driving, Feelies-like guitar interplay.

description: A Melbourne group with members of Total Control and UV Race debuts with wiry, deadpan guitar-pop songs about everyday minutiae. It sounds closer to a shaggier Flying Nun update than to noise rock, for fans of dry humor and trebly guitars.
lineage: Grows out of Melbourne's DIY jangle/post-punk scene and sounds related to the same Australian guitar-pop wave as Rolling Blackouts Coastal Fever and Twerps.

description: Molina strips away Dissed and Dismissed's crunchy guitar for mostly acoustic, Bee Gees- and Byrds-indebted miniatures that rarely stretch past a couple of minutes. It's a hardcore lifer distilling pop songcraft into brief, gutting fragments.
lineage: A quieter turn from the Weezer/Teenage Fanclub-sounding power pop of Dissed and Dismissed toward the acoustic Big Star and Byrds side of the same lineage.

description: A big step up for the band, with keyboards and horns thickening the rowdy garage-jangle sound and the songwriting reaching for Stones- and Faces-style classic-rock scope. It is looser and warmer than Wild Onion, for listeners who like their bar-band rock young and ragged.
lineage: Builds on Wild Onion's Chicago garage-jangle sound while sounding newly indebted to '70s classic rock.

description: Warehouse's second album is a more concise, confident follow-up to Tesseract, keeping the interlocking guitar jams and Elaine Edenfield's fiery frontperson presence. The songs are leaner and more tightly wound, suiting listeners who like angular post-punk with a jangling edge.
lineage: Follows directly from Tesseract's jangling post-punk template, refined after the band's move to Bayonet Records.

description: A genre-hopping record that swings from fiddle-laced country pastiche to noisy skronk to gentle folk within its short, restless tracklist. It's Alex G at his most eclectic, refusing to settle into one style for more than a couple of minutes at a time. It's for listeners who want the fullest picture of his range.
lineage: Broadens the bedroom-pop template of Beach Music with country and folk textures that anticipate his later, more song-oriented Domino albums.

description: Casper Skulls' full-length debut expands their college-radio jangle into bigger, more anthemic arrangements while keeping the dual-vocal chemistry between Melanie St-Pierre and Neil Bednis at the center. The lyrics lean into storytelling and small-scale drama over ringing, layered guitars. It's for fans of R.E.M.-descended Canadian indie rock.
lineage: Follows directly from Lips & Skull on Buzz Records, continuing Toronto's jangle-pop lineage into a fuller studio sound.

description: A loose, conversational set of duets and trade-off songs between two of indie rock's most deadpan drawlers, built on unhurried fingerpicked guitar interplay. The two swap verses and harmonize in a way that feels like eavesdropping on old friends. It's for anyone who wants Vile's haze and Barnett's wit in the same room.
lineage: A direct collaboration linking the American slacker-guitar lineage (Vile) with the Australian deadpan-songwriter tradition (Barnett), each feeding the other's fanbase.

description: A quieter, more acoustic-leaning record built around fingerpicked guitar and synth textures, dealing with DeMarco's relationship with his father. Still slacker in tone but more reflective than his earlier records.
lineage: Shows the slacker-rock lineage bending toward hushed singer-songwriter territory.

description: Troper's second album sharpens Beloved's melodic instincts, trading some of the lo-fi scrappiness for slightly cleaner hooks while keeping the rapid-fire, hyper-referential songwriting intact. Short, bright songs pile up quickly, for fans of power pop that never overstays its welcome.
lineage: Continues the GBV-indebted power-pop songwriting of Beloved, tightening the hooks in a way that anticipates Natural Beauty's more melodic turn.

description: The second half of NE-HI's two-album run, with sharper songwriting and more melodic hooks. The same jangly, fuzz-toned guitar interplay drives it, now with cleaner production and more room to breathe.
lineage: Continuation of NE-HI's jangle/garage-rock songwriting within Chicago's DIY scene.

description: A murky, distorted slacker-punk record from a San Francisco band steeped in 90s indie rock, mixing hooky riffs with intentionally lo-fi, gnarled production.
lineage: Descends from Pavement/GBV-style shambling guitar-pop crossed with West Coast noise-punk.

description: Sam Cook-Parrott's project crams scrappy, hook-heavy songs into a short runtime, fuzzy guitars and bright, reedy vocals up front. It keeps the cassette-born intimacy of Something Wild and Torch Song while widening the emotional range.
lineage: Sounds of a piece with the Swearin'/Waxahatchee axis of DIY guitar-pop, sharing its fuzzy, confessional directness.

description: Their breakout EP, picked up by Sub Pop for US release, sharpens the interlocking three-guitar jangle of Talk Tight into tighter, more anthemic songs. It is the record that took the band from Melbourne club shows to international festival stages ahead of Hope Downs.
lineage: Bridges Talk Tight's homemade jangle-pop and the fuller, driving sound of Hope Downs, with an interlocking-guitar approach that sounds indebted to the Feelies.

description: The Melbourne art-punk quartet's second album keeps the terse, sing-song melodies and four-way vocal trades of their debut across punchy, wiry guitar songs. It is wry, hooky punk with a jangling underside, closer to Swell Maps than to hardcore.
lineage: Part of the Melbourne DIY scene around Total Control/UV Race members, extending Terry HQ's terse punk-pop into slightly more orchestrated territory.

description: Produced with John Agnello and her touring band, this is Waxahatchee's loudest, most straightforwardly indie-rock record, about the end of a relationship. It trades the lo-fi hush of her earlier albums for full-band immersion and sharper, angrier hooks.
lineage: The full-band endpoint of Waxahatchee's slacker/DIY period before she moved toward the more countryish Saint Cloud and Tigers Blood.

description: Lili Trifilio's breakout EP pairs bright, hooky power-pop guitars with plainspoken lyrics about body image and self-doubt, catching viral attention that pushed Beach Bunny from bedroom project to touring band. The songs are short, direct, and instantly catchy. It's for fans of Chicago's guitar-pop scene at its most immediate.
lineage: Grows out of Chicago's DIY guitar-pop scene, sounding kin to acts like Dehd; connects bedroom-pop songwriting to the bigger power-pop sound of the later Blame Game EP.

description: A warm, sleepy-eyed sophomore record that became a slow-burn cult favorite, pairing loose, unpolished guitar interplay with plainspoken lyrics about heartbreak and drift. Its patient tempos and conversational vocals put it squarely in the Woodsist label's slacker lineage. It's for fans who want comfort-food indie rock that never raises its voice.
lineage: Continues the band's hushed country-folk sound on the Woodsist label, sounding close to the broader 2010s Kurt Vile/Real Estate axis.

description: A full-band re-recording of Toledo's 2011 Bandcamp album, keeping the original's confessional, wordy songwriting about a doomed teenage relationship while giving it a much bigger, more anthemic sound. The original self-released Twin Fantasy holds the same songs in rawer, lo-fi form and is worth hearing alongside it.
lineage: A direct remake of Toledo's own Bandcamp-era masterpiece, connecting his DIY lo-fi songwriting roots to his mature full-band sound.

description: A heavier, more direct record than her debut, with fuzzed-out guitars backing pointed lyrics about self-doubt, sexism, and anger. The production is thicker and the tempos slower, giving her deadpan delivery more room to sting. It's for listeners who want Barnett's wit turned toward something angrier.
lineage: Follows directly from Sometimes I Sit and Think..., sharpening the same slacker-guitar and deadpan-lyric approach into more overtly political territory.

description: A brief burst of ringing, mid-fi guitar pop from another corner of Lame-O's Philadelphia power-pop stable, all hooks and no filler. Bright, chiming guitars and easy melodies keep it light on its feet. It is a quick hit for fans of short, sweet jangle.
lineage: Sounds akin to the Philadelphia jangle-pop of Hurry and 2nd Grade.

description: A sprawling, patient record full of long, meandering songs that stretch his laconic style to its most spacious extreme, including several tracks that pass the nine-minute mark. It trades the tighter pop songwriting of Lotta Sea Lice for hypnotic, repetition-based jams. It's for fans who want to sink into Vile's world for a while rather than get a quick hit.
lineage: Extends the loose, hypnotic guitar-drone side of his songwriting from Smoke Ring for My Halo, sounding indebted to Crazy Horse's long-form jams.

description: A slightly more polished, full-band record that keeps Nigel Chapman's signature talk-singing but adds more melodic hooks and confident guitar solos. It is the band's most accessible entry point, warm and ringing without losing its bookish, self-questioning lyrics.
lineage: Third album in Nap Eyes' jangle/talk-song lineage, moving toward a bigger label and wider audience.

description: A tighter, more anthemic record than the band's early lo-fi releases, mixing power-pop hooks with the same wry, self-aware lyrics. Carmen Perry's bright, direct voice leads punchy, fuzzed guitars built for singing along.
lineage: Continues the Philadelphia DIY-to-power-pop path, sounding of a piece with the later power-pop revival of Lawn and Sharp Pins.

description: Three guitarists trading melodic, chiming lines over motorik rhythms, with plainspoken, road-trip lyrics about growing up and moving on. It is one of the cleanest modern distillations of the Flying Nun/Go-Betweens jangle sound.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Antipodean jangle-pop (The Clean, The Go-Betweens); part of the 2010s Australian guitar-pop wave alongside The Goon Sax and Twerps.

description: Sun-bleached, reverb-drenched jangle-pop that recalls the Byrds by way of Real Estate. Sumi Choi's calm, plainspoken vocals float over chiming and occasionally surging guitars, for listeners who like their indie rock pristine and wistful.
lineage: Continues Say Sue Me's jangle-pop songwriting, which sounds indebted to Flying Nun and the Byrds.

description: Lindsey Jordan's teenage debut pairs plainspoken, diaristic lyrics with clean, jangly guitar leads that build into big, cathartic choruses. A defining record of the 2010s slacker-rock revival's younger generation.
lineage: Sounds indebted to 90s and 2000s guitar songwriters like Liz Phair and Rilo Kiley and to the Bandcamp-era DIY scene; it became a touchstone for the wave of young guitar-pop songwriters that followed.

description: Sophie Allison's breakout record moves her Bandcamp bedroom-pop into full-band arrangements. It is still built on quiet, confessional verses and 90s-alt-rock-indebted guitar hooks about jealousy and self-doubt.
lineage: Grows out of the Bandcamp/DIY bedroom-pop network and 90s alt-rock guitar songwriting; a borderline case whose pop instincts push toward Context-lane crossover on later records.

description: Sadie Dupuis's band follows Foil Deer by sharpening its knotty, dissonant guitar interplay into more outright pop structures. The hooks are bigger and the tempos brisker, but the lyrics stay confrontational about power and consent, for fans who like their guitar-pop with feedback and bite.
lineage: Continues Speedy Ortiz's noisy, angular guitar-pop lineage from Major Arcana and Foil Deer, tightening the pop hooks without losing the dissonant guitar tangle.

description: Swearin's reunion album, its first for Merge, keeps the fuzzed, bittersweet guitar-pop of its Salinas Records releases while sounding fuller and more confident, with Allison Crutchfield and Kyle Gilbride trading songwriting duties as before. Harmonized guitars swing between bright jangle and noisy feedback, for fans of heart-on-sleeve Philadelphia DIY rock.
lineage: A return, after a mid-2010s hiatus, to Swearin's own Philadelphia DIY guitar-pop lineage, a scene it shares with Waxahatchee, the project of Allison Crutchfield's twin sister Katie.

description: Terry's third LP in three years keeps their formula of terrace-chant choruses and terse, witty verses, alternating scrappy Wire-like guitar scrambles with gentler, synth-shimmered passages. Its lyrics turn a sharper eye on nationalism and colonial history than the earlier records.
lineage: A continuation of the Melbourne post-punk/pop songwriting of Total Control and UV Race's overlapping membership, staying close to Terry HQ's terse jangle-punk template.

description: Molina brings full-band arrangements back after Confront the Truth's acoustic minimalism, opening with a twelve-string tune that could sit on a Byrds record and closing with gentle, Elliott Smith-like fingerpicking. Nothing is padded; every short song is all melody.
lineage: Splits the difference between Dissed and Dismissed's full-band crunch and Confront the Truth's acoustic intimacy, still sounding rooted in the Byrds/Big Star power-pop seam.

description: A woozy, unsettling record that folds pitch-shifted vocals, folk fingerpicking and eerie electronic textures into some of his most emotionally direct songwriting, circling addiction and loss. Songs like 'Hope' and 'Southern Sky' hold the collage together with plain, aching melodies. It's the most cohesive-feeling statement in Alex G's catalog.
lineage: Builds on the genre-collage approach of Rocket while tightening the emotional focus, setting up the more expansive God Save the Animals.

description: Self-released on DeMarco's own label, this record strips his sound to its most repetitive and hypnotic, with simple, mantra-like song structures and titles. A deliberately low-key follow-up that trades hooks for mood.
lineage: DeMarco's move to self-release on his own label echoes the DIY spirit this lane traces.

description: Truth Club's debut pairs Chris Davis's conversational, self-lacerating lyrics with tense, angular guitar interplay that snaps between quiet verses and squalling choruses. It sounds like a Raleigh house-show band that grew up on Pavement and Cap'n Jazz in equal measure. Good for listeners who want their slacker rock a little more wound-up and anxious.
lineage: Grows out of the Pavement/GBV lineage of loud-quiet indie rock filtered through Raleigh's DIY basement scene; feeds directly into the tighter, more melodic songwriting of Running From the Chase.

description: A warmer, more classic-rock-leaning record that rounds out the band's transition from scrappy garage kids to accomplished songwriters. Piano, harmonies and relaxed grooves replace much of the old rowdiness, for fans of easygoing '70s-style rock.
lineage: Later-period Twin Peaks, still rooted in the band's Chicago garage-jangle scene origins.

description: Peter Gill's debut as 2nd Grade crams hook after hook into a scrappy, GBV-scaled power-pop sprawl, rarely settling into one idea for more than two minutes. It set the template for the project's compulsively prolific, miniature-song aesthetic.
lineage: Sounds directly descended from Guided by Voices' song-fragment power pop, and comes out of the same Philadelphia scene as Hurry and Golden Apples.

description: A deliberately polarizing pivot toward synths, drum machines and EDM-adjacent production, while keeping Toledo's anxious, funny-sad lyricism intact. It traded the noisy guitar rock of Teens of Denial for something colder and more electronic. It's for fans willing to follow the band away from its guitar-rock comfort zone.
lineage: A deliberate break from the Crazy Horse and jangle-rock guitar sound of Teens of Denial, showing the DIY-to-major-indie pipeline can still take creative risks.

description: Written in response to ghostly samples McKiel found on a used reel-to-reel tape, this record blends hushed, fingerpicked songwriting with warped found-sound textures into something inventive and haunting. It's a quieter, more experimental turn than straightforward jangle-pop but keeps a strong melodic core. It's for fans of Canadian DIY songwriting with a spectral edge.
lineage: Part of the You've Changed Records roster connecting Maritime Canada's indie scene to the wider lo-fi/jangle underground; feeds into Hex's continued collaboration with Jay Crocker.

description: Kiwi Jr.'s debut full-length sets the template the band would refine on later Sub Pop records: chiming, Pavement-indebted guitar lines, deadpan sing-speak vocals, and lyrics stuffed with dry pop-culture asides. It's rougher around the edges than Cooler Returns but already has the band's melodic hooks in place. It's for fans who want the origin point of their jangle-pop run.
lineage: Grows out of Toronto's DIY guitar-pop scene and the Pavement/Guided by Voices lineage; set up the band's jump to Sub Pop for Cooler Returns and Chopper.

description: Lawn's second album expands on the duo's breezy power-pop hooks across unhurried songs, with a relaxed, roomy sound ahead of the tighter Bigger Sprout. It's a warmer, looser record than what came before or after, for fans of easygoing guitar pop.
lineage: Sits between Lawn's earlier, more post-punk-tinged material and the tighter power pop of Bigger Sprout and God Made The Highway.

description: Troper's third album swaps the earlier records' snottiness for plainer, more durable storytelling, anchored by the Kinks-indebted 'Jas From Australia'. Clean, chiming guitars and sweeter melodies make it his most approachable record, for fans of classic power-pop craft.
lineage: A more melodically direct turn from Troper's earlier GBV-style scrappiness, sounding closer to the Kinks and Teenage Fanclub end of the power-pop lineage.

description: Nap Eyes' most direct, hook-forward record, still built on Chapman's conversational delivery but with brighter, more confident arrangements.
lineage: Continues the band's jangle/talk-song lineage into a fourth album.

description: A sunnier, more confident sequel to Hope Downs, with the same three-guitar interlock but bigger choruses and warmer production. Written partly about touring and homesickness.
lineage: Sounds like second-generation Flying Nun-indebted jangle-pop, continuing the band's refinement of the sound.

description: Slow Pulp's debut full-length was finished amid health crises and a pandemic, blending blown-out shoegaze guitar with unusually direct, hooky songwriting. It channels the band's explosive live intensity into a more controlled studio record.
lineage: Grows out of Slow Pulp's Chicago/Madison shoegaze-pop beginnings, a lighter, poppier cousin to Wednesday's countrygaze template.

description: A tighter, more polished EP than Prom Queen, with Beach Bunny's power-pop hooks pushed toward arena-ready choruses while the lyrics stay pointed and personal. It followed their first full-length and shows the band's most immediate, radio-ready songwriting.
lineage: Continues the Chicago guitar-pop lineage of Prom Queen, sharpening the hooks as the band's audience grew.

description: A more confident, dynamically varied record than their debut, still anchored by ringing guitar interplay and dual-vocal storytelling but pushing into denser arrangements and darker lyrical territory. It's the sound of a band settling comfortably into its own identity within Toronto's jangle-pop scene. It's for fans who followed the band from their Buzz Records beginnings.
lineage: The most developed entry in Casper Skulls' Buzz Records run, later followed by Kit-Cat on Next Door Records.

description: A calmer record that trades some of Barnett's wordplay density for spacious, drum-machine-inflected slacker pop. Hushed, breezy arrangements suit its themes of patience and care.
lineage: Barnett's songwriting, which sounds indebted to Pavement, softened toward indie-pop.

description: Ducks Ltd.'s debut full-length sets the duo's template of chiming, propulsive guitar interplay over brisk rhythms, drawing on '80s college-rock jangle filtered through a modern anxious lyric sheet. Tom McGreevy's plainspoken vocals ride on top of Evan Lewis's careening guitar lines. It's for fans of Sarah Records-style jangle brought into the present.
lineage: Comes out of the Toronto DIY scene and sounds indebted to the Flying Nun/Go-Betweens jangle-pop lineage; set up Harm's Way's fuller studio sound.

description: The Brisbane trio add synths and sheen to their jangle-pop, its three songwriters trading plainspoken, bittersweet verses. Close harmonies and deadpan delivery keep it wry and tender.
lineage: Founding member Louis Forster is the son of the Go-Betweens' Robert Forster; the band's jangle sounds descended from the Go-Betweens and Flying Nun.

description: Charlie Martin and Will Taylor's duo makes soft-focus, mid-fi slacker pop, warm and unhurried. Plain-spoken affection rides gentle drum-machine pulses and hushed, lullaby-like vocals, for listeners who want indie rock as a quiet comfort.
lineage: Sounds descended from the lo-fi college-radio-to-Bandcamp lineage of Duster and Alex G.

description: Matt Scottoline's project turns plainspoken heartbreak into tight, hook-forward power pop recorded with an easy, unfussy jangle. It sits alongside Philadelphia's current power-pop revival, for fans of short, sweet, sad songs.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Big Star and Superchunk, filtered through the Philadelphia DIY scene.

description: Toronto's Kiwi Jr. sharpen their Pavement- and GBV-descended jangle into a wry, hooky second album. Deadpan vocals trade in pop-culture references and small stories over bright, clipped guitars.
lineage: Sounds directly indebted to Pavement and Guided by Voices.

description: A cohesive, jittery-warm record of jangle-pop songwriting from a Grand Rapids band. It mixes heavy rock'n'roll textures with pop hooks, built to be heard as a full album.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Big Star/Flying Nun jangle-pop songwriting by way of the Midwest DIY circuit.
