description: A tighter, more melodic version of Pardoner's slacker-punk sound, still caked in fuzz but with clearer hooks poking through the murk. Fast, messy guitars and yelped vocals make it for listeners who like their indie rock loud and a little unhinged.
lineage: Continuation of Pardoner's Pavement/GBV-descended noisy slacker-pop songwriting.

description: Remember Sports' third Father/Daughter album builds on Slow Buzz's expanded arrangements, with the four members trading instruments and adding synths and drum machines to the guitar-pop core. Carmen Perry sings her sharpest lyrics yet about self-forgiveness, for listeners who like power pop with rough edges.
lineage: The most ambitious entry in Remember Sports' arc from scrappy basement pop-punk (All of Something) toward richly arranged power pop.

description: A more produced, emotionally raw follow-up to Lush, adding synths and string arrangements to Jordan's core jangle-guitar sound. Her voice pushes into more theatrical territory, for listeners who want the heartbreak bigger and glossier.
lineage: Second chapter of Snail Mail's slacker-to-art-pop evolution.

description: 2nd Grade's second album keeps the compulsive hook-density of Hit to Hit but tightens the songwriting, with titles nodding to Keith Richards and Rolling Stone covers. Sixteen songs of unpretentious, Big Star-scaled jangle-pop.
lineage: Continues Peter Gill's GBV-indebted power-pop songwriting, part of Philadelphia's power-pop revival alongside Hurry.

description: Alex Giannascoli's album pairs pitched-up vocal tics and Auto-Tune warps with plainspoken, sometimes menacing songwriting about faith and small-town life. Gentle acoustic arrangements and gospel-tinged hooks sit next to eerie, lo-fi textures. It suits listeners who like songs that are tender and unsettling at once.
lineage: Grew out of Bandcamp-era home recording; its fragmentary lo-fi songcraft sounds indebted to Guided by Voices and Elliott Smith.

description: Elizabeth Stokes writes tight, guitar-heavy songs that read as character studies of relationships' aftermaths. Harmonized guitars and anthemic choruses give the heartbreak a bright, driving lift.
lineage: Sounds akin to the New Zealand jangle-pop tradition around Flying Nun, crossed with American power pop.

description: The Welsh duo's debut album packs deceptively simple garage-pop melodies into a scrappy, ramshackle energy, with the pair's back-and-forth deadpan vocals doing most of the heavy lifting. Songs whip by quickly, favoring hooks over polish. It's the record that set up their prolific run before Sub Pop signed them.
lineage: Sounds of a piece with the UK DIY garage-pop underground that runs parallel to the American slacker/jangle revival; the band later signed to Sub Pop.

description: James Goodson's project crams huge hooks into no-second-wasted power pop, like Fountains of Wayne played at ear-shattering volume. Crazy Horse-style fuzz and anthemic choruses fill short, breathless songs.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Big Star and Fountains of Wayne melodicism, blown out with fuzz-pedal DIY energy.

description: A guitar-forward home-recorded record with hooky choruses that slides between snotty rock, stargazing psych, and introspective folk, part of Graham Hunt's prolific self-released catalog out of Madison, Wisconsin. It leans on a '90s alt-rock sensibility while still sounding distinctly homemade. It's for fans of one-person bedroom rock records with real songwriting range.
lineage: Part of Hunt's ongoing self-released Bandcamp catalog that runs from lo-fi power pop through to the more studio-polished American Pyramid.

description: Three young Chicagoans' debut is an efficient romp through indie rock's post-punk and jangle fringes. Interlocking guitars, feedback, and deadpan vocals keep songs short and sharp. It suits listeners who love noisy, tasteful '90s-style indie rock.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Pavement and Sonic Youth's guitar interplay, filtered through Chicago's all-ages DIY scene.

description: Joe Glass's debut showcases his knack for an airtight hook across slightly twangy, ramshackle rockers pulling from Nuggets-style garage pop and '90s indie rock. It's scrappy and fast, for fans of the current Midwestern power-pop underground.
lineage: Sounds of a piece with the Chicago-area DIY power-pop underground around Lifeguard and Sharp Pins, sharing their Nuggets-inspired hooks.

description: Kiwi Jr.'s third album adds synths and sheen to their wit-and-melody formula, sardonic Toronto indie rock that balances humor and hooks. It builds on the jangle of Cooler Returns and Football Money with a glossier, more synth-lit sound.
lineage: Continues the band's jangle, which sounds descended from Pavement and GBV.

description: Vile's first album after leaving Matador for Verve leans further into home-studio synth textures and drum-machine pulses while keeping his familiar mumbled melodies intact. It's looser and more playful than his 2010s work, closer to a solo bedroom record again, for longtime fans curious how his sound kept drifting.
lineage: A return to the DIY, self-produced instincts of his earliest lo-fi tapes, now filtered through two decades of studio experience.

description: A New Orleans duo splitting the difference between breezy power-pop hooks and nervy post-punk edges, with trading vocals and taut, bright guitars. It sits in the same power-pop revival as Dazy, 2nd Grade and Mo Troper.
lineage: Sounds indebted to the Big Star power-pop line crossed with post-punk tension, part of the mid-2020s power-pop revival.

description: Fifteen hook-dense power-pop tracks from a Portland songwriter, pairing clever, self-aware writing with warmth and classic melodies. Troper's own tagline calls his style 'the Conker's Bad Fur Day of power pop,' which captures its mix of nerdy reference and sugar rush.
lineage: Direct descendant of the Big Star/Teenage Fanclub power-pop lineage, part of the 2020s power-pop revival alongside Sharp Pins and Lawn.

description: A darker, more expansive record with longer song structures and heavier guitar tones layered under the band's signature three-guitar jangle. It is the band's most textured album, for listeners who want the chime with more shadow.
lineage: Shows the band stretching its Flying Nun-indebted jangle sound toward denser, more textured arrangements.

description: Say Sue Me's most inward record is built around themes of self-love and realization rather than the surf-jangle bounce of earlier singles. Slower tempos and softer arrangements widen the palette without losing the Busan band's pristine, throwback jangle-pop core.
lineage: Continues the Busan band's pristine throwback indie-pop, which sounds close to Alvvays, turning inward after Where We Were Together.

description: Why Bonnie's debut full-length trades their earlier bedroom dream pop for raw-edged, feedback-streaked indie rock with a Texas twang in the melodies. Blair Howerton's clear, unhurried voice rides over fuzzy guitars and road-trip imagery. It suits listeners who like their '90s-style alt-rock with a hint of country dust.
lineage: A Texas band's move from dream pop toward a more country-and-alt-rock-inflected sound, resembling the wider indie-twang turn without being a straight country record.

description: An early record mixing jangly guitar with drum machines and synths in an off-kilter, homemade pop style. It feels like a bedroom experiment in progress, for listeners who enjoy lo-fi indie rock that wanders.
lineage: Part of the DIY/Bandcamp jangle-pop network this lane traces from Flying Nun and college radio.

description: Detroit's Bonny Doon make their ANTI- debut breezier and more accessible than past records, with lyrics that sneak up on the listener over unhurried, conversational arrangements. Close harmonies and hushed, deadpan vocals keep it gentle.
lineage: Slacker-folk that sounds indebted to the Silver Jews and Palace, filtered through Detroit's indie scene.

description: A sprawling, hour-long set of relentlessly catchy, fuzz-wrapped garage pop with great dual-singer chemistry. Most songs are short and rowdy, stacking jokes and hooks at speed.
lineage: Continues the band's garage sound, which sounds indebted to Nuggets, at maximalist length.

description: Blue Broderick's Diners project goes full power-pop on this breezy guitar-pop record, with clear DNA from Tom Petty, Big Star and Fountains of Wayne. Every song is built for maximum hum-along appeal, bright guitars and stacked harmonies up front. It's for fans who want classic power-pop songcraft filtered through a bedroom-pop sensibility.
lineage: Moves Broderick's earlier lo-fi Diners records toward the wider power-pop revival, sounding indebted to Petty, Big Star and Fountains of Wayne.

description: Golden Apples' hookiest, most fuzzed-out set is packed with memorable choruses in the power-pop and jangle vein. Distorted guitars and bright melodies push the songs forward without losing their homemade Philadelphia feel.
lineage: Big Star melodicism via Philadelphia's power-pop revival.

description: A self-released Wisconsin power-pop record with effortless hooks and a '90s rock sensibility, continuing Graham Hunt's steady run of home-recorded guitar-pop albums. The songwriting is direct and unfussy, favoring melody over studio polish. It's for fans who want deep-catalog power pop from outside the usual coastal scenes.
lineage: Sits between If You Knew Would You Believe It? and Timeless World Forever in Hunt's self-released discography.

description: Will Anderson's project buries plainspoken, slacker-jangly songwriting under warm shoegaze fuzz and feedback. Cartwheel was his Third Man Records debut, for listeners who like hooks hidden inside a noise wall.
lineage: Sits between shoegaze fuzz and the jangle-pop tradition, sounding indebted to Guided by Voices' song-fragment economy.

description: A dreamier, more polished turn for the garage-glam lifer Kyle Thomas, trading his usual fuzzed-out riffs for jangly, synth-dusted power pop with a wide-eyed, sun-drenched feel. It's a gentler record than his 2010s output but keeps his knack for an instant hook. It's for fans who like their power pop with a cosmic-country glow.
lineage: King Tuff's catalog runs from 2000s garage-punk through Sub Pop glam-rock; Smalltown Stardust pulls him into the same jangly, twang-adjacent revival as his 2010s peers.

description: The Upper Peninsula band's self-titled album crams dense, hooky songs into a very short runtime, sounding indebted to Fountains of Wayne, PUP and Rozwell Kid in equal measure. It is power pop with a Midwestern punk snap, over almost before it starts.
lineage: A Marquette, Michigan strain of pop-punk-inflected power pop, indebted to Fountains of Wayne's hook density and 1990s Midwest punk energy.

description: A wordless, tape-warped song cycle Mac DeMarco pieced together while driving cross-country, all warm Rhodes, brushed drums and looping guitar vamps instead of his usual slack-jawed vocals. It plays like a private travelogue, mixing his usual chorus-pedal haze with lounge and ambient touches. For listeners who want the DeMarco sound stripped of singing.
lineage: Extends the bedroom-pop haze of his Captured Tracks records into instrumental territory, closer to Jim O'Rourke's ambient side than to Pavement.

description: Kai Slater's (Lifeguard, Dwaal Troupe) solo power-pop project delivers bedroom-recorded, Big Star/Teenage Fanclub-style hooks. Short, jangly songs come wrapped in scrappy tape-hiss charm, for listeners who like their power pop homemade.
lineage: Sounds indebted to the Big Star power-pop lineage by way of lo-fi, self-recorded bedroom pop.

description: Slow Pulp's second album warms its shoegaze-scale guitars with Americana hues, slide and acoustic textures, and pristine pop hooks without any filler. It's their most confident synthesis of noise and twang.
lineage: Extends Moveys' shoegaze-pop into more overtly Americana-tinged territory, sounding close to the countrygaze lineage of Wednesday and Great Grandpa.

description: Speedy Ortiz's fourth album pushes the band's gnarled guitar interplay toward a vast, heavier sound, with long solos and walls of feedback. Sadie Dupuis's lyrics confront trauma and music-industry hypocrisy, making it the band's most expansive and pointed record.
lineage: The most expansive entry in Speedy Ortiz's noisy indie-rock lineage from Major Arcana onward, still rooted in the same angular guitar tangle.

description: Superviolet's debut is buoyant, hook-forward power pop full of bright, jangling guitars and warm, earnest vocals. Its unfussy songs read as a career-best distillation of that songwriting style, for fans of sunny, melodic guitar pop.
lineage: A Columbus, Ohio power-pop project in the Teenage Fanclub/Superchunk lineage, part of the same 2020s power-pop revival as Sharp Pins and Hurry.

description: Five years on from I'm Terry, the band's fourth album dresses their terse four-vocal punk-pop in fuller production while lyrically taking aim at Australia's colonial history. The detuned, scrappy guitars and chant-along choruses are still at the core, for fans of wry, political post-punk.
lineage: A late-period expansion of the same Melbourne art-punk lineage, sharing members with Total Control and UV Race, that produced Terry HQ.

description: A more confident, widescreen version of the Truth Club sound, moving from hushed confession to full-band catharsis with a voice that cracks at the edges of big, hooky choruses. It plays like a document of getting older and more self-aware without losing any of the tension of the debut.
lineage: Continues Truth Club's basement-scene, Pavement/GBV-descended jangle-and-noise songwriting into a more polished, emotionally direct register.

description: A Welsh band's debut applies ringing, Byrds/Feelies-style jangle guitar to raw, personal songwriting about grief and family, one of the sharpest post-2020s jangle-revival records.
lineage: Direct descendant of classic jangle-pop (The Feelies, early R.E.M., Flying Nun bands).

description: A New Orleans duo's fourth LP moves away from disco nostalgia toward more personal, unselfconscious songwriting. Its effortless-sounding hooks and smooth pop craft recall Steely Dan and the Beach Boys.
lineage: Descends from breezy 70s pop-rock songwriting filtered through 2010s New Orleans indie pop.

description: 2nd Grade's third full-length is its most expansive yet, still built from the same rapid-fire jangling hooks and wry titles as its predecessors. It is Peter Gill's project at its most prolific and melodically confident, for fans who like their power pop in short, bright bursts.
lineage: The latest entry in 2nd Grade's GBV/Big Star-indebted-sounding power-pop project, part of Philadelphia's mid-2020s jangle-pop scene.

description: The Welsh band's Sub Pop debut is Modern Lovers-meets-Nuggets garage rock with sarcastic dual vocals and clanging riffs. Songs are short, rowdy and funny-sad, often done in under two minutes.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Nuggets garage and the talky deadpan of Jonathan Richman and the Modern Lovers.

description: Ducks Ltd.'s most fleshed-out record is precise and propulsive jangle-pop with careening riffs and power-pop melodies. Bright guitars and a fuller band sound frame the duo's anxious, plainspoken lyrics. It's the fullest realization yet of their college-rock-meets-anxiety songwriting.
lineage: Builds on Modern Fiction's jangle foundation with a bigger, more collaborative studio sound.

description: An early-2024 power-pop full-length released on the emo/indie label Tiny Engines, part of a wave of DIY guitar-pop records flagged in Josh Terry's most-anticipated list that year. Details on its sound are limited, but its label and placement put it squarely in the jangle/power-pop underground. It's a deep-cut pick for listeners exploring Tiny Engines' current roster.
lineage: Released on Tiny Engines, a label historically associated with emo and twangy emo crossovers, connecting it to the C9 emo-crossover lane as well as straight power pop.

description: This Columbus power trio's three-song EP is pummeling, loud and varied, with each track sounding markedly different but united by an animated heaviness. It's a live-wire document of a genuinely ferocious band, for fans of noisy Midwestern guitar rock that hits hard in short bursts.
lineage: Sounds of a piece with the current Midwest DIY noise-rock underground where it overlaps with the slacker/jangle scene at its loudest edge.

description: A long, double-LP-length set with stronger melodies and more hi-fi recording than earlier Hovvdy work. Hushed, lullaby-soft vocals and gentle pulses keep the duo's intimacy intact even as the sound fills out.
lineage: Continues Hovvdy's lo-fi slacker-pop arc toward fuller production.

description: A second collaboration with producer Jay Crocker, this record folds more synths and studio texture into McKiel's hushed songwriting without losing the strange, homemade intimacy of Bobby Joe Hope. Murmured vocals sit inside warm, slightly warped arrangements. It's for fans of understated, atmosphere-first Canadian indie rock.
lineage: Continues the Crocker/McKiel partnership begun on Bobby Joe Hope, part of the same You've Changed Records lineage.

description: Twin Peaks' Cadien Lake James steps out solo here, trading his main band's raw garage-pop for glimmering, tastefully electronic jangle-pop. It is a more polished, atmospheric record than his band's work, for listeners who like breezy guitar-pop with soft synth shading.
lineage: A solo offshoot of Twin Peaks' garage-jangle songwriting, filtered through cleaner electronic production.

description: Grand Rapids trio Major Murphy follows Access with a warm, psychedelic-tinged set that weaves classic-rock and vintage soft-rock touches into their usual blend of 1990s indie looseness and 1970s AM-radio warmth. It's an emotionally direct record, for listeners who like their guitar pop mellow and melodic.
lineage: Extends Major Murphy's own hybrid of 1990s indie rock and 1970s soft-rock songwriting established on Access, sounding indebted to Big Star's more orchestrated moments.

description: The band pairs its conversational, bookish lyrics with sunny organ and strong, ringing guitar work. Nigel Chapman's half-spoken delivery stays at the center, making it a warm late-career entry for fans of talky, unhurried guitar rock.
lineage: Latest chapter in Nap Eyes' jangle songwriting, which sounds indebted to Silver Jews and the Velvet Underground.

description: Rui Gabriel's solo debut uses a light palette of fun grooves and Summerteeth-grade hooks to write self-aware songs about class and miscommunication. It is bright, sing-along power pop for listeners who like wry lyrics over tuneful, loose-limbed studio pop.
lineage: A solo power-pop outlet that sounds indebted to Wilco's Summerteeth-era studio pop.

description: Nate Amos's (Water From Your Eyes) solo project delivers warped, hooky pop songs that recall the Postal Service, Big Star and the Magnetic Fields. Drum machines and home-recorded synths sit under genuine power-pop songwriting, sweet and slightly off-kilter.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Big Star power-pop songwriting, filtered through home-recorded, synth-augmented indie pop.

description: Indiana songwriters Kevin Krauter and Nina Pitchkites blend shoegaze haze, grunge fuzz and power-pop hooks on their debut LP. It moves between pillowy atmospherics and scathing distortion, for fans of melodic, loud '90s-style guitar rock.
lineage: Sounds indebted to the Big Star power-pop line crossed with 90s alt-rock guitar tones.

description: Alex G's major-label debut keeps his warped, intimate production but pushes toward higher fidelity. Latter-day R.E.M. and Daniel Johnston echoes are folded into the same gentle-menace songwriting that runs through his earlier records, with the title track 'Headlights' as the clearest example.
lineage: Continues Alex G's arc from Bandcamp lo-fi into a wider, still jangle-rooted indie-pop palette.

description: Chicago songwriter Ben Astrachan's solo debut is maximalist and ambitious, packing its songs with wailing guitars and a multitude of '60s-and-'70s-indebted melodic twists. It's conceptual rock music delivered in an off-kilter, deliriously infectious way rather than as straight pastiche. It's for fans of Chicago's current crop of detail-obsessed guitar-pop songwriters.
lineage: Sounds of a piece with Chicago acts like Smushie and Shoulderbird, connecting classic-rock revivalism to the current power-pop/jangle underground.

description: This sophomore LP from Melbourne's the Belair Lip Bombs is frenetic, interlocking power pop fronted by the commanding Maisie Everett. The guitars careen and lock together in a way that recalls Australia's jangle-rock lineage while the choruses aim straight for arenas, for fans of big, direct guitar pop.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Melbourne's interlocking-guitar jangle rock in the Rolling Blackouts C.F. mold, now on Third Man Records' power-pop and garage-rock roster.

description: The Bug Club's second Sub Pop record streamlines their oddball garage-pop into catchier, tighter songs, with the jokes landing harder and the choruses stickier than ever. The dual vocals of Sam Willmett and Tilly Harris trade lines with an easy chemistry throughout. It's for listeners who want slacker-pop songwriting that's actually secretly very well-crafted.
lineage: Continues the band's garage-punk-to-power-pop evolution begun on Green Dream in F#, now filtered through a major indie label's reach.

description: A concept album set at a fictional university, this record returns Car Seat Headrest to a bigger, more guitar-driven full-band sound after the electronic detour of Making a Door Less Open. Toledo's wordy, theatrical songwriting is at its most ambitious here, built around a cast of recurring characters. It's for longtime fans who wanted the band's rock muscle back.
lineage: A return to the anthemic guitar-rock lineage of Teens of Denial after the band's synth-pop experiment, keeping Toledo's literary songwriting intact.

description: Loud, relentlessly hooky rock that channels Summerteeth-era Wilco and Ty Segall's frantic energy. Crazy Horse fuzz and Telecaster twang back small-town storytelling at full tilt.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Neil Young & Crazy Horse fuzz, with Wilco's Americana-pop as a touchstone.

description: Casper Skulls' latest LP has the dual-vocal chemistry and college-radio jangle of a band drawing on Pavement, R.E.M. and Superchunk, full of lived-in warmth. Guitars ring and interlock while the vocal trade-offs keep the songs feeling conversational. It's for longtime fans of the band's steady evolution.
lineage: Continues the jangle-pop lineage established on Buzz Records, now on Next Door Records with a warmer, more assured sound.

description: New Orleans slacker-pop trio The Convenience deliver thirteen loose, deadpan-sung tracks built on jangling, lightly lo-fi guitars. The songwriting is plainspoken and wry, closer to a conversation than a performance, in the same Crescent City DIY scene as Lawn.
lineage: Part of New Orleans' current jangle/slacker cluster alongside Lawn.

description: Cult New York duo Frog's latest album is folky, lo-fi and scrappy, like Modest Mouse playing Pinegrove-style heart-on-sleeve songs. A piano-led opener and banjo-anchored tracks wrap aching lyrics in charmingly unadorned production. It's for fans who want deadpan, funny-sad songwriting without any studio gloss.
lineage: A long-running New York DIY act that sounds indebted to Drag City-style funny-sad songwriting, filtered through the lo-fi Bandcamp underground.

description: Russell Edling's group turns its own songwriting process inside out across a spacious, nervy set of fuzzed and jangling power pop. Dreamy mellotron cuts against scrubby guitars, with a playful, Elephant 6-style looseness.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Big Star and Elephant 6 melodicism, sitting within Philadelphia's current power-pop scene.

description: Adventurous, stylistically shifting indie rock that still flows front to back, with Built to Spill and Pavement echoes throughout. Jangling guitars stretch into long solos beneath deadpan vocals.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Pavement's loose song-suite structure and Built to Spill's guitar interplay.

description: A twee-punk-leaning collection of home recordings, full of pristine, thoughtful jangle-pop with big hooks and surging punk energy. Lo-fi fidelity and short songs keep it scrappy and small-town intimate.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Guided by Voices and Beat Happening's DIY-jangle lineage.

description: Another entry in Graham Hunt's prolific self-released catalog, continuing his blend of hooky, home-recorded power pop with wide-ranging classic-rock and psych touches. Bright guitars and direct melodies keep it unfussy, for listeners tracking his steady, low-key discography.
lineage: Part of Hunt's ongoing solo catalog that runs directly into American Pyramid's bigger studio sound.

description: A more direct second album of ramshackle, perfect pop songs, with grooves and glowing harmonies replacing the debut's noisier fringes. Clean, jangling guitars and deadpan vocals keep the songs short and spare.
lineage: Continues Horsegirl's post-punk and jangle sound, akin to Pavement, toward cleaner pop songwriting.

description: Lawn's most confident record yet, a scrappy blend of post-punk and power-pop with dual lead vocals trading off across hook-heavy songs. It is a punchy distillation of the New Orleans band's sound, wiry guitars and all.
lineage: Continues Lawn's power-pop/post-punk hybrid songwriting into a bigger, punchier register.

description: Mac DeMarco's Guitar returns to vocal pop songwriting after the instrumental detour of Five Easy Hot Dogs, foregrounding warm guitar tone and his familiar half-mumbled melodies. It is unhurried, private-sounding pop built for headphones on a walk. Fans of Salad Days will find the same loose, wobbly charm.
lineage: A return to the vocal jangle-pop songwriting of Salad Days and This Old Dog after an instrumental record, still rooted in his Captured Tracks-era slacker sound.

description: A warm, crisp midtempo jangle record built around layered melodies and unvarnished lyricism, with pedal steel coloring several tracks. It stakes out its own lane of graceful, inviting jangle-pop for listeners who like their guitar pop gentle.
lineage: Sounds indebted to the DIY jangle/college-radio line (Big Star, Flying Nun), filtered through 2020s Midwest indie rock.

description: A sprawling set from Kai Slater, packed with 1965-styled jangle hooks and bright, trebly guitars. It is the most maximalist Sharp Pins record yet, stringing together short, hook-forward pop songs with barely a pause between them.
lineage: Extends Sharp Pins' Nuggets/Big Star-sounding jangle-pop into a longer, more song-crammed format, released through K Records and Perennial.

description: Kai Slater's Sharp Pins project follows Turtle Rock with fourteen driving, Nuggets-indebted power-pop songs, tighter and more melodically direct than before. Calvin Johnson's K Records/Perennial imprint released it, cementing Sharp Pins' place in the Big Star-to-GBV jangle-pop lineage.
lineage: Follows Turtle Rock in the 1960s-garage-into-Big-Star jangle-pop lineage; its release through K Records/Perennial places it in a long-running indie-pop label network.

description: Nate Amos (also of Water From Your Eyes) re-recorded songs from across his sprawling This Is Lorelei back catalog, tracked quickly to keep the straight-to-Bandcamp spirit of the originals. It works as a breezy, guitar-pop-facing entry point to his catalog rather than a best-of.
lineage: A deliberate reconnection to Amos's earlier lo-fi Bandcamp songwriting, following Box for Buddy, Box for Star.

description: A follow-up that keeps The Tubs' chiming jangle-pop core while broadening the arrangements. It continues the band's run of sharply written, classic-sounding guitar-pop, with bright leads and a dry, baritone lead voice.
lineage: Continues The Tubs' jangle-pop, which sounds indebted to '80s British and Antipodean guitar pop.

description: A knotty, chameleonic indie rock record mixing jangle, synths and drum machines. At least one song sounds like a lost Pavement track, making it a rewarding listen for fans of homemade, shape-shifting guitar pop.
lineage: Continues Zook's homemade jangle/synth-pop hybrid songwriting, which sounds indebted to Pavement's slacker guitar-pop.

description: A sprawling double set of concise, hook-driven power pop split into 'Girls' and 'Boys' halves, led by Peter Gill, who also plays in Friendship. The songs are quick, bright and jangly, flying past before they can outstay their welcome. It suits listeners who like power pop in big, generous doses.
lineage: Gill's membership in Friendship ties 2nd Grade to the same Philadelphia scene as Friendship and Hurry; the songwriting sounds indebted to Big Star and Guided by Voices.

description: This New York quartet's self-titled debut is a hooky, jangly and twangy power-pop rock record with blistering riffs and meaty choruses, released by the fast-rising Ever/Never label. It's punchy and immediate, favoring rock and roll swagger over polish. It's for fans who want the twang-adjacent side of the current power-pop wave.
lineage: Signed to the New York label Ever/Never, which ties the band into the current DIY jangle/twang underground.

description: A sprawling grab-bag from a home-recording project, Well Once There Was A King cycles through folk, slacker jangle, country, doom-metal detours and Beach Boys harmonies without pausing for breath. It rewards the same magpie curiosity that draws people to Guided by Voices' overstuffed records.
lineage: Sounds indebted to the lo-fi, kitchen-sink home-taping tradition of GBV and Sebadoh, filtered through a 2020s Bandcamp DIY sensibility.

description: This trio's debut full-length channels raucous energy into hook-forward, dynamic indie rock, packing frantic drive and earworm melodies into a lean runtime. Delicate falsetto verses give way to explosive, unrelenting choruses across the tracklist. It's for fans who want their power pop with real teeth.
lineage: Released via Fire Talk's Angel Tapes imprint, which ties the band into the current DIY guitar-pop underground.

description: Hunt's most maximalist record yet trades home recording for a fuller studio sound, with frantic late-'90s pop-rock hooks, autotuned detours and euphoric grooves recalling Screamadelica. It still sounds instantly familiar despite its left turns, the fullest treatment his songwriting has gotten to date.
lineage: Hunt's self-released catalog moving from bedroom recording toward a bigger studio sound while keeping the same playful, hook-heavy songwriting.

description: This Brooklyn band's debut, originally formed in North Carolina, eschews the twang-and-shoegaze sound of their home-state peers for something more its own: brutal, pounding riffs paired with dual lead vocals and patiently pastoral arrangement shifts. Released by the Texas label Keeled Scales, it stands apart from the countrygaze pack while sharing its scene. It's for fans who want the loudest, least twangy corner of the current DIY guitar-rock underground.
lineage: Formed within North Carolina's twang-and-shoegaze scene before relocating to Brooklyn; its sound sits between C4 countrygaze and straighter, heavier guitar rock.

description: A Brooklyn songwriter's guitar-and-synth indie rock record, made with players from the Ruination Record Co. circle. Clean guitars and glowing synths frame understated vocals and mid-tempo songs. It suits listeners who like thoughtful, low-key indie rock.
lineage: Part of the same small Brooklyn songwriter-collaborator scene as Adeline Hotel, Office Culture and The Bird Calls.

description: A batch of scrappy rock sketches built on Telecaster-driven hooks and guitar charm. The earworm rippers mix Nuggets garage and '90s indie jangle with punk swagger, most of them over in about two minutes.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Nuggets-era garage rock and '90s indie jangle.

description: kitship's am i a rock? is low-key acoustic singer-songwriter fare and understated lo-fi indie rock, built on commanding vocals and instant, unfussy melodies. It suits listeners who like scrappy, tuneful home recordings.
lineage: Sounds akin to the current Chicago Bandcamp slacker/lo-fi network around acts like Sharp Pins.

description: Cooper's third album trades the jam-guitar sound of her earlier band for a crisper, Beck-like mix of fuzz bass, piano and twinkling synths. It is warm, direct pop-rock songwriting with a slacker's DIY informality, for listeners who like hooks with a homemade edge.
lineage: Sounds like a former jam/psych-rock guitarist moving toward a more concise, jangle-adjacent indie-pop songwriting style.

description: An anthemic yet intimate pop-rock record that sits between energetic and vulnerable songwriting. It continues the band's move from scrappy Philadelphia basement pop-punk toward bigger power-pop hooks.
lineage: Latest chapter of Remember Sports' Philadelphia DIY power-pop lineage.

description: Slow Pulp's third album continues the band's move toward pristine, contemporary alt-rock that melds 1990s shoegaze scale with direct pop songwriting. The emotional stakes run higher and the production is more polished, for fans who liked Yard's balance of noise and melody.
lineage: A continuation of Yard's shoegaze-meets-Americana synthesis, pushing further into polished, radio-ready alt-rock.

description: Lindsey Jordan's third Snail Mail album follows Valentine with clear-eyed, jangling guitar-pop, keeping the conversational, unadorned vocal delivery that made Lush a breakout. Harmonized guitars and a breezy, hushed touch carry songs about heartbreak, for listeners who want confessional indie rock without much studio gloss.
lineage: Continues Snail Mail's own lineage from Lush through Valentine, staying within confessional, guitar-led jangle-pop songwriting.

description: A Los Angeles band's debut LP, blending frantic C86-style jangle-pop with post-punk urgency and a touch of Flying Nun. Ten songs of tightly wound guitar interplay and restless energy.
lineage: A direct 2020s continuation of the Flying Nun/C86 jangle lineage that runs through this whole lane.

description: The London 'Celtic jangle boyband' moves to Merge for its third album, pushing its shimmering, virtuosic guitar-pop further with folk touches and a second, steelier vocal presence arguing against Owen Williams's familiar persona across songs about grief and regret. It's the most ambitious Tubs record yet.
lineage: Builds directly on Dead Meat and Cotton Crown's jangle-pop songwriting, deepening the band's British folk-jangle hybrid.

description: The Indianapolis band's follow-up to Triple Seven continues their blend of fuzzy shoegaze guitar textures with unabashedly sweet, jangling pop melodies. It keeps the same sugar-and-noise balance that made Triple Seven a breakout.
lineage: Continues Wishy's fusion of shoegaze guitar-wall production with 1990s power-pop songwriting established on Triple Seven.

description: The Boston trio's self-titled debut sets Dimitri Giannopoulos's deadpan, half-sung vocals over slow, heavy, effects-laden guitar figures. It is a foundational document of the 2010s Boston slowcore-adjacent scene, closer to Duster's hazy drift than to any twang.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Duster and Codeine-style slowcore fed through a melodic, riff-driven Boston indie-rock lens; precedes the band's run of Run for Cover albums.

description: Imbecile is an early, self-recorded document from Boone Patrello's Dead Sullivan project, raw, hushed songs made before his work in the Texas slowcore band Teethe. It is rougher and more diaristic than his later work, for listeners curious about where that sound started.
lineage: A direct predecessor to Teethe, tying Dead Sullivan to the same Texas slowcore lineage that runs through this lane.

description: Friendship's early album stretches Dan Wriggins' plainspoken, funny-sad songwriting over synthesizer, pedal steel and Rhodes piano, mixing live and programmed drums. It is patient, homemade-sounding Americana about work, loneliness and friendship, closer to a whisper than a shout.
lineage: Early Philadelphia-era record; the twisted, ambient-pedal-steel take on Americana heard on Friendship's later Merge records seems to start here.

description: Thx is Hannah Read's hushed, homespun early full-length as Lomelda, short songs of plainspoken lyrics over sparse acoustic and electric guitar, recorded with the DIY intimacy of her Silsbee, Texas project. It sits at the quiet, unresolved end of the 2010s Bandcamp folk scene, closer to a diary than a studio record.
lineage: An early Lomelda record and precursor to M for Empathy and Hannah; its hushed songs sound akin to the 2010s Bandcamp folk scene.

description: Expect the Best is Widowspeak's heaviest, most nocturnal record, a mix of somber indie rock, dream pop and grungy twang. Molly Hamilton's melodies stay pretty even as the songs sit in dread and self-doubt, over glacial tempos and Telecaster crunch.
lineage: Follows All Yours and lays groundwork for the country-tinged twang that deepens on Plum and The Jacket.

description: Produced with BJ Burton, 'Double Negative' buries Sparhawk and Parker's harmonies under distorted, glitching electronics and collapsing beats, sounding less like a band recording live and more like a slowcore album being digitally destroyed in real time. The tempos are still slow and the mood still devotional, but the texture is closer to noise music than to the hushed folk-rock of the band's debut. It is for listeners willing to hear a thirty-year-old sound radically rebuilt.
lineage: A late-career reinvention of Low's own slowcore template, pushed into noise and glitch textures that resemble what younger hushed and noise-leaning bands were exploring in the 2010s.

description: Released after a reissue campaign by Numero Group revived interest in Stratosphere and Contemporary Movement, this self-titled reunion album picks up the band's hazy, slow-motion four-track sound almost exactly where they left off nearly two decades earlier. The songs are just as murky and unhurried as the '90s records, proof that the trio's aesthetic was never really a product of its era's recording limits alone. It arrived into a scene of younger bands who had spent years citing Duster as an influence, closing a loop between original slowcore and its 2010s revival.
lineage: A 2019 reunion by a 1990s V12 band that lands squarely in the modern slowcore revival it helped inspire; filed primary in C8 with V12 as secondary.

description: Dreamin' trades Friendship's earlier drum machines for a warmer, more organic sound built on acoustic guitars, soft drums and a haunting pedal steel. Dan Wriggins' lyrics sit in the gap between intimacy and loneliness, sung in a plainspoken near-murmur.
lineage: A bridge between Friendship's rougher early records and the fuller Merge albums to come; its unhurried, country-inflected hush sounds akin to Lomelda.

description: So Divine widens Horse Jumper of Love's palette slightly while keeping their signature slow tempos and heavy-lidded, half-mumbled vocals. Guitars still swell into distorted crescendos, but the songwriting is more direct and melodic than the debut.
lineage: First album for Run for Cover, the label that would house the band through its most acclaimed run; still sounds indebted to Duster/Codeine slowcore.

description: M for Empathy is Hannah Read's most stripped-down Lomelda record, brief, whispery songs built from silence, half-finished phrases and spare guitar. It feels like things long unsaid finally let out, a record about making peace with her own voice.
lineage: The quietest turn in Lomelda's catalog between Thx and Hannah, sounding akin to the hushed Texas and Bandcamp folk of the 2010s.

description: Hannah is Read's most fleshed-out Lomelda album, tender, unhurried songs that move between fragile solo passages and warmer full-band arrangements while keeping her plainspoken, diaristic lyrics at the center. It is patient, intimate Texas indie folk built for close listening.
lineage: Consolidates the hushed songwriting of Thx and M for Empathy into a fuller sound.

description: Ella O'Connor Williams's debut as Squirrel Flower is a hushed, unsettled record full of water imagery, quiet indie folk-rock that occasionally breaks into noise. It set the template for her louder, twangier records to come.
lineage: An early, quieter entry in a catalog that grows steadily louder and sounds more countrygaze-indebted with each release.

description: Teethe's self-titled debut is a self-produced, self-mixed set of slow, hushed Texas indie rock. It is an early, raw document of the slowcore group.
lineage: Sounds rooted in Texas DIY slowcore; a rawer predecessor to the more polished Magic of the Sale.

description: Plum is Widowspeak's warmest, most unhurried record. Molly Hamilton's honeyed voice sits over dusty, sun-worn guitars and easy tempos that lean further into the band's country and '90s dream-pop touchstones than the darker Expect the Best before it.
lineage: Follows Expect the Best and precedes The Jacket in Widowspeak's later-career turn toward a twangier, more overtly country-inflected version of their dream-pop sound.

description: Bnny's debut, written by Jess Viscius in the years after her partner's death, is inky, minimalist noir-pop delivered in a half-whispered voice. It draws on the Velvet Underground's two-chord simplicity for its lo-fi, grief-centered songs.
lineage: The record that established Bnny's hushed, grief-soaked sound, setting up the fuller-band, more shoegaze-inflected One Million Love Songs.

description: Friendship's Merge Records debut is gentle, curious and patient, built around Dan Wriggins' plainspoken baritone and lyrics that reward close listening. It is quietly funny and often devastating, evoking a very particular strand of hushed, country-tinged indie rock.
lineage: Friendship's move to Merge after earlier small-label records carried their slow-burn, country-tinged indie rock to a wider audience.

description: Talk Soon is Carolina Chauffe's raw, introspective phone-fi bedroom folk record. It is intimate and homey, songs caught close to the mic between long drives.
lineage: Early, fully self-recorded hemlock LP that establishes the hushed, song-a-day approach Chauffe later builds on; sounds close to Lomelda's plainspoken Texas hush.

description: Natural Part is a tighter, more focused set of songs than the band's earlier records, still built on Dimitri Giannopoulos's murmured deadpan and slow-burn guitar dynamics. It is a good entry point for the band's core sound of hushed verses breaking into fuzzed-out release.
lineage: Continues the band's Run for Cover run; sounds akin to Duster and Bedhead and sits among 2020s slowcore revival bands.

description: Marketplace is The Namby Pamby's debut, sparse but pretty slow-burn indie rock with quiet guitars and understated vocals. It favors patient builds and understated melody over hooks, suited to fans of slowcore's gentler side.
lineage: A small-market Midwest counterpart to the slowcore-adjacent bands (Horse Jumper of Love, Teethe) this lane tracks.

description: The Jacket is built from layered guitars, dusty percussion and ambling bass, with Widowspeak leaning fully into outlaw-country and slowcore reference points like Neil Young and Cowboy Junkies. Molly Hamilton's voice stays front and center over road-song imagery.
lineage: The most explicitly twangy Widowspeak record, extending the country turn begun on Plum.

description: Sounds is a side project from villagerrr's songwriter, a set of hushed, lo-fi songs leaning into a wandering, small-town Americana feel. It is looser and more homemade than villagerrr's main output, for listeners who like sketches as much as finished songs.
lineage: A side outlet for villagerrr's songwriter, sharing that band's hushed, homespun sound.

description: Newfoundland's Aaron Powell makes quiet, grainy, homespun songwriting on Midnight Society, his most dynamic Fog Lake record. A few rockers recall You Forgot It in People-era Broken Social Scene amid the usual hush.
lineage: Part of Powell's long-running, prolific solo bedroom-folk catalog; sounds like a lo-fi Canadian counterpart to the American hushed-twang scene this lane tracks.

description: Hataałiinez Wheeler's debut LP as Hataałii is mysterious, hypnotic Arizona indie rock. His deep-voiced surf-country croon, with shades of Jim Morrison and Lou Reed, sits against sparse, slow arrangements.
lineage: First widely heard record from Hataałii; establishes the slow, serene surf-country sound he expands on Waiting for a Sign and I'll Be Around.

description: Heartbreak Rules keeps Horse Jumper of Love's slow, weighty tempos while pushing the vocals closer to the front of the mix. It is a moody, unhurried record about heartbreak, delivered with the band's usual dry understatement.
lineage: A steady continuation of the band's Run for Cover-era sound between Natural Part and Disaster Trick.

description: A short EP of slow-motion, synth-tinged dream-folk from Carly Bond's Bay Area project: sparse arrangements, cavernous reverb and a fragile, close-mic'd vocal at the center. The songs drift rather than build, suited to late-night, headphone listening.
lineage: Extends Meernaa's hushed songwriting, which sounds suspended between Duster-style haze and modern indie folk.

description: Justin Morris's Sluice project makes open-hearted, lyrically dense songwriting, loose and lived-in with pastoral, fingerpicked arrangements. It is quiet, plainspoken music about time, faith and place.
lineage: Sounds akin to the Durham/Triangle DIY folk-rock circle around Fust; its hushed, country-tinged songwriting leads into Companion.

description: Lily of the Valley is Will Kennedy's second 22º Halo album, hopeful, lively songs with real weight underneath. It sits between folk, slacker rock and bedroom pop, its plainspoken hush carrying emotion without turning maudlin.
lineage: Sounds akin to Philadelphia's hushed, homemade strand of indie folk.

description: Heart of the Artichoke is Iris James Garrison's delicate, perceptive record about connection and healing, built from spacious, full-bodied folk songs. Earworm melodies and warm, unfussy arrangements keep it intimate without excess polish. It suits listeners who like gentle indie folk with strong hooks.
lineage: Sounds akin to the hushed-folk collaborator network around Babehoven and Lomelda.

description: Bnny's second album is a slowcore, shoegaze and garage record about life after grief. Jess Viscius's hushed vocals sit over heavier, more fleshed-out arrangements than the debut.
lineage: Continues the grief-driven songwriting of Everything with a fuller, noisier Chicago band sound.

description: Fine's debut Rocky Top Ballads is impeccably crafted minimalist songwriting with rootsy, bluegrass-tinged elements and a Hope Sandoval-style hush over every track.
lineage: Part of the current hushed-twang wave that pairs slowcore dynamics with bluegrass instrumentation, in the vein of Duster-descended acts.

description: Waiting for a Sign is impressionistic and obliquely Nick Cave-like, Hataałii's warbling baritone floating over slow, eerie Americana. It is late-night roadhouse music, all reverb and slow sway.
lineage: Second Dangerbird Records LP, continuing the hushed, ornate Americana Hataałii built on Singing Into Darkness.

description: 444 reimagines twelve of Carolina Chauffe's phone-recorded songs with a full Chicago band, crunchy and enthralling, split between intimate homespun folk and twangy indie rock. It was recorded in a two-day session the week Chauffe left Chicago for the road.
lineage: hemlock's most fully-realized full-band record to date, built from years of solo song-a-day recordings; a direct peer to Lomelda and Little Mazarn's Texas/Midwest hushed-folk circle.

description: amen! gives Carolina Chauffe's solo intimacy full-band urgency, recorded live as a trio. The songs keep hemlock's hushed, plainspoken core while the band pushes them forward.
lineage: Bridges hemlock's earlier solo phone-fi work and the full-band 444; sounds rooted in the same Texas hushed-folk orbit as Lomelda.

description: Another slow, heavy-lidded set of Horse Jumper of Love songs, all murmured vocals and guitars that build toward distorted release. It is the band's most refined take on hushed-to-heavy dynamics, for slowcore fans.
lineage: The band's most recent full-length, continuing its Run for Cover run as one of the most visible modern slowcore-adjacent groups.

description: Little Kid's Orindal Records debut sets Kenny Boothby's urgent, soft-spoken voice against intimate, relentlessly hummable slow-tempo songs. Exploratory jazz touches color the arrangements.
lineage: Toronto songwriter Kenny Boothby's project shares Orindal Records with Friendship and sounds akin to that label's quiet, folk-leaning roster.

description: Any Light is a sophisticated, deliberately paced folk record from Victoria, BC's Loving, unhurried songs built on close harmony and patient arrangement. It favors restraint over hooks, rewarding slow, careful listening.
lineage: A Canadian counterpart to the hushed American folk-rock this lane tracks, working at its own unhurried pace outside any particular scene.

description: Molly Meehan's debut as vega is gentle, adventurous Burlington indie rock. Soft vocals and patient guitars lean toward the folk-indebted side of the scene.
lineage: Sounds akin to the Burlington, Vermont DIY scene around Greg Freeman that feeds this lane's softer end.

description: Golden Caravan swings between pummeling noise and jangle, with moody slowcore passages. A subtle twang runs underneath the loud-quiet dynamics.
lineage: Sounds akin to the Boston indie-rock underground of Horse Jumper of Love, mixing slowcore heaviness with a lighter, country-tinged jangle.

description: Body is a dynamic debut swinging from homespun quiet to raging catharsis, recalling Elliott Smith, Pinback and Owen through natural, unpolished harmonies. It favors emotional whiplash over consistency of mood, suiting listeners who like slowcore with emo's sudden surges.
lineage: Sits at the emo-adjacent, slowcore-leaning edge of this lane, closer to Horse Jumper of Love and Joyer than to overt twang.

description: Friendship's second Merge album widens their idea of country music further, setting shambolic guitars against flute pads and a Motown-ish rhythm section under bleary poetry. Dan Wriggins' ragged baritone cuts through murky, wry songs like 'Betty Ford'.
lineage: Continues Friendship's slow, twang-inflected songwriting with more polish and range, staying rooted in the same understated, funny-sad register.

description: Hannah Pruzinsky threads Wurlitzer, saxophone and synth through an explorative, quiet folk framework on Red sky at morning. It is a meditation on love, control and domesticity that never rises above a gentle murmur.
lineage: Sounds akin to the Florist/Told Slant hushed-folk orbit that also feeds the C8 lane.

description: I'll Be Around continues Hataałii's ornate, eerie Americana. It is a modern crooner's take on heartbreak set over slow, serene surf-country arrangements.
lineage: Third full-length, moving from Dangerbird to the Panther Mountain imprint while keeping the same hushed, baritone-led sound.

description: A live album gathered from Hour's DIY touring, capturing the shifting chamber-folk ensemble in intimate, informal rooms. Winds, strings and quiet percussion breathe around slow, meditative pieces, with the audience close enough to hear. It is a touring-diary counterpart to the studio records.
lineage: A touring-diary document in Hour's catalog before Ghost Bridge, part of the same Dear Life Records world as Cormier-O'Leary's band Friendship.

description: Brothers Nick and Shane Sullivan dial back Joyer's shoegaze leanings for folkier touches on this LP. Pastoral twang runs through cuts like 'Cure' and 'Glare of the Beer Can' alongside spidery, more explosive rock songs.
lineage: Its pull toward folk and twang, after a more purely shoegaze-pop prior record, sounds akin to Horse Jumper of Love and places it at this lane's edge.

description: Little Mazarn pairs Lindsey Verrill's heart-opening vocals and singing saw with bombastic drums and dissonant synths. The record recasts the Austin group's primitive-folk origins into something more expansive.
lineage: Austin's Little Mazarn sounds rooted in the same hushed, Texas folk network as Lomelda and hemlock, following Texas River Song.

description: into a pretty room is lots of hands' Fire Talk debut, a winsome, ramshackle collage of reworked bedroom demos, flickering electronics and processed vocals about grief, growing up and letting go. It sounds fragile and homemade, suited to listeners who like bedroom recordings with an experimental streak.
lineage: Shares Fire Talk Records with Bnny and Fran, part of that label's hushed, home-recorded strand of indie rock.

description: Devin McKnight's Maneka album sits at the combustible intersection of slowcore and shoegaze. It alternates quiet, acoustic reflection with head-splitting noise while staying cohesive.
lineage: McKnight (formerly of Speedy Ortiz and Grass Is Green) built Maneka as a showcase for genre-crossing songwriting; the slowcore passages sound akin to Horse Jumper of Love and Joyer.

description: Otto Benson's first vocally focused album is pretty but austere guitar folk, built around a bassy croon and shimmering pedal steel over a sparse palette. It is quiet driving music for long, empty stretches of American road.
lineage: Released through the WNOADIARWB collective; its hushed, pedal-steel-laced sound is akin to Friendship and Lomelda's country-tinged quiet.

description: The Spot is a stripped-back, wistfully optimistic bedroom-pop record of brief songs favoring hushed, homemade warmth over polish. Soft vocals and simple guitar keep it light and close, for listeners who like gentle, low-key home recordings.
lineage: A small, self-recorded entry in the same breezy, low-key bedroom-folk vein as klark sound and kitship.

description: A level-up for the Texas slowcore group, Magic of the Sale is dark and enveloping. Its nostalgic atmospherics are filled out with strings and pedal steel.
lineage: Teethe's sophomore LP, refining the slow, hushed sound of their self-titled debut with richer, more country-tinged arrangements.

description: I See Them, I See Me finds Maya Bon's Babehoven pushing into full-band indie folk-pop with country and Americana touches, its soaring vocals and explosive production a marked step up from the duo's lo-fi beginnings. It keeps the emotional directness of earlier records while widening the arrangements.
lineage: Babehoven's move toward a fuller, more countrified sound, still close to the hushed-folk network of this lane.

description: tiarn is delicate, immersive ghostly folk from Hana Stretton, built on spectral harmonies and slow, fingerpicked arrangements. It leans toward folk-ambient at its most hushed.
lineage: A quieter, ambient-leaning entry that sounds akin to the modern hushed-folk scene this lane tracks.

description: Michael Cormier-O'Leary's chamber-folk project Hour opens up into a larger ensemble of winds, strings and mallet percussion for slow, meditative pieces. It sits closer to instrumental chamber music than a rock record, patient and quietly mournful. For listeners who like slowcore's pacing without the guitars.
lineage: Cormier-O'Leary also plays in Friendship, and Hour shares Dear Life Records with that Philadelphia deadpan/slowcore circle.

description: Four Days in June has Joseph Shabason and Nicholas Krgovich reaching for '90s CD-era songcraft in the vein of Neil Young's Harvest Moon and k.d. lang. Brushed drums and understated pedal steel, banjo and fiddle give their usual wry chamber-pop a country-rock glow. It suits listeners who like soft, grown-up country-tinged pop.
lineage: Sounds indebted to '90s pop-country and Cosmic American touchstones while keeping the duo's own understated, plainspoken songwriting.

description: Blanket is hazy, meditative folk rock pairing gorgeousness with eeriness and wonkiness. Its slow tempos and murky production sit close to the lane's slowcore-adjacent end.
lineage: Follows Shep Treasure's earlier EPs; its hushed, murky sound is akin to Joyer's East Coast DIY folk-rock.

description: Companion is weirder and more interior than Radial Gate, with fiddle, Wurlitzer and tape-echo textures around Justin Morris's plainspoken songs. Room noise and found sound are left in the mix.
lineage: A follow-up to Radial Gate, deepening Sluice's hushed, conversational folk-rock.

description: beacon, how blue pairs soft, openhearted, melancholic indie rock with woozy twang and waltz-like arrangements. It follows trust me, i'm trying with a gentler country lean.
lineage: Second vega LP, continuing Molly Meehan's plainspoken, gently twangy Burlington indie-folk songwriting.

description: Roses is airtight, soaring Widowspeak songwriting with woozy Americana flourishes. Its twangy signifiers push beyond pure mood-setting toward the country side of the band's dream-pop sound.
lineage: Follows Widowspeak's quieter Captured Tracks albums (Expect the Best, Plum, The Jacket), continuing what sounds like a late-career drift from dream pop toward the C8 sound.

description: Hop Along's second full-length introduced Frances Quinlan's cracked, yelping voice to a wider audience over ramshackle, folk-punk-adjacent indie rock. There is little literal twang here, but the loose, front-porch informality of the arrangements and the plainspoken storytelling put it on the emo/DIY side of the Core's borderline territory.
lineage: Originally released on Hot Green Records; its emo-adjacent songwriting sounds like an antecedent to later Core bands such as Cusp.

description: Pinegrove's self-released debut lays out the template before the band had fully found it: Evan Stephens Hall's literary, run-on lyricism over loose, country-tinged indie rock. Rougher and less confident than what followed, it is mostly for the committed who want to trace the band's arc from house-show DIY act to genre touchstone.
lineage: Grew out of New Jersey DIY house shows; the seed that Cardinal refined into an alt-country/emo hybrid that later Core bands sound indebted to.

description: Hop Along's Saddle Creek debut sharpens the loose folk-punk of Get Disowned into tighter, more melodic songwriting. Frances Quinlan's voice is still the main instrument but now framed by fuller, more anthemic arrangements.
lineage: First Hop Along album on Saddle Creek; sounds like an antecedent to the emotionally direct, character-driven indie rock of younger Core bands such as Cusp and Wednesday.

description: Pinegrove's breakthrough: eight songs of confessional, run-on-sentence lyricism set to alt-country-inflected indie rock, softening emo's sincerity into something closer to a bar-band singalong. Evan Stephens Hall's talk-singing delivery and the band's tight, chiming interplay made it a touchstone for the emo-twang crossover.
lineage: Followed the self-released Meridian and the Everything So Far anthology; its blend of Crazy Horse-lite guitar and confessional emo phrasing is echoed by Slaughter Beach, Dog, Cusp and other Core bands.

description: Jake Ewald's first record outside Modern Baseball trades that band's pop-punk urgency for loose, talky Americana, its narrators drifting through small towns and diners in a warm, unhurried drawl. It is a quieter, more countrified debut than anything in Ewald's emo background, setting up the storytelling mode Slaughter Beach, Dog would keep refining.
lineage: Jake Ewald's post-Modern Baseball project, moving from pop-punk toward the alt-country and heartland-rock songwriting of Slaughter Beach, Dog's later records.

description: Released under the band's earlier name Sioux Falls, this debut LP lays out the emo-tinged, twangy indie rock that would carry into Strange Ranger's later records. Quiet, hushed verses give way to sudden bursts of noise, for fans of sprawling emo-leaning guitar rock.
lineage: The starting point of what became Strange Ranger's emo-twang crossover songwriting; it sounds akin to the Tiny Engines-adjacent DIY scene of bands like Free Cake for Every Creature.

description: Slaughter Beach, Dog's second LP fleshes out the full-band sound only sketched on Welcome, with warmer arrangements and closer harmonies behind Jake Ewald's short-story-style narratives of small-town Pennsylvania life. It leans further into alt-country structure while keeping the plainspoken, novelistic detail that separates it from Ewald's emo past.
lineage: Follows Welcome; continues the band's move from Modern Baseball-adjacent emo toward a full alt-country and heartland-rock sound.

description: Strange Ranger's second album leans into a rawer, more spacious sound than their debut. It still balances hushed indie-folk passages against noisier emo-indebted guitar surges, suiting listeners who like quiet-loud dynamics with a twang.
lineage: Continues the twangy emo-crossover songwriting begun as Sioux Falls, moving toward the fuller sound of Remembering the Rockets.

description: Hop Along's third album adds string arrangements and more elaborate production to the band's yelping, emotionally raw songwriting, widening its scope without losing Frances Quinlan's idiosyncratic phrasing. It is the most polished Hop Along record, and the closest the band gets to the anthemic, full-band scale that defines the wider Core sound.
lineage: Third full-length from the Philadelphia band; its emo-to-indie-rock arc sounds akin to fellow Philadelphia acts like Slaughter Beach, Dog.

description: Recorded before the allegations that led to the band's year-long hiatus and released independently once the group returned, Skylight is quieter and more inward than Cardinal, trading some of its predecessor's forward motion for slower, more reflective songs still built on the same alt-country-emo frame. It reads as a transitional record between the band's DIY years and their later, more polished Rough Trade albums.
lineage: Bridges Cardinal and the Rough Trade era; released independently in 2018 after the band's hiatus.

description: A more polished, expansive record than its predecessors, Safe and Also No Fear widens Slaughter Beach, Dog's palette with strings and richer arrangements behind Jake Ewald's character-driven songwriting. It keeps the band's core alt-country-emo hybrid intact while pushing toward a more widescreen, adult-contemporary version of the sound.
lineage: Third LP; deepens the alt-country storytelling of Welcome and Birdie with more ambitious production.

description: The last Strange Ranger album before their turn toward electronic production, capping the band's emo-tinged indie rock era. Its arrangements are fuller and more anthemic than Rot Forever or Daymoon, for listeners who like big, yearning guitar rock.
lineage: The culmination of Strange Ranger's twangy emo-crossover songwriting before the band moved toward electronic textures on later records.

description: Pinegrove's Rough Trade debut is warmer and more settled than the band's earlier records, its alt-country and emo elements now fully integrated into a smooth, mid-tempo sound built for singing along in a crowd. It is less jagged than Cardinal but keeps the same core: banjo and pedal steel under Hall's rambling, diaristic lines.
lineage: First album on Rough Trade, following the band's independent years; represents the emo-twang crossover moving toward a more polished, festival-ready sound.

description: Caleb Cordes's Sinai Vessel moved from twinkly emo toward a heavier, more patient indie-rock sound here. Slide guitar glides through confessional songs about guilt, grief and the exhaustion of trying to be good, several of them long and slow-building.
lineage: Follows the more emo-scaled Brokenlegged; sounds like a step toward the twangier indie rock of the Core.

description: A looser, lower-stakes Slaughter Beach, Dog record that lets songs stretch out and drift. It is still built on Jake Ewald's storytelling, with patient, jammy arrangements and a relaxed, late-night mood.
lineage: Follows Safe and Also No Fear in the band's run on Lame-O Records.

description: Home Is Where's breakout debut crams whirlwind hardcore aggression and warm, harmonica-flecked folk melancholy into a short record. Bea MacDonald's voice ranges from an intimate, Dylan-esque croon to a full-throated scream, often within the same song, splitting the difference between gothic post-punk and twangy Americana.
lineage: Set the template for the band's fusion of American Football-style emo with country and folk instrumentation that the whaler expanded on.

description: Elise Okusami's second Oceanator album pairs big, emo-scaled guitar hooks with disarmingly direct lyrics about anxiety and dread. The songs move between crunchy pop-punk and more open, twangy indie-rock passages, for fans of cathartic, hook-heavy guitar music.
lineage: Sounds descended from 2000s emo and pop-punk filtered through 2020s indie-rock production, close in spirit to the emo-twang crossover of bands like Strange Ranger.

description: A more overtly political and climate-anxious record than its predecessors, 11:11 keeps Pinegrove's alt-country-emo blend intact while widening the lyrical lens from personal confession to collective dread. The band's interlocking guitars and pedal steel still carry the emotional weight, but the songs lean more anthemic than introspective.
lineage: Second Rough Trade album; continues the band's move from DIY confessional songwriting toward larger, more communal themes.

description: Cusp's full-length debut fuses twinkling, twangy indie-rock guitar with grungy, alt-gaze fuzz. Its dynamic tracks move between haunting quiet passages and unsettled, noisy choruses, grappling lyrically with powerlessness and the limits of ambition.
lineage: Sounds close to the Chicago emo-twang axis of Friko and to Warehouse, Mothers and Ovlov.

description: A concept record about getting used to the world getting worse, the whaler adds pedal steel, trumpet and banjo to Home Is Where's anxious, apocalyptic emo. Its interconnected songs take as many cues from Bob Dylan as from American Football, ambitious and exhilarating by turns.
lineage: Second LP, following the breakout i became birds; sounds like proof the emo-twang crossover extends beyond the Wednesday/MJ Lenderman axis, alongside Cusp and Twine.

description: Slaughter Beach, Dog's fifth LP is warm, intimate storytelling wrapped in muted, gentle Americana, with Erin Rae guesting. 'Float Away', an ode to the Delaware River, is the clearest statement of Jake Ewald's plainspoken, place-obsessed songwriting a decade into the project.
lineage: Fifth full-length; the fullest, most settled version yet of the alt-country songwriting Ewald began developing after Modern Baseball.

description: Strange Ranger return to guitar-based songwriting after an electronic detour, with a warmer, more settled sound. It closes out the emo-twang arc that began as Sioux Falls, for longtime fans and newcomers who like reflective, gently twangy indie rock.
lineage: A return to guitar-based twangy indie rock after a synth-pop detour, closing the band's arc from Rot Forever through Remembering the Rockets.

description: Friko's debut LP is huge, cathartic, theatrical indie rock built on Niko Kapetan's powerhouse vocals, which build from hushed verses to hair-raising, screamed peaks. Orchestral swells and emo-scale dynamics are layered over anthemic guitar rock.
lineage: Emerged from Chicago's DIY scene; folds Midwest emo's emotional extremity into anthemic indie rock that sounds as close to Broken Social Scene and Neutral Milk Hotel as to twangier Core peers.

description: A move from Caleb Cordes's earlier emo toward resonant heartland indie rock about the toll of making music for a living, with pedal steel making the shift audible. Plainspoken songs move between road-worn resignation and moments of quiet hope, closer to Slaughter Beach, Dog's storytelling than to Sinai Vessel's twinkly beginnings.
lineage: Third full-length; the clearest example yet of Sinai Vessel's drift from emo toward Americana-inflected indie rock.

description: Heartland twang and Dirty Three-style violin sit inside a post-hardcore band's dynamics, with feedback swelling behind heart-on-sleeve, grief-stricken lyrics. It sounds close to Songs: Ohia and the Frames, pulling between noise and twang throughout.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Unwound and Fugazi's post-hardcore dynamics, carried into the twangier, string-laced emo of the 2020s Core scene.

description: Cusp's Exploding In Sound debut pairs anthemic, '90s-styled rock with pedal steel and squiggly synths, wrapping anxious lyrics in the band's grungiest, most confident arrangements yet. It holds emo's emotional rawness inside a full, twangy band sound.
lineage: Follows You Can Do It All; the move to Exploding In Sound places them near other Chicago and Northeast emo-twang crossover acts.

description: A tighter follow-up to New Old Horse, keeping the band's post-hardcore-meets-heartland-twang balance intact across shorter, more direct songs about restlessness and dead-end relationships. It is a stopgap EP rather than a statement, but it confirms the sound was no fluke.
lineage: Follows New Old Horse; continues the Fugazi-to-countrygaze pull the earlier LP set out.

description: Friko's second album pushes the band's frantic, explosive sound toward longer, more compositionally ambitious pieces without losing the crescendos that made their debut a breakout. It is a cathartic record for anyone who wants indie rock that swings for the rafters.
lineage: Follows Where We've Been, Where We Go From Here; the band's continued expansion of Chicago DIY emo-rock into more orchestral, art-rock territory.

description: A ten-song record where big hooks and feedback crash into banjo, mandolin, accordion and toy instruments, with shouted, harmonized vocals and loose studio chatter left in. It swings hard between hushed folk moments and punk blowouts, which puts it on the emo-twang side of the map. For listeners who like their folk-punk messy and their emo with a string band in the room.
lineage: Folk-punk-leaning emo that sounds indebted to Titus Andronicus's rowdier moments and the Pinegrove-era emo-twang crossover; its acoustic instruments tie it to the DIY folk revival around the Core.

description: This band's debut LP is a collaborative, cathartic mix of '90s alternative dynamics, 2010s emo phrasing, and pedal-tinged bedroom folk. The jams build from hushed verses to full-band peaks, running toward heartbreak rather than away from it.
lineage: Released on Good English Records; sounds akin to the emo-into-twang wave of Cusp and Twine, but with a more explicitly folk, pedal-steel palette.

description: Will Johnson's debut full-length as Centro-matic is scrappy, fuzzed-out guitar rock cut fast and cheap. It sounds like a home-recorded garage band with a country streak rather than a polished studio act, closer to lo-fi indie rock than to alt-country proper. It marks the start of the prolific Denton output that Centro-matic and South San Gabriel would build out over the next two decades.
lineage: Launches Will Johnson's Centro-matic and, with it, the Denton, Texas wing of the Molina/Magnolia orbit.

description: Released the same year as the Songs: Ohia debut, this early EP collects spare, plainly recorded songs like 'Pass' and 'Defenders' that feel closer to sketches than finished songs. It shares the debut's stark voice-and-guitar sound and dark, allusive titles. It is a minor, early document more than a destination record, useful mainly for hearing how quickly Molina was already writing and releasing material.
lineage: A same-year companion to the Songs: Ohia debut LP, part of the flood of early Secretly Canadian releases that established Molina's stark solo sound before the full band arrived.

description: Jason Molina's debut as Songs: Ohia, nicknamed 'the Black Album' for its plain dark sleeve, is little more than his high, reverb-soaked voice and a spare guitar, cut fast and plainly. The songs sit over almost no percussion, just repeated, incantatory phrases about ghosts, rivers and the Midwestern dark. It set the stark, haunted template Molina returned to for the rest of his career.
lineage: Molina's first single came out on Will Oldham's Palace Records, and this album sounds kin to the same lo-fi, DIY folk underground; it established the voice-and-guitar minimalism that later Songs: Ohia and Magnolia Electric Co. records built from or reacted against.

description: Molina's second Songs: Ohia LP keeps the rough, homemade feel of the debut but lets a looser, shifting cast of players clatter behind him, giving songs like 'An Ace Unable to Change' a more unsettled pulse. The songs drift between hushed voice-and-guitar pieces and ramshackle band takes, with titles that hint at a private mythology. It is rougher and more obscure than the albums that followed, a transitional record between bedroom tape and full-band songwriter.
lineage: Bridges the stripped-down debut and the fuller-band Axxess & Ace, part of Molina's rapid early run of Secretly Canadian-adjacent releases out of the Bloomington/Chicago underground.

description: Centro-matic's second album thickens the fuzz-guitar rock of the debut with more developed arrangements while keeping Johnson's frayed, unpolished vocal delivery up front. The songs still sound cut live and fast, prioritizing feel over finish. It shows Centro-matic edging from lo-fi noise-rock toward the more country-inflected sound of their 2000s records.
lineage: Continues Centro-matic's fast, fuzz-heavy development toward the fuller alt-country/Crazy Horse sound of 'Distance and Clime' and 'Love You Just the Same'.

description: Axxess & Ace tightens Molina's songwriting into something closer to conventional verse-chorus structure while keeping the hushed, echo-drenched production of his earliest work. 'Captain Badass' stretches out as a slow-burning centerpiece, while 'Love & Work' and 'Redhead' show a plainer, more direct kind of heartbreak song. It is the record where Molina's songwriting starts to catch up with his atmosphere, and a good first stop for newcomers.
lineage: Continues the Secretly Canadian run that runs from Songs: Ohia's debut through The Lioness, tightening the songwriting that would fully bloom on Didn't It Rain and Magnolia Electric Co.

description: Released on the Netherlands-based Munich label, this album keeps pace with Centro-matic's rapid-fire recording habits, another set of scuffed-up, guitar-forward rock songs built around Will Johnson's plainspoken drawl. The same fuzzed, Crazy Horse-tilted core of their celebrated 2000s records is already in place. It underlines how prolifically Centro-matic worked in their first Denton decade.
lineage: One of several rapid-fire early Centro-matic releases building the fuzz-guitar, alt-country sound the band would refine through the 2000s.

description: Ghost Tropic is the slowest and most drone-like Songs: Ohia record, built from long, barely-moving pieces like 'Not Just a Ghost's Heart' and 'Incantation.' Molina's guitar and voice sit in wide, reverberant space with sparse percussion rather than pushing toward a chorus, closer to American slowcore than to a folk or country record. It is for patient listeners who want Molina at his most spectral.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Low- and Codeine-style slowcore more than any other Songs: Ohia record, sitting between the folk-noir of The Lioness and the gospel-country turn of Didn't It Rain.

description: A solo, mostly acoustic album sold at live shows, Protection Spells is one of Molina's least-heard records, closer in spirit to the stark debut than to the full-band records surrounding it. The songs are recorded plainly, voice and guitar with little else, slow and hushed. It is a tour artifact for committed fans rather than a starting point.
lineage: A between-albums tour-only release from the same 2000 stretch that produced The Lioness and Ghost Tropic, showing the stripped-down solo mode Molina kept returning to between full-band records.

description: Recorded in Scotland with Alasdair Roberts and members of Arab Strap, The Lioness pairs Molina's voice with a chillier, more atmospheric backing than his American records, opening on the slow drone of 'The Black Crow.' Songs like 'Lioness' and 'Tigress' move at a near-funereal pace, closer to Scottish folk-noir than to Americana. It is one of the clearest points of contact between the Songs: Ohia catalog and the Drag City/Will Oldham circle, via Roberts.
lineage: Made with Alasdair Roberts and members of Arab Strap in Scotland, linking the Songs: Ohia catalog directly to the UK folk underground that also produced Roberts's own records.

description: Will Johnson's quieter alter-ego project to Centro-matic, South San Gabriel's debut was originally released under the Centro-matic name before Johnson split his catalog into a loud band and a hushed one. Sparse, slow, and largely acoustic, it points toward the slowcore-adjacent side of the Denton scene rather than Centro-matic's fuzzed-out rock. It is the origin point of a project Johnson would keep alive alongside Centro-matic for another decade.
lineage: Splits off from Centro-matic as Will Johnson's hushed, slow-tempo alter ego, establishing a quieter parallel track to the Crazy Horse fuzz of his main band.

description: Centro-matic's fourth full-length pushes the band's fuzzed-out guitar rock into longer, more patient arrangements, trading some of the earlier records' scrappiness for a fuller, more deliberate sound. Will Johnson's songwriting stays plainspoken and drawled, but the band -- now a steadier four-piece with Scott Danbom and Mark Hedman -- plays with more room to stretch out. It sits at the midpoint between Centro-matic's lo-fi 1990s records and the more assured 'Love You Just the Same'.
lineage: Marks Centro-matic settling into its core lineup (Johnson, Pence, Danbom, Hedman), the same band that would carry through 'Love You Just the Same' and 'Fort Recovery'.

description: Recorded live in Italy and released there by a small label, this set captures the full-band version of Songs: Ohia on the road, reworking songs like 'Tigress' and 'Being in Love' from The Lioness alongside looser, newer material. It is louder and more electric than the studio records of the same period, with longer, looser arrangements. It documents the road band rather than making a studio statement.
lineage: A snapshot of the touring Songs: Ohia band, showing how the sound opened up once Molina had a full electric group behind him, pointing toward Didn't It Rain and The Magnolia Electric Co.

description: A one-off project pairing Jason Molina with Will Oldham and Scotland's Alasdair Roberts, this is plain, unplugged folk balladry, closer to a front-porch song-swap than any of the three writers' main bands. Tracks like 'Maa Bonny Lad' and 'The Gypsy He-Witch' lean on traditional-sounding melodies and close, unpolished harmonies. It is a minor but telling document of how tightly the Molina and Will Oldham/Drag City circles overlapped.
