'Cast Iron Skillet' strings together small-town parables about judgment and consequence, and the closing 'Miles' runs past seven minutes as a slow-building meditation on aging. It is the sound of the full band playing to its own strengths rather than chasing a single studio mood.
lineage: Returns to the full-band, harmonized-guitar approach of The Nashville Sound after the more orchestrated Reunions, keeping Isbell's storytelling lineage running from Drive-By Truckers through his own solo catalog.

description: Isbell's first fully solo acoustic record since Sirens of the Ditch, cut fast with no 400 Unit and just his own voice and guitar filling the space. 'Bury Me' and the title track work through the end of his marriage in blunt, unsparing detail, while 'Good While It Lasted' takes a plainer, more forgiving view of the same breakup. It strips away nearly two decades of full-band arrangements to leave just the bare songwriting.
lineage: A return to the unaccompanied, acoustic-singer-songwriter mode of Isbell's pre-400 Unit debut Sirens of the Ditch, after seven straight albums made with the full band.

description: An early record credited to Sam Doores and Riley Downing, who would go on to front The Deslondes, played in a ramshackle country-blues style they'd carry into that band. It leans on upright bass, loose acoustic guitars, and weathered group harmonies, closer to a porch session than a studio record. It's for anyone tracing the roots of the Deslondes' street-corner sound back before the band had its name.
lineage: Sam Doores and Riley Downing, both credited here, later co-founded The Deslondes; this is the pre-Deslondes form of their shared songwriting.

description: Doores' debut solo record moves away from the Deslondes' New Orleans R&B-and-country stew toward quieter, piano- and acoustic-led songwriting. Songs like 'Let It Roll' and 'Other Side of Town' keep his easy, conversational drawl but trade the full band's boogie for more intimate arrangements. It's for Deslondes fans curious what one member sounds like on his own.
lineage: A solo record from Deslondes co-founder Sam Doores, released on the band's label, New West.

description: Downing's first solo album is a leaner, more straightforwardly honky-tonk record than his main band, built on twangy electric guitar, pedal steel, and plainspoken breakup songs. The title track and 'Coleman Rose' lean into a classic country shuffle. It's the record for listeners who want the Deslondes' rootsier, more countrified side isolated and pushed forward.
lineage: A solo record from Deslondes co-frontman Riley Downing, released on the band's label, New West.

description: A stripped-back, road-worn Deslondes record built on the band's habit of trading lead vocals and songwriting among members. 'Hold on Liza' and 'Pour Another Round' keep the barroom piano and multi-voice harmonies that define the band's sound, with less studio polish than 'Hurry Home' or 'Ways & Means'. It's for longtime fans following the band's New Orleans country-and-R&B blend.
lineage: The Deslondes' fourth studio album, continuing the shared-songwriting band founded by Sam Doores and Riley Downing.

description: A three-song demo session released on Sam Doores' Mashed Potato Records, catching Casey Jane Reece-Kaigler and Camille Wind Weatherford's paired voices before they had a full band identity. The recordings are spare and rough-edged, built on close harmony over simple guitar backing. It's a curiosity for tracing the Lostines back to their earliest New Orleans sessions.
lineage: Released on Sam Doores' Mashed Potato Records, placing the duo in the same New Orleans DIY-country circle as the Deslondes.

description: The New Orleans duo's proper debut EP, built on the two singers' tightly stacked harmonies over spare guitar and rhythm section. Tracks like 'Faith In Love' and 'Who's Your Love' favor early rock-and-roll and girl-group phrasing filtered through a country-folk band. It's the entry point for the Lostines' pre-full-length sound.
lineage: Follows their 2016 demos on Sam Doores' Mashed Potato Records; released on Nick Shoulders' Gar Hole Records, tying them to the same New Orleans DIY-country scene.

description: A split EP pairing two songs from The Lostines with two from Nick Shoulders & the Okay Crawdad, released jointly by Gar Hole Records and Sam Doores' Mashed Potato Records to mark their overlapping years coming up in New Orleans. The Lostines' side moves from the electric-guitar dancehall stomp of 'A Tear' to the string-and-keyboard hush of 'Last Night'. It documents the small-label, shared-scene connections around the New Orleans Americana underground.
lineage: A cross-label collaboration linking The Lostines' Mashed Potato Records roots to Nick Shoulders' Gar Hole Records, both offshoots of the same New Orleans DIY country scene.

description: The Lostines' full-length debut folds 1960s girl-group harmony singing into a New Orleans roots-band frame, with fiddle, pedal steel, and swooning strings behind Casey Jane Reece-Kaigler and Camille Wind Weatherford's tightly entwined voices. Songs like 'Neon Lights' and 'Full Moon Night' move between late-night dancehall pop and quieter, string-laced balladry. It's the best entry point to the duo's sound.
lineage: Follows EPs released on Mashed Potato Records and Gar Hole Records, both New Orleans DIY-country labels; the girl-group-meets-honky-tonk sound is indebted to '60s pop harmony groups.

description: Winslow-King's second Bloodshot Records album blends New Orleans R&B, ragtime-inflected fingerpicking, and slide guitar into a warm, gospel-tinged roots-rock sound. It's brighter and more arranged than straight blues, built around his easy tenor. Good for listeners who want the city's brass-band and blues traditions filtered through a songwriter's frame.
lineage: Esther Rose sang and played in his band before her solo career; he also shares the early-2010s New Orleans roots scene with Hurray for the Riff Raff and The Deslondes.

description: A follow-up to 'Everlasting Arms' built on slide-guitar blues, New Orleans rhythm, and concise, hook-forward songs, with a looser, more electric feel than its predecessor. 'Esther Please' shows its plainspoken, personal side. It suits listeners drawn to the city's blues-and-roots lineage more than pure country twang.
lineage: Continues Winslow-King's run on Bloodshot Records; sits geographically and stylistically near the New Orleans roots circle of the Deslondes and Hurray for the Riff Raff.

description: A folk-songwriting record that mixes in the French, Cajun, and R&B threads of New Orleans. It's a quiet, singer-songwriter set built around acoustic guitar and a clear, unforced voice, closer to porch-folk than her later, more band-driven work. For listeners tracing New Orleans folk voices adjacent to the Riff Raff/Deslondes scene.
lineage: Sounds akin to the early-2010s New Orleans street-folk and traditional-jazz crossover scene around Hurray for the Riff Raff.

description: A river-titled set pairing Quintana's folk guitar and voice with jazz- and Cajun-inflected arrangements. It's more fleshed-out than her debut, with a full band supporting story-songs about place and water. Good for fans of literate, regionally rooted folk songwriting.
lineage: Sounds rooted in New Orleans folk and traditional jazz, near the city's Americana scene.

description: A short, intimate EP of acoustic story-songs, smaller in scale than her full-lengths but continuing the plainspoken folk style of her earlier records. It functions as a between-albums release rather than a major statement. Best for listeners already following her catalog.
lineage: A small release between 'Miss River' and her later, more produced work.

description: Fronted by a full electric band, this album leans harder into vintage New Orleans R&B and Cajun two-step rhythms than her earlier folk-leaning records. It's a looser, more rhythmic record built for dancing, with the rolling piano-and-horns feel of the city's '50s and '60s R&B. Good for listeners who want Quintana's most fully arranged, band-forward work.
lineage: Sounds indebted to vintage New Orleans R&B in the Fats Domino/Irma Thomas vein, plus Cajun dance music.

description: A hard-country record steeped in honky-tonk shuffles and blue-collar songwriting, with Reedy's plainspoken voice out front. It's twangier and more traditionalist than the Deslondes' genre-blending, closer to classic Bakersfield/outlaw phrasing than to R&B. For listeners who want working-class honky-tonk played straight.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Bakersfield and outlaw country; kin in spirit to the New Orleans street-country of the Deslondes.

description: A record built around travel and homesickness, keeping the band's classic honky-tonk instrumentation of twangy electric guitar and pedal steel under Reedy's plainspoken, working-class songwriting. It's a more settled record than the band's earlier, rowdier output. For fans of traditionalist country songwriting with a road-worn edge.
lineage: Sounds indebted to classic honky-tonk and outlaw country, continuing the sound of 'That's All There Is (And There Ain't No More)'.

description: The debut album by New Orleans songwriter Kelcy Mae Wilburn under the band name Ever More Nest, an Americana record centered on place and rootedness. It pairs a plainspoken, weathered alto with pedal steel and understated full-band arrangements, closer to alt-country balladry than to the city's brass-and-R&B side. It's for listeners who like quiet, place-rooted Americana songwriting.
lineage: Sounds akin to the 2010s New Orleans Americana scene around Hurray for the Riff Raff and The Deslondes.

description: A Cajun record that runs traditional two-step fiddle and French-language singing through distortion pedals and rock-band volume, closer to a noisy roots-punk gig than a dancehall set. It's trad-Cajun instrumentation (fiddle, accordion) pushed into feedback and fuzz. It's for listeners exploring how far a traditional Louisiana form can be pushed toward rock.
lineage: Sits in the trad-Cajun/newgrass Context lane rather than the Deslondes/Riff Raff alt-country lineage, but shares the same New Orleans-area roots-music community and stages; the split is genre (trad Cajun vs. country-rock songwriting) rather than geography.

description: A Grammy-winning Cajun record that folds synthesizers and studio effects into traditional fiddle-and-accordion two-steps, continuing the band's project of modernizing Cajun music without abandoning its French-language core. It's denser and more electronic than 'Mammoth Waltz', while keeping the same two-step dance rhythms. For listeners wanting the trad-Cajun wing of the wider Louisiana roots scene.
lineage: Same trad-Cajun lineage as 'Mammoth Waltz'; connected to the broader New Orleans-area Americana community by geography and shared festival stages, not by songwriting style.

description: Life on the Lawn is a Philadelphia band's plodding, guitar-forward indie rock record, with the loping, anxious 'Wasting the Weekends' as a standout. The songs move at a deliberate, slowcore-adjacent pace, wrapped around conversational, downcast lyrics. It sits closer to the scene's slacker and power-pop wing than to overt country, but the tempo and mood put it near the Core's quieter side.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Pavement-descended slacker rock, with a slowcore undertow that recalls the hushed-twang lane.

description: This self-titled debut is a spare, home-recorded set of guitar rock from Philadelphia's A Country Western. The songs are short and plainly played, favoring direct, diary-like lyrics over polish. It's for listeners who like their slacker rock small, quiet, and unvarnished.
lineage: A DIY, pandemic-era continuation of the Bandcamp slacker-rock tradition that the band would later sharpen on Life on the Lawn.

description: Spent is a ten-song set of plainspoken, guitar-driven folk-rock from St. John's songwriter Andrew Smith, tagged by the artist himself as folk and alt-country. The songs are built from long, narrative verses about touring, fading friendships, and small-town memory, sung in a conversational near-talk-sing delivery. It's for listeners who like wordy, unhurried songwriting with a small-town eye.
lineage: Continues the plainspoken, guitar-and-voice songwriting line that runs from '90s alt-country through 2010s Bandcamp singer-songwriters.

description: Glutton For Punishment is Kansas City band Big Fat Cow's fuzzed-out country-rock record, self-tagged 'fuzz folk' and 'post rock' alongside 'country' and 'folk'. A song called 'Goodbye Gram Parsons' makes the band's cosmic-country reference points explicit, while the rest of the record piles distorted guitar onto loose, rootsy song structures. It's for listeners who want their twang loud and ragged.
lineage: The song 'Goodbye Gram Parsons' names a direct reference point; the fuzz-over-country sound resembles 2010s-2020s loud indie-twang bands.

description: A five-song follow-up EP that opens with 'Yellow Belly Boy' and keeps Big Fat Cow's fuzzy, country-tagged guitar rock intact in a shorter format. The band again tags itself 'fuzz folk' and 'post rock' alongside straight 'country,' and the songs keep the loose, rowdy energy of their full-length in a tighter run of tracks.
lineage: A shorter continuation of the band's cosmic-country/fuzz-folk sound established on Glutton For Punishment.

description: Good Grief is Birmingham, Alabama band Bitter Calm's debut full-length, self-tagged 'chamber rock' and 'slowcore.' The eight songs move at a hushed, unhurried pace with sparse arrangements built around clean guitar and restrained vocals, matching the band's own description of itself as 'big big sad.' It is the quieter, earlier half of the band's Core-era catalog.
lineage: Sits in the Low/Duster-descended slowcore-and-sadcore line, rendered by a young indie band rather than a '90s one.

description: Eternity In The Lake of Fire is Bitter Calm's nine-song second record, again tagged 'chamber rock', 'indie rock', and 'slowcore' on the band's own page. The band's notes frame it around self-annihilation and hopelessness, and the arrangements add violin, bass, and percussion to the hushed guitar-and-voice core. 'Sinner' is the clearest way in.
lineage: Extends the slowcore, sadness-as-method tradition into a darker, more full-band-oriented record than the debut.

description: There Will Be Chicken Wings is a twelve-song Raleigh, North Carolina record self-tagged 'southern rock', 'alt country', 'countrycore', and 'countrygaze' on Bandcamp. It moves between rowdy, full-band roots rock and slower, heavier passages, with plainspoken lyrics about small-town Southern life. It's for fans of loud, wall-of-guitar country in the Wednesday mold.
lineage: Sounds indebted to the Wednesday-style template of loud, distorted guitars under country song structure.

description: Sunfall is an Austin songwriter's ten-track home-recorded record, self-tagged 'americana,' 'california country,' and 'psychedelic folk.' The songs are warm and unhurried, built on acoustic fingerpicking and drifting, sun-bleached melodies rather than twang or fiddle. It plays like a bedroom-scale entry in the Laurel Canyon-descended cosmic-country revival.
lineage: Channels the breezy, Gram Parsons/Laurel Canyon-descended cosmic-country sound through a solo, DIY bedroom recording.

description: A seven-song companion EP from the same year as Sunfall, tagged with the same 'americana', 'folk-psych', and 'psychedelic' terms. It keeps the same hazy, acoustic-led sound in a shorter run of songs such as 'Naturally' and 'Winds'. It's for listeners who liked Sunfall and want more of its sun-bleached drift.
lineage: A shorter, same-year sibling to Sunfall in Buckley Willis's cosmic-country/psych-folk catalog.

description: Famous Lunch is New Orleans songwriter Chris Acker's ten-song full-length, tagged 'alt country', 'americana', and 'country folk' by the artist. Backed by a band with pedal steel, Acker sings plainspoken, funny-then-heartbreaking narrative songs with a loose, live-sounding feel. 'Wouldn't Do For You (Buddy)' is one of the record's centerpieces.
lineage: Sounds indebted to the Prine/Townes line of plainspoken storytelling, filtered through a New Orleans dancehall-country band.

description: Odd, Ordinary, & Otherwise is Chris Acker's thirteen-song full-length, again tagged 'alt country', 'americana', and 'country folk'. The Bandcamp notes say it ranges from quiet, introspective tunes to barn burners, written partly during 2020 isolation. It shows the same plainspoken, detail-heavy songwriting that runs through his catalog.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Prine-style storytelling; an earlier stage of the songwriting heard on Famous Lunch.

description: Slow Country is a twelve-song record from Chicago's Conor Lynch, self-tagged 'folk rock', 'indie rock', and 'singer-songwriter' with a self-described 'mid-fi' aesthetic. Song titles like 'Steam Whistle' and 'Long Ways From Home' point to the record's rural, travel-worn imagery, set over loose, unpolished guitar arrangements. It's for listeners who like home-recorded folk-rock with rough edges left in.
lineage: A lo-fi, home-recorded take on folk-rock storytelling in the Bandcamp singer-songwriter tradition.

description: Cooper Kenward's self-titled twelve-song debut is tagged 'alternative', 'folk', and 'singer-songwriter' by the Los Angeles artist. The songs favor plain, conversational lyrics over polish, in the vein of the barroom and bedroom-folk wing of the Core scene. It's a DIY-scale starting point for listeners who later found 'Dying in a Diner'.
lineage: Early, DIY-scale entry in the same LA singer-songwriter lane later refined on Dying in a Diner.

description: Dying in a Diner is Cooper Kenward's ten-song Soggy Anvil Records release, still tagged 'alternative', 'folk', and 'singer-songwriter'. The artist's notes frame the record around memory, like paging through old photos, with songs that range from loose and unguarded to slow-built. 'Orbit' and 'Over Easy' are good ways in.
lineage: Continues the plainspoken LA singer-songwriter thread of his self-titled debut; sounds akin to MJ Lenderman-adjacent conversational songwriting.

description: Always The Moon is a nine-song Pensacola, Florida record self-tagged 'folk', 'country', and 'indie'. The songs are guitar-and-voice driven, with plainspoken, downcast titles ('Father Time', 'Treading Water', 'Sycophant To Sorrow') typical of the singer-songwriter side of the scene. It's for listeners who like small, sad country-folk songs.
lineage: A small-scale, self-released entry in the plainspoken new-country/singer-songwriter lane.

description: sending is a six-song EP from Harrisonburg, Virginia band Dogwood Tales. It includes an early version of 'mt jackson', a song about a family member's hospitalization that the band would later re-record for a full-length. The EP's tone is plainspoken and small-town-focused, consistent with the rest of the band's catalog.
lineage: An early sketch of songs the band would develop further on Every Star in Rockingham County.

description: Rodeo is a six-song vinyl EP played by a full band of acoustic and electric guitar, bass, pedal steel, and drums. It is a straightforward alt-country record built on real pedal steel and full-band arrangements rather than fuzz or distortion. It's for listeners who want the band's most traditionally country side.
lineage: Represents the more traditionally country-instrumented side of Dogwood Tales' catalog, released through the same regional vinyl label as 13 Summers 13 Falls.

description: 13 Summers 13 Falls is a five-song vinyl EP released the same year as Rodeo through WarHen Records. It keeps the band's plainspoken, small-town songwriting in a shorter, quieter set than its companion release, with songs like 'Hard To Be Anywhere' and 'Since Yesterday'.
lineage: A same-year, same-label companion to Rodeo in Dogwood Tales' developing alt-country catalog.

description: Every Star in Rockingham County is Dogwood Tales' twelve-song Born Losers Records full-length. The label copy describes pedal steel chords, delicate harmonies, and power-pop drumming set against lyrics about small-town Shenandoah Valley life, hospital bills, and pop-culture touchstones like Princess Peach and McDonald's. It re-records 'Mt. Jackson', first heard on the EP 'sending', as its emotional centerpiece.
lineage: Its label copy places it in a Townes Van Zandt-descended songwriting tradition; musically it sounds akin to current lo-fi indie country.

description: Fat, Evil Children's self-titled six-song EP is tagged 'americana,' 'indie folk,' and 'indie rock' by the Los Angeles band. It includes 'Weedpuller,' the playlist's entry point, alongside plainspoken, mid-tempo songs that lean folk and Americana rather than punk or fuzz despite the band's name.
lineage: A small-scale LA entry in the 2010s-2020s Bandcamp Americana/indie-folk lane.

description: Can't Stop is Fat, Evil Children's second six-song EP, tagged with the addition of 'emo' alongside the band's usual 'americana' and 'indie folk' tags. The songs keep the same plainspoken, mid-tempo approach as the debut EP, with slightly more emotionally direct, anthemic moments.
lineage: A continuation of the band's Americana/indie-folk sound with a newly added emo edge, connecting it to the scene's emo-twang crossover wing.

description: swan is the second full-length from New Zealand project Fazed on a Pony, tagged 'alt-country', 'emo', and 'indie rock'. The label copy says it expands from the project's earlier Pavement-esque indie rock into arrangements with pedal steel, fiddle, drum machines, and synths, and compares it to MJ Lenderman, David Berman, and Sparklehorse. 'Heart Goes Blank' is the clearest way in.
lineage: Its label copy compares it to MJ Lenderman, David Berman, and Sparklehorse; it sounds indebted to that line of wry, twangy indie songwriting.

description: it'll all work out is Fazed on a Pony's earlier eight-song full-length, tagged 'alt-country,' 'emo,' and 'indie rock' like its follow-up. It represents the more straightforwardly 'Pavement-esque' indie-rock sound that swan's own liner notes say the project later expanded outward from.
lineage: The earlier, leaner version of the alt-country/indie-rock songwriting Fazed on a Pony built out further on swan.

description: Chicago quartet's debut EP mixes big fuzzed-out guitar riffs with twangy pedal steel, mandolin, and bass harmonica. The four songs move from house-show stomp to honky-tonk shuffle, with abstract, personal lyrics giving the psychedelic country-rock an introspective edge. It plays like a scrappy, DIY-recorded take on '60s-'70s country-rock on a practice-space budget.
lineage: Self-described as a 'Country and Folk, Power Pop and Rock n' Roll' band drawing on 60s-70s country production, in line with the pedal-steel-and-fuzz indie-twang scene.

description: GracieHorse's early full-length is billed on Bandcamp under alt-country and 'bummer jams' tags, a Los Angeles songwriter working a direct, unguarded confessional style over rock-leaning arrangements. Tracks like 'Youth is a Fire' and 'Tightrope' pair plainspoken, heartbreak-adjacent lyrics with a loose, road-worn band sound. It is the record that established the storytelling, no-frills approach she carried into her later work.
lineage: Sounds indebted to plainspoken alt-country and rock songwriting; early work from an LA singer-songwriter Bandcamp files under alt-country.

description: Idle County bill themselves as 'WNC farm-rock' out of Asheville, and their debut LP is tagged country, alt-country, and rock n roll on Bandcamp. Song titles like 'Lebanon, TN' and 'Sin City' point to travelogue, small-town storytelling over a straightforward country-rock band sound. The plainspoken, guitar-forward feel recalls late-'90s alt-country.
lineage: Sounds indebted to '90s alt-country (Wilco/Uncle Tupelo-adjacent) as filtered through the 2020s Asheville scene.

description: Jacob Tremont's ten-song junebug is tagged countrygaze alongside folk, acoustic pop, and lo-fi indie-folk on Bandcamp, a bedroom-recorded singer-songwriter set built around fingerpicked guitar and plainspoken lyrics. Song titles ('garden', 'diner', 'steamboat') suggest small, quiet vignettes rather than big statements. It's an intimate, home-recorded record from the hushed end of DIY singer-songwriter music.
lineage: Self-tagged 'countrygaze'; sounds akin to the hushed, DIY bedroom-folk wing of the current indie-twang scene.

description: A six-song follow-up to junebug, carrying the same countrygaze/lo-fi indie-folk tags on Bandcamp. Tracks like 'no, i'm not afraid' and 'seven years of bad luck' continue the plainspoken, home-recorded singer-songwriter approach in shorter form. It reads as a between-albums EP rather than a full statement.
lineage: Sounds like a continuation of the countrygaze-tagged, DIY bedroom-folk sound of junebug.

description: Billed a 'New York songman,' Josh Bolin's four-song debut EP is tagged cosmic americana alongside folk and indie rock on Bandcamp. The songs favor warm, unhurried arrangements over acoustic-and-electric guitar interplay, in keeping with the cosmic-country lineage of buttery lead guitar and easy tempos. It's a compact introduction rather than a full statement.
lineage: Tagged 'cosmic americana' by the artist; sounds indebted to the Gram Parsons/Laurel Canyon-descended cosmic country revival.

description: This Canton, Ohio band's debut is tagged Americana, classic rock, and garage rock on Bandcamp, and its notes pitch a 'son-rock' aesthetic of heartland tunes and Rust Belt blues. 'On the Road Again, Again' sets a truck driver's meditations over a Willie Nelson-style loop. It's raspy, tape-hiss Midwestern rock about family friction and dead-end towns.
lineage: Self-described 'son-rock'; sounds indebted to heartland rock and Rust Belt Americana.

description: Kitchen, a solo bedroom-pop project from Rochester, New York, released this sprawling 20-track album, home-recorded and plainly designed. Songs like 'Real Estate Agent' pair conversational, self-lacerating lyrics with spare, lo-fi arrangements. It's DIY slacker songwriting rather than country per se, closer to the bedroom end of the Bandcamp indie-rock scene than to twang.
lineage: A solo lo-fi/DIY bedroom-indie project without an explicit country lineage; included here for its conversational, home-recorded slacker songwriting.

description: Local Superstar's self-titled album is tagged indie rock, alt-country, and folk rock on Bandcamp. Song titles like 'Passing By Waco', 'Dog Song', and 'Drinkin' to Write' point to loose, road- and drinking-song-flavored guitar rock. It's an eight-song set from a Savannah, Georgia project working the alt-country-leaning indie-rock lane.
lineage: Sounds akin to the current alt-country-leaning indie-rock scene of the Southeast.

description: Lowell Thompson's ten-song Stranger's Advice is tagged rock, alt-country, and 'vermont' on Bandcamp. Songs like 'Bradley Street' and 'Meadow Lane' point toward plainspoken, place-named storytelling over straightforward alt-country arrangements. It's for listeners who like unfussy, band-backed songwriter records.
lineage: Sounds akin to the 2010s wave of indie-scene alt-country singer-songwriters.

description: Wellington, New Zealand's Mudgoose tags this ten-song album lofi folk, outsider folk, loner folk, and experimental folk on Bandcamp. 'Mary's Lost' and the title track sit in hushed, homemade arrangements typical of the record. It's quiet, DIY loner-folk rather than country, closer to the lo-fi/outsider end of the current Bandcamp singer-songwriter underground.
lineage: Self-tagged loner/outsider lo-fi folk, part of the DIY Bandcamp network rather than a country lineage.

description: Los Angeles band New Rose's eleven-song Morning Haze is tagged 'country' on Bandcamp, with a tracklist ('Country Noise', 'Should've Been A Wedding', 'Pearl Buttons') that reads as a set of plainspoken country-rock songs about heartbreak and small betrayals. It's a straightforward, guitar-and-twang alt-country record from an LA band.
lineage: Self-tagged 'country,' part of the current alt-country-leaning West Coast indie scene.

description: Washington, DC's Heaven Forbid bill themselves 'High Faultin' Rootin' Tootin' Sons of Guns', and their eight-song debut album is a straightforward honky-tonk record mixing originals with country classics such as 'Make The World Go Away'. The band's own copy promises '8 new favorites and country classics in high fidelity'. It's for listeners who want classic honky-tonk played straight by a young band.
lineage: Sounds indebted to classic honky-tonk and '60s country standards.

description: Alabama songwriter Jameson Hubbard's debut album under the name Haysop is billed in its notes as a rock 'n' roll album through and through. It pairs Muscle Shoals-flavored guitar and Wurlitzer with Hubbard's deadpan-tinged, Kurt Vile-esque songwriting about a budding relationship. It's a 13-song set that swings from full-throttle rockers to loose front-porch picking.
lineage: Sounds indebted to Muscle Shoals-style Southern soul-rock and Kurt Vile's drawled songwriting.

description: A five-song debut EP from a Jackson, Mississippi band that pairs pedal steel with fuzzed-out, loosely played guitar rock. The band's own Bandcamp tags it alongside twangcore and countrygaze, and songs like 'Built to Rust' and 'Nebraska' lean into ragged, mid-tempo indie-twang. It plays like a rougher-edged cousin to the Wednesday/MJ Lenderman school of loud guitar country.
lineage: Sounds indebted to the countrygaze/indie-twang wave (Wednesday, MJ Lenderman) that puts pedal steel inside noisy indie-rock guitars.

description: A follow-up five-song EP from Rose Haven Motor Hotel, tagged on Bandcamp as country-alt, indie folk, and indie rock. It closes with 'Just Fine, Thanks', a quieter, more resigned song than the debut EP's rowdier moments, showing a band moving between loud indie-twang and hushed indie folk within the same short release.
lineage: Continues the band's countrygaze/indie-twang lane established on their debut EP.

description: A four-song EP from this Nashville band, whose Bandcamp bio promises "Rocking & Rolling & Twanging & Banging" and tags itself twang rock and alt-country. Ringing, jangly guitars sit over straightforward rock rhythm section, closer to loose bar-band indie-twang than polished Americana.
lineage: Part of the 2010s-2020s Nashville DIY scene folding twang and jangle into indie rock songwriting.

description: A four-song live recording taped in Allston, Massachusetts, tagged twang rock and alt-country on the band's Bandcamp. It captures Save Henry's ringing, jangly guitar approach in a bar-show setting rather than the studio.
lineage: Documents the same Nashville twang-rock project in a live setting.

description: A ten-song Philadelphia record self-tagged on Bandcamp as Americana, alt-country, art rock, and emo at once. 'Michigan' and the rest of the album move between twangy indie rock and more anxious, emo-inflected structures, putting it close to the emo-twang crossover strand of the current scene.
lineage: Sounds akin to the emo-and-DIY-punk-into-twang strand of bands like Truth Club and MJ Lenderman's peers.

description: A ten-song debut album from Toronto's Spirit Josh; the Bandcamp tags run alt-country, indie folk, and lo-fi. Songs like 'hank, paint & country star' wear their country-folk debt openly inside plain, home-recorded arrangements.
lineage: Sits in the lo-fi/indie-folk end of the 2010s Bandcamp twang scene, closer to home-taped folk than loud guitar rock.

description: A ten-song follow-up tagged alt-country, bedroom pop, indie folk, and lo-fi on Bandcamp. It keeps Spirit Josh's plainspoken, home-recorded style, moving between quiet folk arrangements and slightly fuller indie-pop structures across songs like 'Hotel Motel' and 'Terminal Love'.
lineage: Continues the same lo-fi indie-folk-into-alt-country project as the 2019 debut.

description: An eight-song album tagged alt-country and indie folk, closing with 'Staying Up & Drinkin' Wine'. Song titles like 'Straight Outta Dodge' and 'Trout! Fishing!' keep the wry, plainspoken tone of Spirit Josh's earlier records inside a slightly more full-band arrangement.
lineage: Third album in the same Toronto lo-fi/alt-country project.

description: A ten-song Chicago record the band tags on Bandcamp as Americana, alt-country, country punk, and cowpunk all at once. Songs like 'Funeral Home' and 'Gas' move at a fast, punky clip with twangy guitar leads, putting it squarely in the punk-kids-play-country tradition.
lineage: Sounds indebted to cowpunk (X, Jason & the Scorchers) filtered through 2010s-2020s DIY indie-rock recording.

description: A ten-song self-titled record, again tagged alt-country, country punk, and cowpunk by the band. 'Eggs' and 'Drunk at the Airport' keep the same fast, twangy cowpunk attack as the earlier record, with titles that lean into deadpan, everyday absurdity.
lineage: A later entry in St. Marlboro's cowpunk/alt-country catalog.

description: A nine-song debut album with pedal steel throughout, built around what the band calls a 'dynamic and improvisational' live style. 'Sandy' and the rest of Country River lean breezy and jam-friendly rather than raw or fast, closer to the cosmic-country/'70s-revival end of the current scene than to punk-adjacent twang.
lineage: Sounds indebted to the Dead/Gram Parsons-descended cosmic-country revival of buttery lead guitar and pedal steel over relaxed tempos.

description: The debut LP from this self-described 'alt-country quintet' out of Nashville, a nine-song set that includes 'Weatherman'. The band's own copy calls it the product of several years' work, and the Bandcamp tags (Americana, alt-country, folk punk) place it as a full-band, recognizably country-structured record rather than a noisier indie-twang one.
lineage: A straightforward continuation of 2010s-2020s alt-country bands playing recognizable country structures with indie-scene provenance.

description: The band's first EP, four songs tagged acoustic, americana, classic country and country rock on Bandcamp. It is a more stripped-down, acoustic-leaning start for a band that would fill out into a full alt-country quintet on their debut LP.
lineage: Founding release of The Downstreamers' Nashville alt-country project.

description: A ten-song record from the solo project Walker Rider, tagged countrygaze and lofi country on Bandcamp. 'Falling' and 'Keep True' sit among plainspoken, lo-fi arrangements; the project's own bio describes the songs as queer love songs leaning into limerence, set to alt-country and indie guitar.
lineage: Part of the lo-fi/countrygaze wing of the current indie-twang scene, closer to bedroom recording than full-band rock.

description: An earlier ten-song Walker Rider record, tagged alternative country and lofi country. Songs such as 'North Country' and the title track keep the same hushed, home-recorded alt-country approach as the later Fair, with a title track that leans directly into cowboy-song imagery.
lineage: Earlier entry in Walker Rider's lo-fi alt-country catalog.

description: A ten-song folk record released on twosyllable records, tagged simply 'folk' on Bandcamp. 'Berry on a Briar' and songs like 'Sheep Guts' and 'Letting Go' are quiet, fingerpicked, and plainspoken, closer to hushed indie folk than twangy rock.
lineage: Sits in the folk-songwriting line running from Townes/Gillian Welch through the 2010s Bandcamp scene.

description: A ten-song Charlottesville record the band's own bio describes as pulling from "regional forebears Sparklehorse and Dave Berman": "shoegaze with eye contact, country without the cowboy hat." The Bandcamp tags (alternative, indie, slacker, soft rock) fit a slack, mid-tempo indie-rock record with a country undertow rather than an overt twang band.
lineage: Follows the Sparklehorse/Silver Jews line of soft, slack indie rock with a country undertow, feeding into the current slacker/jangle revival.

description: A ten-song Brooklyn record on Born Losers Records; the band's own copy frames it as a folk-rock project in the Liz Phair/Jenny Lewis mold, equal parts polished pop songwriting and loose band-practice energy. 'Big Parking Lot' and the rest keep a wry, conversational tone over jangly, mid-fi guitar pop.
lineage: The band's own copy names Liz Phair and Jenny Lewis as models; the jangly guitar pop sounds indebted to the slacker/jangle revival.

description: A ten-song debut LP from this Asheville band, whose Bandcamp tags run alt-country, noise rock, shoegaze, and slowcore together. The songs move slowly and heavily, with country structure buried under guitar noise. It's for listeners who want countrygaze at its heaviest and most downcast.
lineage: Sounds indebted to the countrygaze template (Wednesday) of shoegaze-scale guitar walls under country song structure.

description: A second ten-song LP tagged the same way as the debut (alt-country, noise rock, shoegaze, slowcore). It meets shoegaze with country, with steel guitar meshing into the band's dense, slow-building arrangements. The title track shows the band's heavy, slow-burning approach.
lineage: Sounds indebted to countrygaze and slowcore; continues the approach of their debut LP.

description: An eight-song debut LP on PNKSLM Recordings, tagged alternative and alt-country on Bandcamp. The songwriting is dryly funny and plainspoken, closer to talk-sung indie-country than polished Americana, as on 'creative director blues' and 'modern love'.
lineage: Sounds akin to deadpan, talk-sung indie-country songwriting in the Berman/Lenderman vein.

description: A nine-song second LP on PNKSLM, framed in the band's own copy around dryly funny songwriting with real sadness underneath. 'birkenstocks' and other pop-culture-referencing titles keep the same dry, talk-sung alt-country tone as the debut.
lineage: Continues the deadpan indie-country sound of 'things are gonna be alright'.

description: An eleven-song debut album the band describes on its own Bandcamp page as modern DIY indie alt-country, with an earnest, twangy vocal delivery and a hint of distortion behind nimble guitar lines. 'Frontyard' and the rest of the record match that description closely, and Bandcamp tags it country alongside indie, rock, and acoustic.
lineage: Sounds like indie-raised musicians playing directly toward alt-country structure and twang.

description: A fourteen-song second album, tagged rock, acoustic, indie and pop on Bandcamp. It keeps the same twang-inflected, DIY indie-rock approach as the debut, with a title track that appears in both a "loud" and a "quiet" version bookending the record.
lineage: Second full-length from hey i'm outside's alt-country project.
